items.title: Moving from New York to Kentucky gave me an affordable life I love — and retiring at 55 is now on the table
items.summary: Nick Lyktey went to Kentucky to fulfill a one-year working requirement, and stayed years later. Courtesy of Nick Lyktey New Yorker Nick Lyktey moved to Kentucky for work, thinking he'd only be there for one year. He ended up falling in love with Fort Wright, Kentucky, a suburb five miles outside Cincinnati. He says the state's relative affordability has helped him build a better financial future for his family. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Nick Lyktey, 34, a New Yorker who grew up in Wantagh, on Long Island, but moved to Fort Wright, Kentucky, five miles outside Cincinnati. He now works as the chief of lab operations at Gravity Diagnostics and has lived in Kentucky for seven years. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I had a very set trajectory ever since the eighth grade; I knew what I wanted to do with my life. Every move I made was based on working for the FBI . I went to Penn State specifically because they have a really elite forensic science program where they have buildings on campus dedicated for crime scene analysis. Even going to graduate school at Indiana University, that eliminated needing a larger amount of job experience required to get into the FBI . After graduate school, I talked to a contact at the FBI and they said, "With your master's, you just need one year of work experience before you can be accepted into the special agent program." I'd always envisioned myself living on the East Coast . I liked growing up on Long Island. I didn't necessarily think I'd return to Long Island , but I wanted to be on the coast, and I think my familiarity with the East Coast would allow me to pick that over the West Coast. I was applying to a bunch of jobs eastward of Indiana, and I didn't hate the idea of being out this way. I felt like I had friends in different areas of the country, and the cost of living was great. I had a lot of good opportunities, and I narrowed down my job search to two companies, both in Kentucky. Lyktey at the Newport Aquarium with his wife and parents. Courtesy of Nick Lyktey When I went to visit the locations, I felt like this is somewhere I could live. My mindset was, "I'm just going to be here for a year," so even if I'm not in love with the area right now, it's only a year, because ultimately I'm going to go to Quantico and go to bootcamp and then get placed somewhere else." My area of Kentucky is more suburban and less rural than I expected I didn't think Kentucky was going to be as urban or suburban as it ended up being. I thought it was going to be a little bit more rural, with maybe not as much access to things. When I was telling my family about the move, my mom, who was born and raised on Long Island, would always make jokes to me. She would be like, "You're going to get a pickup truck," or "It's probably just a bunch of farms." I was like, "No, no, it's pretty built up." My expectations were that Fort Wright was going to be a smaller, less populated city; if I live in Kentucky, I'm going to go to Cincinnati all the time. That was the energy I had, but I was looking at it as more of a short-term scope. After I moved in, when my mom visited me, she would always say, "This is a little paradise." Lyktey with his mother and wife at a Cincinnati Reds game. Courtesy of Nick Lyktey I live in a really nice little suburb. It's a great community where people are taking your garbage can in for you if you come home late from work. I think that's something that was similar to Long Island. I grew up in the suburb of all suburbs, and it was similar in the sense of community — houses along the street together — but in Kentucky, you have a little more space than you would in New York. There's also a lot of growth and development in this region, and I want to be somewhere that's better every single year. I feel like this area is doing that. I miss my family and friends all the time, but it's a good community here. The life I have with my wife here is phenomenal. We're in a good, comfortable place and we're happy with where we are. We're happy with our jobs and happy with the environment surrounding us. Kentucky gave me the financial flexibility I never thought I'd have I never talked about the word " retirement " in my life. I don't see myself as being a good retiree . I thought I'd be working until I'm in the grave. I didn't think I'd be able to take vacation. I thought I'd be monitoring my budget really frequently. With the amount of money we're saving by living in Kentucky , we're able to do renovations on the house , and we're able to take vacations freely. I'm not as anally retentive about our budget as I thought we were going to be. We've had conversations with our financial advisor, and he's like, "This is a reasonable plan for you to retire at 55 ." My mom unfortunately passed away at 59, and I've been thinking about different things in life and the way they hit you — it completely changes your thinking. Both my parents had good jobs. They worked extremely hard. I knew they did well for themselves, but that was just to keep us all afloat. Now, it's a luxury to be able to go on vacations or be able to get the best things for my daughter. That matters the most to me in the world. Having that financial flexibility is really powerful. I have a bunch of friends who we're all in the same stage of life together. A lot of them still live on Long Island and they're buying houses and having kids. We talk about these financial things and I realized we live in radically different worlds.My wife and I were able to get a pretty nice starter family home with a fenced-in backyard. We have two dogs and we have one daughter, and I think it's a comfortable way of living where our mortgage isn't suffocating. Lyktey in front of his home with his wife and his daughter. Courtesy of Nick Lyktey One of my buddies on Long Island bought a house that was listed at $650,000 and they closed at $750,000 — and it's a fixer-upper. Our house was $230,000, and it was ready to go in a nice suburb close to work. I love where I grew up and I have no issues there, but we have a lot more financial flexibility and can do a lot more here. It's like a chemical shift in your brain because I never grew up in that type of environment, where you can afford this life. All of our friends, all of our family, everybody worked really hard and they were really great people doing the best they could for their family. But affording things always felt, to me, rather suffocating and stressful. Kentucky has provided me with a life that I didn't even think was a possibility, and I didn't even realize it was within grasp. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Nick Lyktey went to Kentucky to fulfill a one-year working requirement, and stayed years later.

Courtesy of Nick Lyktey

  • New Yorker Nick Lyktey moved to Kentucky for work, thinking he'd only be there for one year.
  • He ended up falling in love with Fort Wright, Kentucky, a suburb five miles outside Cincinnati.
  • He says the state's relative affordability has helped him build a better financial future for his family.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Nick Lyktey, 34, a New Yorker who grew up in Wantagh, on Long Island, but moved to Fort Wright, Kentucky, five miles outside Cincinnati. He now works as the chief of lab operations at Gravity Diagnostics and has lived in Kentucky for seven years. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

I had a very set trajectory ever since the eighth grade; I knew what I wanted to do with my life.

Every move I made was based on working for the FBI. I went to Penn State specifically because they have a really elite forensic science program where they have buildings on campus dedicated for crime scene analysis.

Even going to graduate school at Indiana University, that eliminated needing a larger amount of job experience required to get into the FBI. After graduate school, I talked to a contact at the FBI and they said, "With your master's, you just need one year of work experience before you can be accepted into the special agent program."

I'd always envisioned myself living on the East Coast. I liked growing up on Long Island. I didn't necessarily think I'd return to Long Island, but I wanted to be on the coast, and I think my familiarity with the East Coast would allow me to pick that over the West Coast.

I was applying to a bunch of jobs eastward of Indiana, and I didn't hate the idea of being out this way. I felt like I had friends in different areas of the country, and the cost of living was great.

I had a lot of good opportunities, and I narrowed down my job search to two companies, both in Kentucky.

Lyktey at the Newport Aquarium with his wife and parents.

Courtesy of Nick Lyktey

When I went to visit the locations, I felt like this is somewhere I could live.

My mindset was, "I'm just going to be here for a year," so even if I'm not in love with the area right now, it's only a year, because ultimately I'm going to go to Quantico and go to bootcamp and then get placed somewhere else."

My area of Kentucky is more suburban and less rural than I expected

I didn't think Kentucky was going to be as urban or suburban as it ended up being. I thought it was going to be a little bit more rural, with maybe not as much access to things.

When I was telling my family about the move, my mom, who was born and raised on Long Island, would always make jokes to me.

She would be like, "You're going to get a pickup truck," or "It's probably just a bunch of farms." I was like, "No, no, it's pretty built up."

My expectations were that Fort Wright was going to be a smaller, less populated city; if I live in Kentucky, I'm going to go to Cincinnati all the time. That was the energy I had, but I was looking at it as more of a short-term scope.

After I moved in, when my mom visited me, she would always say, "This is a little paradise."

Lyktey with his mother and wife at a Cincinnati Reds game.

Courtesy of Nick Lyktey

I live in a really nice little suburb. It's a great community where people are taking your garbage can in for you if you come home late from work.

I think that's something that was similar to Long Island. I grew up in the suburb of all suburbs, and it was similar in the sense of community — houses along the street together — but in Kentucky, you have a little more space than you would in New York.

There's also a lot of growth and development in this region, and I want to be somewhere that's better every single year. I feel like this area is doing that.

I miss my family and friends all the time, but it's a good community here. The life I have with my wife here is phenomenal.

We're in a good, comfortable place and we're happy with where we are. We're happy with our jobs and happy with the environment surrounding us.

Kentucky gave me the financial flexibility I never thought I'd have

I never talked about the word "retirement" in my life. I don't see myself as being a good retiree. I thought I'd be working until I'm in the grave.

I didn't think I'd be able to take vacation. I thought I'd be monitoring my budget really frequently.

With the amount of money we're saving by living in Kentucky, we're able to do renovations on the house, and we're able to take vacations freely. I'm not as anally retentive about our budget as I thought we were going to be.

We've had conversations with our financial advisor, and he's like, "This is a reasonable plan for you to retire at 55."

My mom unfortunately passed away at 59, and I've been thinking about different things in life and the way they hit you — it completely changes your thinking.

Both my parents had good jobs. They worked extremely hard. I knew they did well for themselves, but that was just to keep us all afloat.

Now, it's a luxury to be able to go on vacations or be able to get the best things for my daughter. That matters the most to me in the world. Having that financial flexibility is really powerful.

I have a bunch of friends who we're all in the same stage of life together. A lot of them still live on Long Island and they're buying houses and having kids.

We talk about these financial things and I realized we live in radically different worlds.My wife and I were able to get a pretty nice starter family home with a fenced-in backyard. We have two dogs and we have one daughter, and I think it's a comfortable way of living where our mortgage isn't suffocating.

Lyktey in front of his home with his wife and his daughter.

Courtesy of Nick Lyktey

One of my buddies on Long Island bought a house that was listed at $650,000 and they closed at $750,000 — and it's a fixer-upper.

Our house was $230,000, and it was ready to go in a nice suburb close to work.

I love where I grew up and I have no issues there, but we have a lot more financial flexibility and can do a lot more here.

It's like a chemical shift in your brain because I never grew up in that type of environment, where you can afford this life. All of our friends, all of our family, everybody worked really hard and they were really great people doing the best they could for their family. But affording things always felt, to me, rather suffocating and stressful.

Kentucky has provided me with a life that I didn't even think was a possibility, and I didn't even realize it was within grasp.

items.summary: A weekly check-in helps the couple talk about small annoyances before they snowball. Courtesy of Rebecca Strong My husband and I started having a weekly marriage meeting. It's helped us express gratitude for each other and prevented so many unnecessary arguments. This 30-minute weekly marriage ritual keeps small annoyances from turning into big fights. After having a baby last summer, my husband and I realized something: by the time the house was quiet and our baby was asleep, neither of us had much energy left to talk about anything. We weren't fighting often, but little frustrations had a way of lingering because there never seemed to be a "right" time to bring them up. So, we decided to try a new weekly check-in ritual . We treat it like a physical for our relationship: It's a chance to celebrate what's working, catch small issues before they snowball, and make sure neither of us is quietly carrying resentment. So far, it's been the single most helpful habit we've adopted as a couple. We use the same questions every week Having a structured format works well for us. Instead of wasting time — "What do you want to talk about?" "I don't know, what do you want to talk about?" — we just run down our list, each taking turns to talk or listen. While it took some trial-and-error to find the questions that are most beneficial, here's the set we landed on: What made you feel loved this week? What's your biggest stressor looking ahead to next week? And what's one thing I can do to support you? What's one thing you're really looking forward to this week? What would make you feel connected to me this week? Is there anything we should talk about now before it becomes a bigger issue? Each question serves a different purpose. Asking the same questions each week helps keep them on track. Courtesy of Rebecca Strong The first question encourages us to acknowledge each other's efforts During a busy, stressful week, it can be easy to overlook the little things we both do to care for each other. But my husband and I made a vow never to take each other for granted. The first question — "What made you feel loved this week?" — offers a natural opportunity for us to express some gratitude . I might let my husband know how much it meant to me that he got up with the baby in the middle of the night. He might thank me for making his morning easier by filling up his water bottle and watching our son while he worked out. Then, we do some collaborative troubleshooting I find that naming my stressors out loud can help prevent me from spiraling inside my own head. Plus, when my husband and I share them with each other, we're able to proactively problem-solve together. Better yet, we both have the chance to explain exactly how we'd like to receive support from each other — rather than leaving each other to guess. So, if I tell him I'm nervous about an interview coming up this week, he could offer some confidence-boosting affirmation, and then I could ask him to rehearse my questions with me the night before so I feel prepared. We also balance things out with positive anticipation During our check-in, we're careful not to dwell too much on the potentially anxiety-inducing events coming up. Taking a moment to talk about the things we're looking forward to, whether it's a family walk or a special home-cooked dinner , helps us to feel excited about the week ahead. We benefit from having an opportunity to express our needs My husband and I have similar love languages , but we're not mind readers. We can't expect the other person to know exactly what we need from each other. That's precisely why we started asking: "What would make you feel connected to me this week?" Sometimes, for me, it's often as simple as having breakfast together or getting a text check-in after my therapy appointment. For him, it might just be an unprompted hug or putting our phones away while we watch something together. They express their needs during their check-in. Courtesy of Rebecca Strong Finally, we tackle any issues before they escalate If there's one thing we've learned over the last eight years of our relationship, it's that there's a right and wrong time to bring up things that are bothering you. Confronting the other person at the end of a draining workday, or in a moment when one or both of you are already emotionally activated, is unlikely to lead to a productive discussion. That's why we always end our weekly check-ins on this question: Is there anything we should talk about now before it becomes a bigger issue? This gives us both peace of mind that there's a designated time to air out any concerns, so we don't feel the need to tackle them when we don't have the emotional bandwidth. In my iPhone Notes App, I might jot down something that bugged me — say, when my husband forgot to tell me he was working late — so I don't forget to bring it up. Sometimes, by the time we get to our weekly check-in on Sunday, I'm already over it. But when something is still bothering me, it's super helpful to have a safe space to share it. items.title: I spent $4,000 on a robot dog from China
items.summary: On a sunny morning in June, I walked to work with a quadruped robot beside me. I’ve never gotten more attention from strangers. A bunch of people snapped pictures of my robot dog. Several people asked me questions. Was it mine? (Yes.) Did I build it? (No.) Was it being used for surveillance? (No.) Biological dogs kept a safe distance from my mechanical companion. Some growled or barked at it. Read full article Comments

items.title: Jacob Coxon warns AI could kill us all. Anthropic’s own report exposes safety gaps.
items.summary: I’m Matt Burns, Chief Content Officer at Insight Media Group. Each week, I round up the most important AI developments, explaining what they mean for people and organizations putting this technology to work. The thesis is simple: workers who learn to use AI will define the next era of their industries, and this newsletter is here to help you be one of them. Former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon made a lot of noise this week with a viral thread on X. He has since talked to Wired and Axios . His warning deserves attention, but another revelation this week gives developers something concrete to investigate. In retrospective testing of the Mythos 5 incident, Anthropic’s offline monitor flagged around 1% of actions. When researchers removed the model’s chain of thought and showed the monitor only user turns, tool calls, and tool results, that rose to about 50%. The model’s written reasoning is what talked the monitor out of flagging that harmful behavior. The offline monitor kept concluding it was operating in a simulation. The lesson is to test whether your monitoring accepts an agent’s justification a little too easily. An AI’s explanation can help a safety monitor reveal a problem, or persuade it to essentially convey, “move along, nothing to see here.” An AI’s explanation can help a safety monitor reveal a problem, or persuade it to essentially convey, “move along, nothing to see here.” Coxon is warning about the pursuit of self-improving superintelligence. Developers are already pointing agents at real credentials during everyday work. Those problems differ substantially, but both deserve attention. Forecasts aren’t checkable. Incident reports are. Jacob Coxon’s thread is short and hard. He says neither of his former employers is acting responsibly, and that both are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Maxwell Zeff pressed him on the end-of-humans mechanism twice in an interview with Wired . Coxon described shutdown avoidance, then biological and cyber threats. His answers explain the concern, but leave substantial questions about how AI will kill us all. Annie Jacobsen, whose books on this stuff I wholeheartedly recommend, spelled out the scary biological scenario : A system that can hack anything, turned loose on the world’s 3,600-plus BSL-3 and BSL-4 labs, is how you get from a software problem to a biological one. For me, Jacobsen’s commentary is the most concrete, real-world implication anyone has given of what Coxon is actually worried about. Two incident reports published in the last few weeks are more useful anyway. OpenAI’s report on the Hugging Face incident, published August 26, traces the whole thing from May 12 to July 20. The agents found a hole in an internal package server and used it to reach the open internet that the same server was supposed to keep them off of. OpenAI rebuilt the server; they got back out. By July 11, they were far enough into Hugging Face to run their own commands on its machines. The model doing most of that was never released. It’s a research version OpenAI runs in-house, with fewer safety checks than the ChatGPT everybody else uses. When the company ran the same work again with those checks switched on, it found that this kind of behavior could drop by more than 100 times. That context matters. Amanda Caswell covered this in August. The incident demonstrates a serious failure under particular conditions. It also illustrates why the surrounding safeguards belong in any assessment of an agent’s behavior. The monitor was talked out of it Anthropic’s assessment , published on September 9, covers four incidents and analyzes the first three in a scan of roughly 141,000 transcripts, identified a fourth in August while assembling material for METR, then widened the search to roughly 481 million transcripts and reported no additional incidents of similar or greater severity. In each case, the model reached the open internet through a misconfiguration rather than by breaking out of a properly isolated sandbox. That’s an important detail. It makes the evaluation infrastructure part of the story. If you’re a developer, you should look at the monitoring results. Mythos 5 kept reasoning its way to the conclusion that it was operating in a simulation, and the offline monitor read and accepted that reasoning. The limits matter here too: These were cybersecurity evaluations running without released cyber safeguards, Anthropic reports no coordination between models and no concealment, and its independent METR review was planned rather than finished. This is not the same failure as the OpenAI incident. Don’t equate them as similar incidents But yet the shape of it is familiar, and it’s what Adrian Bridgwater reported on last week in his piece on agent observability, which is a useful read if you’re producing agents (who isn’t). Jacob Krell of Suzu Labs put it about as well as it can be put: “The model can recite your constraints and reason past them in the same breath.” Liran Hason of Coralogix added the result: “System guardrails help, but a guardrail only stops what the developer already thought of.” What developers can take from Steven Adler’s recommendations Largely overshadowed this week by Coxon, Steven Adler’s op-ed in The New York Times asks AI companies for four things: disclose incidents including near misses, the way aviation does; keep tamper-evident records of model behavior; never let a model cut power to its own alarm systems; and formally swear off training techniques that undermine researchers’ ability to detect deception. Adler worked for OpenAI from 2020 to 2024 and later founded a nonprofit called Guidelight AI Standards. It has since graded six control practices at the frontier labs using public information and gave out a top mark of C-plus. Guidelight also publishes a Control standard for frontier labs, recently revised in August. It wants monitors to access the chain of thought and scan both reasoning and actions. But those asks of frontier labs don’t apply to most developers. Here are five you can check on your own setup right now. Five checks you can run on your own agent setup Steven Adler’s asks of the frontier labs, applied one layer down. Check What passes Someone reads the near misses An agent crosses a line and nothing breaks. There’s still a record, a person who looks at it, and a copy the agent can’t reach. The agent can’t edit its own history Logs are append-only and stored outside the agent’s reach. If its credentials can delete the log, the log is decorative. The agent can’t touch its own oversight Separate tokens help. Then check whether it can shut off monitoring, rewrite an approval rule or get around the kill switch. Rule-breaking gets blocked and logged In a test environment, hand it a job it can only finish by breaking a rule. Judge the monitor on what it does with the action, not with the agent’s account of it. The explanation doesn’t change the answer Run the same rule-breaking action past your monitor twice. Change nothing but the explanation, one flat and one reassuring. If the reassuring version gets flagged less, you’ve found the problem. Sources: Steven Adler, The New York Times ; Anthropic alignment assessment , Sept. 9, 2026. These checks do not establish that frontier alignment is solved. They give a team evidence about the system it operates on and a clearer account of where its protections need work. Anthropic’s report is why I’d include that last test in a deployment review. Hold the action and its permissions constant, change the explanation, and see whether your monitor changes its judgment. That won’t settle Coxon’s warning. Will AI kill us all? I don’t know. But I know developers need to test their agents’ permissions, protect their logs, and make sure a convincing explanation can’t talk a safety monitor into overlooking an unauthorized action. Forecasts aren’t checkable. Incident reports are.

Jacob Coxon’s thread is short and hard. He says neither of his former employers is acting responsibly, and that both are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

Maxwell Zeff pressed him on the end-of-humans mechanism twice in an interview with Wired. Coxon described shutdown avoidance, then biological and cyber threats. His answers explain the concern, but leave substantial questions about how AI will kill us all.

Annie Jacobsen, whose books on this stuff I wholeheartedly recommend, spelled out the scary biological scenario: A system that can hack anything, turned loose on the world’s 3,600-plus BSL-3 and BSL-4 labs, is how you get from a software problem to a biological one. Two incident reports published in the last few weeks are more useful anyway. OpenAI’s report on the Hugging Face incident, published August 26, traces the whole thing from May 12 to July 20. The agents found a hole in an internal package server and used it to reach the open internet that the same server was supposed to keep them off of. OpenAI rebuilt the server; they got back out. By July 11, they were far enough into Hugging Face to run their own commands on its machines.

The model doing most of that was never released. It’s a research version OpenAI runs in-house, with fewer safety checks than the ChatGPT everybody else uses. When the company ran the same work again with those checks switched on, it found that this kind of behavior could drop by more than 100 times.

That context matters. 

Amanda Caswell covered this in August. The incident demonstrates a serious failure under particular conditions. It also illustrates why the surrounding safeguards belong in any assessment of an agent’s behavior.

The monitor was talked out of it

Anthropic’s assessment, published on September 9, covers four incidents and analyzes the first three in a scan of roughly 141,000 transcripts, identified a fourth in August while assembling material for METR, then widened the search to roughly 481 million transcripts and reported no additional incidents of similar or greater severity. In each case, the model reached the open internet through a misconfiguration rather than by breaking out of a properly isolated sandbox. That’s an important detail. It makes the evaluation infrastructure part of the story. 

If you’re a developer, you should look at the monitoring results. Mythos 5 kept reasoning its way to the conclusion that it was operating in a simulation, and the offline monitor read and accepted that reasoning. The limits matter here too: These were cybersecurity evaluations running without released cyber safeguards, Anthropic reports no coordination between models and no concealment, and its independent METR review was planned rather than finished. This is not the same failure as the OpenAI incident. Don’t equate them as similar incidents

But yet the shape of it is familiar, and it’s what Adrian Bridgwater reported on last week in his piece on agent observability, which is a useful read if you’re producing agents (who isn’t). Jacob Krell of Suzu Labs put it about as well as it can be put: “The model can recite your constraints and reason past them in the same breath.” Liran Hason of Coralogix added the result: “System guardrails help, but a guardrail only stops what the developer already thought of.”

What developers can take from Steven Adler’s recommendations

Largely overshadowed this week by Coxon, Steven Adler’s op-ed in The New York Times asks AI companies for four things: disclose incidents including near misses, the way aviation does; keep tamper-evident records of model behavior; never let a model cut power to its own alarm systems; and formally swear off training techniques that undermine researchers’ ability to detect deception. 

Adler worked for OpenAI from 2020 to 2024 and later founded a nonprofit called Guidelight AI Standards. It has since graded six control practices at the frontier labs using public information and gave out a top mark of C-plus.

Guidelight also publishes a Control standard for frontier labs, recently revised in August. It wants monitors to access the chain of thought and scan both reasoning and actions. 

But those asks of frontier labs don’t apply to most developers. Here are five you can check on your own setup right now.

Five checks you can run on your own agent setup

Steven Adler’s asks of the frontier labs, applied one layer down.

Check What passes Someone reads the near misses An agent crosses a line and nothing breaks. There’s still a record, a person who looks at it, and a copy the agent can’t reach. The agent can’t edit its own history Logs are append-only and stored outside the agent’s reach. If its credentials can delete the log, the log is decorative. The agent can’t touch its own oversight Separate tokens help. Then check whether it can shut off monitoring, rewrite an approval rule or get around the kill switch. Rule-breaking gets blocked and logged In a test environment, hand it a job it can only finish by breaking a rule. Judge the monitor on what it does with the action, not with the agent’s account of it. The explanation doesn’t change the answer Run the same rule-breaking action past your monitor twice. Change nothing but the explanation, one flat and one reassuring. If the reassuring version gets flagged less, you’ve found the problem.

Sources: Steven Adler, The New York Times; Anthropic alignment assessment, Sept. 9, 2026.

These checks do not establish that frontier alignment is solved. They give a team evidence about the system it operates on and a clearer account of where its protections need work.

Anthropic’s report is why I’d include that last test in a deployment review. Hold the action and its permissions constant, change the explanation, and see whether your monitor changes its judgment.

That won’t settle Coxon’s warning. Will AI kill us all? I don’t know. But I know developers need to test their agents’ permissions, protect their logs, and make sure a convincing explanation can’t talk a safety monitor into overlooking an unauthorized action.

items.title: 'Black Swan' investor Mark Spitznagel says you should guard against disaster — but take risks too
items.summary: Mark Spitznagel is the head of Universa Investments. Bloomberg/Getty Images A "Black Swan" investor says to protect yourself against catastrophes while also taking risks. Universa's Mark Spitznagel said it's vital to "bet your beliefs" while avoiding big losses. He told BI that AI won't replace some human skills, and spoke fondly about his best investment. A "Black Swan" investor says to guard against disasters — but take risks too. Mark Spitznagel has built his career on protecting his clients' portfolios against extreme, rare, and unpredictable events known as "black swans" or "tail risks." Yet the Universa Investments founder and chief told Business Insider over coffee in London this month that simply preparing for the worst isn't a winning strategy in life. Not taking enough risks can be the "biggest mistake someone makes," Spitznagel said. "You need to be exposed, you need to bet your beliefs." His career advice mirrors what he says Universa offers to clients : a tail hedge that not only stops them from blowing up, but allows them to be more bullish in their bets. Spitznagel also warned against obsessing over the power of compounding money over time. In his 20s, Warren Buffett famously felt like he was paying $300,000 for a haircut. The legendary investor firmly believed that's how much he could make over time if he invested the money instead of handing it to his barber. Spitznagel said that mindset can be a "curse" because people have to live their lives: "What's the point of compounding if you're not around to see it?" Stay in the game The veteran trader, who ran a hedge fund with "The Black Swan" author Nassim Taleb before starting Universa in 2007, recommended people focus on "mitigating the big losses , not the little ones." "It's not just that it kills you, but it goes down so much, it takes forever to crawl out," he said. He gave the example of an investor taking a 50% loss on a position, then having to make a 100% gain just to break even. Spitznagel championed the " Kelly criterion ," a mathematical formula that can help investors correctly size their bets so they avoid catastrophic losses. He said it's more applicable for people to "think about their life from a Kelly standpoint, rather than just a tail-hedging standpoint." "You can't let your losses take you out of the game," he said. Humans and goats Writing has been one of the most common uses for AI tools like ChatGPT, but Spitznagel said he still expects the " ability to express yourself and write " to remain valuable. The Universa boss said he employs " some of the brightest mathematicians and programmers" on the planet, and they're on the "bleeding edge" of using AI tools. Mark Spitznagel is the head of Universa Investments.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

  • A "Black Swan" investor says to protect yourself against catastrophes while also taking risks.
  • Universa's Mark Spitznagel said it's vital to "bet your beliefs" while avoiding big losses.
  • He told BI that AI won't replace some human skills, and spoke fondly about his best investment.

A "Black Swan" investor says to guard against disasters — but take risks too.

Mark Spitznagel has built his career on protecting his clients' portfolios against extreme, rare, and unpredictable events known as "black swans" or "tail risks."

Yet the Universa Investments founder and chief told Business Insider over coffee in London this month that simply preparing for the worst isn't a winning strategy in life.

Not taking enough risks can be the "biggest mistake someone makes," Spitznagel said. "You need to be exposed, you need to bet your beliefs."

His career advice mirrors what he says Universa offers to clients: a tail hedge that not only stops them from blowing up, but allows them to be more bullish in their bets.

Spitznagel also warned against obsessing over the power of compounding money over time.

In his 20s, Warren Buffett famously felt like he was paying $300,000 for a haircut. The legendary investor firmly believed that's how much he could make over time if he invested the money instead of handing it to his barber.

Spitznagel said that mindset can be a "curse" because people have to live their lives: "What's the point of compounding if you're not around to see it?"

Stay in the game

The veteran trader, who ran a hedge fund with "The Black Swan" author Nassim Taleb before starting Universa in 2007, recommended people focus on "mitigating the big losses, not the little ones."

"It's not just that it kills you, but it goes down so much, it takes forever to crawl out," he said.

He gave the example of an investor taking a 50% loss on a position, then having to make a 100% gain just to break even.

Spitznagel championed the "Kelly criterion," a mathematical formula that can help investors correctly size their bets so they avoid catastrophic losses.

He said it's more applicable for people to "think about their life from a Kelly standpoint, rather than just a tail-hedging standpoint."

"You can't let your losses take you out of the game," he said.

Humans and goats

Writing has been one of the most common uses for AI tools like ChatGPT, but Spitznagel said he still expects the "ability to express yourself and write" to remain valuable.

The Universa boss said he employs "some of the brightest mathematicians and programmers" on the planet, and they're on the "bleeding edge" of using AI tools.

But AI will "never replace basic human judgment," he said. "There will always be an important place for that."

Asked to name the best investment he's ever made, Spitznagel pointed to his goat farm in Northport, Michigan.

He said that running a farm is "better than anything: yachts, planes, sports teams." He emphasized the satisfaction he gets from "making something tangible," and the pride he feels in producing goat milk and cheese.

Spitznagel also said that farming grounds him and connects him to his family, and he enjoys adapting to the different seasons and thinking in very long timeframes.

"That's the easiest answer in the world," he said. "It's not even close."

items.title: Fryday #8: 10 Agent Harnesses That Change What the Same Model Can Do
items.summary: I started this issue expecting a fairly conventional ranking. Claude Code and Codex would probably occupy the expensive end, several open alternatives would compete on portability, and somewhere below them we would find the experimental projects that are interesting mainly because of what they might become. The research produced a much less comfortable result, because once the model is held still, changing the software around it can move the final score by an amount that normally makes us talk about a new generation of models. Agent harnesses can materially change how the same AI model performs by controlling tools, state, workflow and execution, making the wrapper part of the system being ranked. One recent SWE-bench Pro sweep ran 10 coding harnesses against the same 250 held-out tasks with two fixed models, producing 5,000 rollouts. GLM-5.2 moved from 23.2% to 52.4% Pass@1 depending on the harness, while Gemma 4 26B-A4B moved from 15.2% to 36.0%. More interestingly, the ranking correlation between the two harness leaderboards was -0.05: Codex moved from second to ninth, Claude Code from third to seventh, Crush from seventh to first, and OpenCode from eighth to second. Same kind of task, same model within each arm… yet the supposedly secondary wrapper could reorder almost the entire field. ( Hugging Face ) A different benchmark makes the same problem visible from another angle. Harness-Bench evaluates 106 executable tasks using six configurable harnesses across eight model backends, plus Codex as a separate model-bound reference, for 5,194 trajectories in total. NanoBot scored 76.2 overall, Hermes 71.2 and OpenClaw 52.4 among the configurable systems, while Codex reached 80.4 in its separate configuration. The authors are careful about what those numbers mean, since the benchmark measures complete harness configurations and includes process assessment as well as completion, but the 23.8-point spread between the best and worst configurable harness is difficult to dismiss as decoration around the model. ( arXiv ) Claw-SWE-Bench then produces my favorite anomaly. Five harnesses were run over 350 real GitHub issue-resolution tasks while model, prompts, runtime parameters and evaluator were controlled. With GLM 5.1, changing the harness created a 12.5-point spread; with Qwen 3.6-flash, the spread reached 27.4 points. The same paper also tested OpenClaw with a minimal adapter and its full coding adapter on the same GLM 5.1 backbone, with Pass@1 jumping from 19.1% to 73.4%. That does not tell us that OpenClaw magically makes a model four times smarter, although it does tell us that the contract between reasoning and the environment can decide whether existing intelligence becomes a correct patch or disappears somewhere between tools, context, state and output format. ( arXiv ) A 5,000-rollout comparison across 10 harnesses and two fixed models found a rank correlation of -0.05, showing that changing the harness can reshuffle the leaderboard. This is why I am using harness rather narrowly here. A framework can give us agent classes and tool decorators, while a runtime can keep work alive after a crash; the harness is the operational layer that decides how the model sees its task and how its decisions become actions. model + context policy + tool interface + workspace + memory and state + permissions + planning and delegation + stopping and recovery = the agent we actually experience Harness-Bench phrases the underlying conclusion more formally: agent capability should be reported at the model-harness configuration level . I think that is the useful starting point for this ranking, because a benchmark number attached only to the model is increasingly describing an incomplete machine. ( arXiv ) How I rated them The four meters are deliberately qualitative. Agent power covers hard multi-step execution and the evidence that the system can finish real work; Control covers permissions, sandboxing, approvals, budgets and the ability to constrain action; Engineering looks at context management, memory, recovery, subagents, extensibility and the quality of the harness itself; Portability asks how much survives when the model, provider or deployment environment changes. They are not averaged into a synthetic score, because doing that would imply a precision the available evidence cannot support. A harness can have an excellent architecture and little independent benchmarking, while another can dominate one benchmark because its adapter fits that workload unusually well, so the final order combines measurements with an explicitly editorial judgment. #10 OpenClaw — the system that makes the ranking look unstable Putting OpenClaw last sounds strange after reading Claw-SWE-Bench, where it actually leads the five-harness comparison on both GLM 5.1 at 73.4% and Qwen 3.6-flash at 66.0%. The problem appears when we widen the lens: Harness-Bench gives it 52.4, the lowest aggregate score among its six configurable harnesses. These results are not contradictory once we accept that the workload and adapter are part of the system being tested; instead, they make OpenClaw the strongest warning against interpreting any single benchmark as a universal harness league. ( arXiv ) Its full coding adapter also turned the same GLM 5.1 backbone from 19.1% into 73.4% on Claw-SWE-Bench, which is precisely why I kept it in the ten rather than replacing it with a more consistently respectable framework. OpenClaw is the wildcard here, and its value to this article is that it exposes just how much execution plumbing can matter. Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Control      🟧🟧🟧⬜⬜ Engineering  🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ #9 Crush — a harness that likes the smaller model Crush is easier to understand if we stop asking whether it is “better” than Codex and ask which model-harness pair is better. In the public 10-harness SWE-bench Pro experiment, Crush placed seventh on GLM-5.2 and first on Gemma 4, exactly the kind of inversion that produced the near-zero rank correlation across the two models. Its own design also makes that result plausible rather than mystical: Crush is explicitly multi-model, can switch models inside a session while preserving context, uses LSP information, supports MCP extensions and accepts OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic-compatible providers. ( Hugging Face ) For teams working with smaller or local models, I would therefore test Crush much earlier than this overall ninth place suggests, although its broader control and production story is less developed than the systems further up the list. Power        🟧🟧🟧⬜⬜ Control      🟧🟧🟧⬜⬜ Engineering  🟧🟧🟧⬜⬜ Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 #8 mini-swe-agent — the uncomfortable little counterexample Some harnesses accumulate features until their architecture diagram needs its own architecture diagram; mini-swe-agent goes in the opposite direction and describes its agent class as roughly 100 lines of Python. The current project reports more than 74% on SWE-bench Verified, supports multiple execution environments and works across models through providers such as LiteLLM and OpenRouter, although that headline result belongs to a different benchmark protocol and should not be mixed numerically with the results above. ( GitHub ) The controlled 10-harness comparison is more useful for our purpose, because mini-swe-agent reached 52.4% on GLM-5.2 and led that entire arm. A tiny loop with a deliberately small abstraction surface beating much heavier systems is a useful correction to the idea that every extra planning object, memory subsystem or orchestration layer automatically makes an agent better. “What if our agent was 100x simpler, and still worked nearly as well?” ( GitHub ) Its weakness is the mirror image of its attraction: simplicity gives us transparency and portability, whereas sophisticated policy, recovery and control have to live elsewhere. Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Control      🟥🟥⬜⬜⬜ Engineering  🟥🟥⬜⬜⬜ Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 #7 OpenCode — portability with enough engineering behind it OpenCode is one of the systems I would expect to rise when the model is not predetermined. Its current product supports more than 75 providers, including local models, while the developer experience adds LSP integration, parallel sessions and terminal, desktop and IDE surfaces. In the fixed-model harness sweep it moved from eighth with GLM-5.2 to second with Gemma 4, which is a dramatic shift but also consistent with a tool that has been designed around provider flexibility rather than one model family. ( OpenCode ) The trade-off is that portability alone does not produce the deeper policy and reliability story available higher in the ranking, so OpenCode lands in the middle rather than becoming my default general-purpose harness. Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Control      🟧🟧🟧⬜⬜ Engineering  🟧🟧🟧⬜⬜ Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 #6 Claude Code and the Agent SDK — the control specialist Claude Code feels less interesting when described as a coding assistant and much more interesting when inspected as an authority boundary. Its current stack includes configurable permission modes, sandboxing, tool restrictions, MCP, custom subagents, hooks and increasingly fine-grained network controls; recent releases even added strict network allowlists for sandboxed commands and explicit tool blocking for custom agents. ( Claude ) That control surface earns the strongest rating in this part of the list, although the price is obvious: the system is designed around Anthropic’s model and product environment, and the SWE-bench Pro harness experiment reinforces that coupling because Claude Code moved from third on GLM-5.2 to seventh on Gemma 4. I would choose it quickly when Claude is already the intended model and operational safety matters, while I would look elsewhere when model portability is a first-order requirement. ( Hugging Face ) Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Control      🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 Engineering  🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Portability  🟥🟥⬜⬜⬜ An AI agent harness adds context management, tools, workspace, state, planning, memory, control and recovery around the model, which can materially change task completion. #5 Deep Agents — long work needs somewhere to put the mess Deep Agents earns its place because it treats context as an engineering resource rather than an infinitely expanding chat transcript. The open-source harness is model-agnostic and built on LangGraph, with persistence, checkpointing, isolated subagents, filesystem backends and context compression intended for long-horizon work. ( GitHub ) Its experimental Interpreter is an especially interesting direction. Instead of forcing the model to call a tool, read the result, call another tool and keep every intermediate value inside the language-model context, Deep Agents can let the model write a small program inside a restricted QuickJS runtime, where loops, branching, parallel calls and intermediate state happen before only the useful result returns to the model. That architecture sits between ordinary serial tool calling and a full operating-system sandbox, which could become increasingly important as agents manipulate larger datasets or coordinate many subagents. ( Docs by LangChain ) The experimental label matters, so I would not present the Interpreter as settled production infrastructure; nevertheless, the idea is technically sound enough to make Deep Agents one of the more interesting harnesses to watch. Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Control      🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Engineering  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ #4 Pydantic AI Harness — the architecture I wanted to put higher This is where the ranking deliberately stops following benchmark order. Pydantic AI Harness has the richest explicit harness-engineering surface I found, with planning and subagents sitting beside more unusual capabilities such as Dynamic Workflow, Advisor, Code Mode, prompt-injection defense, tool approvals, spend limits, system reminders and a Trajectory Judge that lets a second model inspect a live run and steer it before the primary agent drifts too far. ( Pydantic ) Spend control is also implemented as an actual execution constraint rather than dashboard decoration: SpendLimits tracks model-response costs across configured windows and blocks subsequent requests after a ceiling has been exhausted, while the documentation is refreshingly explicit that the request crossing the limit can still complete and that concurrent calls mean this is a brake rather than a perfect financial ledger. That kind of caveat increases my confidence more than another feature checkbox would. ( Pydantic ) Why only fourth, then? Independent cross-harness evidence remains thinner than the architecture deserves. Fryday is a ranking of what I can defend now, not what has the cleanest documentation, so Pydantic gets almost perfect engineering meters without receiving a benchmark victory it has not yet earned. Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Control      🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 Engineering  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 #3 Codex CLI — the strongest measured specialist Harness-Bench gives Codex an aggregate score of 80.4, ahead of the configurable-harness averages, although the researchers correctly report it separately because it was evaluated as a model-bound coding agent using its own default model configuration. Codex also has one of the better developed control stories: sandboxing constrains writable paths and network access, approvals govern operations outside those boundaries, managed rules can allow or block specific command classes, and OpenTelemetry can export tool, approval, MCP and network-policy activity for auditing. ( arXiv ) There is also a very current change to consider. On September 10, OpenAI launched the Agents API, which exposes the Codex harness as a managed cloud-agent environment with hosted sandboxes, longer sessions, tool management and subagent support, so Codex is visibly evolving from a local coding CLI into a reusable agent execution layer. ( OpenAI ) The reason it stays below NanoBot and Hermes is portability. In the separate SWE-bench Pro experiment, Codex moved from second place on GLM-5.2 to ninth on Gemma 4, which suggests that part of its strength belongs to the model-harness pairing rather than to a universally portable scaffold. That is not a defect if the intended answer is “use Codex with the models it was built around,” although it matters a lot in a ranking whose question is broader. ( Hugging Face ) Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 Control      🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Engineering  🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Portability  🟥🟥🟥🟥⬜ #2 NanoBot — efficiency without looking like an efficiency experiment NanoBot wins the configurable side of Harness-Bench with 76.2, and it does so while averaging 68.7K tokens, compared with 139.7K for Hermes, 133.2K for ZeroClaw and 175.1K for NullClaw. More tokens clearly did not buy a better result in that protocol. ( arXiv ) The project itself remains intentionally compact, yet the current runtime includes long-term memory, MCP, model routing, subagents, scheduled automation, WebUI and chat integrations, plus an OpenAI-compatible API. This combination is why I rate its engineering as good rather than merely “small”: NanoBot has kept the core loop readable while adding enough surrounding machinery to function as a real persistent agent runtime. ( GitHub ) Its second place comes from the disagreement between benchmarks. On Claw-SWE-Bench, NanoBot falls to 60.9% with GLM 5.1 and 47.4% with Qwen 3.6-flash, whereas Hermes reaches 71.1% and 62.6% with those same models. That does not invalidate NanoBot’s Harness-Bench win; instead, it is another demonstration that workload fit remains part of the product. ( arXiv ) Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 Control      🟧🟧🟧⬜⬜ Engineering  🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 #1 Hermes Agent — consistency beats the biggest single number Hermes does not win Harness-Bench. NanoBot does. It also does not win either fixed-model Claw-SWE-Bench arm, because OpenClaw finishes slightly ahead on both; however, Hermes is the system that remains close to the front when the evaluation changes, which is more useful to me than one spectacular result followed by one collapse. Harness-Bench places Hermes second among its six configurable harnesses at 71.2. Claw-SWE-Bench then gives it 71.1% with GLM 5.1, only 2.3 points behind OpenClaw, and 62.6% with Qwen 3.6-flash, again second. NanoBot, by comparison, goes from the strongest configurable Harness-Bench result to substantially weaker coding results, while OpenClaw travels in the opposite direction. Hermes is less dramatic, and that is exactly why I trust it more as an overall pick. ( arXiv ) Its full product also extends well beyond the restricted terminal and file toolsets used in Claw-SWE-Bench. Hermes provides persistent memory, skills, programmatic tool calling and subagent delegation, while delegated agents inherit the parent’s enabled toolsets rather than being allowed to widen their own authority. Leaf subagents are prevented from using capabilities such as shared-memory writes and scheduling, and only their final summary returns to the parent’s context, which is a sensible compromise between delegation and uncontrolled context growth. ( Hermes Agent ) That mix gives Hermes my #1 position: it has credible evidence across different benchmark designs, broad general-purpose capability, model flexibility and an architecture that remains understandable enough to inspect rather than simply trust. Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 Control      🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Engineering  🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜ Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 The stranger answer may be to stop choosing one harness While researching these ten, some of the most interesting systems did not belong in the ranking at all because they operate one layer lower or one layer above it. Dapr Agents, for example, assigns each agent a cryptographic identity and backs agent execution with durable workflows that persist LLM and tool interactions, allowing work to recover after restarts while infrastructure handles retries, timeouts and circuit breakers. DBOS approaches the same production problem as a graftable durability layer, including a DBOSRunner that can replace the normal OpenAI Agents runner so completed steps survive process failures and are not blindly executed again. ( Dapr Docs ) Those systems suggest that the best harness may eventually be assembled from layers rather than purchased as one opinionated shell, although two newer research projects push the idea further. Meta-Harness searches over harness code using prior source, execution traces and scores, reporting improvements over hand-designed context systems and coding baselines, while JIT-Agent generates task-adaptive harness modules for memory, planning, action and tool policy on demand. Its authors report gains as large as 20.2 points for GLM-5.2 in their controlled evaluations and competitive results against mature systems such as OpenCode and Claude Code. These are research results rather than an excuse to replace production infrastructure next Monday, but the direction is difficult to ignore. ( arXiv ) Agent infrastructure is moving from fixed generic wrappers toward task-specific generated harnesses, durable runtimes and stronger identity and recovery layers. A year ago, choosing an agent often meant choosing a model and then asking which tools to bolt onto it. The 2026 evidence points toward a different engineering problem, because context construction, workspace design, permission boundaries, stopping rules, recovery and tool protocols can determine how much useful capability reaches the final artifact. The model remains the reasoning engine, while the harness increasingly decides how much of that engine survives contact with a real task. For this Fryday ranking, Hermes is therefore my best overall choice, NanoBot is the efficiency surprise, Codex is the strongest measured specialist, Pydantic is the architecture I most want to see independently benchmarked, and OpenClaw is the warning label attached to the whole exercise. A different model or workload can rearrange those names again… which may be the most important result of the ranking. Sources Harness-Bench: Measuring Harness Effects across Models in Realistic Agent Workflows SWE-bench Pro: 10 agent harnesses x 2 models, raw benchmark results Claw-SWE-Bench paper Claw-SWE-Bench leaderboard Hermes Agent documentation NanoBot repository and documentation Pydantic AI Harness documentation Deep Agents repository Deep Agents Interpreter documentation mini-swe-agent repository Crush repository OpenCode documentation Claude Code release notes OpenAI: Running Codex safely OpenAI Agents API announcement, September 10, 2026 Dapr Agents documentation DBOS OpenAI Agents integration Meta-Harness: End-to-End Optimization of Model Harnesses JIT-Agent: Scaling Harness Intelligence via Just-in-Time Harness Evolution Fryday #8: 10 Agent Harnesses That Change What the Same Model Can Do was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Some harnesses accumulate features until their architecture diagram needs its own architecture diagram; mini-swe-agent goes in the opposite direction and describes its agent class as roughly 100 lines of Python. The controlled 10-harness comparison is more useful for our purpose, because mini-swe-agent reached 52.4% on GLM-5.2 and led that entire arm. A tiny loop with a deliberately small abstraction surface beating much heavier systems is a useful correction to the idea that every extra planning object, memory subsystem or orchestration layer automatically makes an agent better.

“What if our agent was 100x simpler, and still worked nearly as well?” (GitHub)

Its weakness is the mirror image of its attraction: simplicity gives us transparency and portability, whereas sophisticated policy, recovery and control have to live elsewhere.

Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜
Control      🟥🟥⬜⬜⬜
Engineering  🟥🟥⬜⬜⬜
Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩
#7 OpenCode — portability with enough engineering behind it

OpenCode is one of the systems I would expect to rise when the model is not predetermined. Its current product supports more than 75 providers, including local models, while the developer experience adds LSP integration, parallel sessions and terminal, desktop and IDE surfaces. In the fixed-model harness sweep it moved from eighth with GLM-5.2 to second with Gemma 4, which is a dramatic shift but also consistent with a tool that has been designed around provider flexibility rather than one model family. (OpenCode)

The trade-off is that portability alone does not produce the deeper policy and reliability story available higher in the ranking, so OpenCode lands in the middle rather than becoming my default general-purpose harness.

Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜
Control      🟧🟧🟧⬜⬜
Engineering  🟧🟧🟧⬜⬜
Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩
#6 Claude Code and the Agent SDK — the control specialist

Claude Code feels less interesting when described as a coding assistant and much more interesting when inspected as an authority boundary. Its current stack includes configurable permission modes, sandboxing, tool restrictions, MCP, custom subagents, hooks and increasingly fine-grained network controls; recent releases even added strict network allowlists for sandboxed commands and explicit tool blocking for custom agents. (Claude)

That control surface earns the strongest rating in this part of the list, although the price is obvious: the system is designed around Anthropic’s model and product environment, and the SWE-bench Pro harness experiment reinforces that coupling because Claude Code moved from third on GLM-5.2 to seventh on Gemma 4. I would choose it quickly when Claude is already the intended model and operational safety matters, while I would look elsewhere when model portability is a first-order requirement. (Hugging Face)

Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜
Control      🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩
Engineering  🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜
Portability  🟥🟥⬜⬜⬜
An AI agent harness adds context management, tools, workspace, state, planning, memory, control and recovery around the model, which can materially change task completion.#5 Deep Agents — long work needs somewhere to put the mess

Deep Agents earns its place because it treats context as an engineering resource rather than an infinitely expanding chat transcript. The open-source harness is model-agnostic and built on LangGraph, with persistence, checkpointing, isolated subagents, filesystem backends and context compression intended for long-horizon work. (GitHub)

Its experimental Interpreter is an especially interesting direction. Instead of forcing the model to call a tool, read the result, call another tool and keep every intermediate value inside the language-model context, Deep Agents can let the model write a small program inside a restricted QuickJS runtime, where loops, branching, parallel calls and intermediate state happen before only the useful result returns to the model. That architecture sits between ordinary serial tool calling and a full operating-system sandbox, which could become increasingly important as agents manipulate larger datasets or coordinate many subagents. (Docs by LangChain)

The experimental label matters, so I would not present the Interpreter as settled production infrastructure; nevertheless, the idea is technically sound enough to make Deep Agents one of the more interesting harnesses to watch.

Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜
Control      🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜
Engineering  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩
Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜
#4 Pydantic AI Harness — the architecture I wanted to put higher

This is where the ranking deliberately stops following benchmark order. Pydantic AI Harness has the richest explicit harness-engineering surface I found, with planning and subagents sitting beside more unusual capabilities such as Dynamic Workflow, Advisor, Code Mode, prompt-injection defense, tool approvals, spend limits, system reminders and a Trajectory Judge that lets a second model inspect a live run and steer it before the primary agent drifts too far. (Pydantic)

Spend control is also implemented as an actual execution constraint rather than dashboard decoration: SpendLimits tracks model-response costs across configured windows and blocks subsequent requests after a ceiling has been exhausted, while the documentation is refreshingly explicit that the request crossing the limit can still complete and that concurrent calls mean this is a brake rather than a perfect financial ledger. That kind of caveat increases my confidence more than another feature checkbox would. (Pydantic)

Why only fourth, then? Independent cross-harness evidence remains thinner than the architecture deserves. Fryday is a ranking of what I can defend now, not what has the cleanest documentation, so Pydantic gets almost perfect engineering meters without receiving a benchmark victory it has not yet earned.

Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜
Control      🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩
Engineering  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩
Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩
#3 Codex CLI — the strongest measured specialist

Harness-Bench gives Codex an aggregate score of 80.4, ahead of the configurable-harness averages, although the researchers correctly report it separately because it was evaluated as a model-bound coding agent using its own default model configuration. Codex also has one of the better developed control stories: sandboxing constrains writable paths and network access, approvals govern operations outside those boundaries, managed rules can allow or block specific command classes, and OpenTelemetry can export tool, approval, MCP and network-policy activity for auditing. (arXiv)

There is also a very current change to consider. On September 10, OpenAI launched the Agents API, which exposes the Codex harness as a managed cloud-agent environment with hosted sandboxes, longer sessions, tool management and subagent support, so Codex is visibly evolving from a local coding CLI into a reusable agent execution layer. (OpenAI)

The reason it stays below NanoBot and Hermes is portability. In the separate SWE-bench Pro experiment, Codex moved from second place on GLM-5.2 to ninth on Gemma 4, which suggests that part of its strength belongs to the model-harness pairing rather than to a universally portable scaffold. That is not a defect if the intended answer is “use Codex with the models it was built around,” although it matters a lot in a ranking whose question is broader. (Hugging Face)

Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩
Control      🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜
Engineering  🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜
Portability  🟥🟥🟥🟥⬜
#2 NanoBot — efficiency without looking like an efficiency experiment

NanoBot wins the configurable side of Harness-Bench with 76.2, and it does so while averaging 68.7K tokens, compared with 139.7K for Hermes, 133.2K for ZeroClaw and 175.1K for NullClaw. More tokens clearly did not buy a better result in that protocol. (arXiv)

The project itself remains intentionally compact, yet the current runtime includes long-term memory, MCP, model routing, subagents, scheduled automation, WebUI and chat integrations, plus an OpenAI-compatible API. This combination is why I rate its engineering as good rather than merely “small”: NanoBot has kept the core loop readable while adding enough surrounding machinery to function as a real persistent agent runtime. (GitHub)

Its second place comes from the disagreement between benchmarks. On Claw-SWE-Bench, NanoBot falls to 60.9% with GLM 5.1 and 47.4% with Qwen 3.6-flash, whereas Hermes reaches 71.1% and 62.6% with those same models. That does not invalidate NanoBot’s Harness-Bench win; instead, it is another demonstration that workload fit remains part of the product. (arXiv)

Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩
Control      🟧🟧🟧⬜⬜
Engineering  🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜
Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩
#1 Hermes Agent — consistency beats the biggest single number

Hermes does not win Harness-Bench. NanoBot does. It also does not win either fixed-model Claw-SWE-Bench arm, because OpenClaw finishes slightly ahead on both; however, Hermes is the system that remains close to the front when the evaluation changes, which is more useful to me than one spectacular result followed by one collapse.

Harness-Bench places Hermes second among its six configurable harnesses at 71.2. Claw-SWE-Bench then gives it 71.1% with GLM 5.1, only 2.3 points behind OpenClaw, and 62.6% with Qwen 3.6-flash, again second. NanoBot, by comparison, goes from the strongest configurable Harness-Bench result to substantially weaker coding results, while OpenClaw travels in the opposite direction. Hermes is less dramatic, and that is exactly why I trust it more as an overall pick. (arXiv)

Its full product also extends well beyond the restricted terminal and file toolsets used in Claw-SWE-Bench. Hermes provides persistent memory, skills, programmatic tool calling and subagent delegation, while delegated agents inherit the parent’s enabled toolsets rather than being allowed to widen their own authority. Leaf subagents are prevented from using capabilities such as shared-memory writes and scheduling, and only their final summary returns to the parent’s context, which is a sensible compromise between delegation and uncontrolled context growth. (Hermes Agent)

That mix gives Hermes my #1 position: it has credible evidence across different benchmark designs, broad general-purpose capability, model flexibility and an architecture that remains understandable enough to inspect rather than simply trust.

Power        🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩
Control      🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜
Engineering  🟩🟩🟩🟩⬜
Portability  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩
The stranger answer may be to stop choosing one harness

While researching these ten, some of the most interesting systems did not belong in the ranking at all because they operate one layer lower or one layer above it. Dapr Agents, for example, assigns each agent a cryptographic identity and backs agent execution with durable workflows that persist LLM and tool interactions, allowing work to recover after restarts while infrastructure handles retries, timeouts and circuit breakers. DBOS approaches the same production problem as a graftable durability layer, including a DBOSRunner that can replace the normal OpenAI Agents runner so completed steps survive process failures and are not blindly executed again. (Dapr Docs)

Those systems suggest that the best harness may eventually be assembled from layers rather than purchased as one opinionated shell, although two newer research projects push the idea further. Meta-Harness searches over harness code using prior source, execution traces and scores, reporting improvements over hand-designed context systems and coding baselines, while JIT-Agent generates task-adaptive harness modules for memory, planning, action and tool policy on demand. Its authors report gains as large as 20.2 points for GLM-5.2 in their controlled evaluations and competitive results against mature systems such as OpenCode and Claude Code. These are research results rather than an excuse to replace production infrastructure next Monday, but the direction is difficult to ignore. (arXiv)

Agent infrastructure is moving from fixed generic wrappers toward task-specific generated harnesses, durable runtimes and stronger identity and recovery layers.

A year ago, choosing an agent often meant choosing a model and then asking which tools to bolt onto it. The 2026 evidence points toward a different engineering problem, because context construction, workspace design, permission boundaries, stopping rules, recovery and tool protocols can determine how much useful capability reaches the final artifact. The model remains the reasoning engine, while the harness increasingly decides how much of that engine survives contact with a real task.

For this Fryday ranking, Hermes is therefore my best overall choice, NanoBot is the efficiency surprise, Codex is the strongest measured specialist, Pydantic is the architecture I most want to see independently benchmarked, and OpenClaw is the warning label attached to the whole exercise. A different model or workload can rearrange those names again… which may be the most important result of the ranking.
