items.title: How INT8 Quantization Made My Neural Network 60% Smaller: A TinyML Model Compression Experiment
items.summary: Exploring what happened when I traded numerical precision for a smaller ECG arrhythmia detection model. Reduction of model size from 87.5 KB to 34.6 KB with INT8 quantization Last time, we looked at what happens behind the simple number on your smartwatch: 72 BPM . Behind that number is a stream of physiological data, computation, and a model trying to make sense of it. But there was one part of that story we hadn’t explored yet. What happens when the AI itself has to get smaller? To find out, I started with the model itself. The first technique I tried was INT8 quantization , a way to reduce the numerical precision of a neural network so it can use less storage and computation. 🧩 The First TinyML Model Compression Experiment In Part 1, I started with a simple question: How much could I compress a TinyML model for ECG arrhythmia detection before its performance started to suffer? If you haven’t read it yet, you can start here: Part 1: What Happens When You Shrink an AI That Reads Heartbeats to Just 35 KB? To answer that, I first needed a starting point. The FP32 1D CNN had the following metrics on the reported MIT-BIH evaluation setup: Reported FP32 baseline metrics on the MIT-BIH evaluation setup. This was the model I was going to shrink. The first compression experiment was INT8 quantization . Unlike pruning, which removes or zeroes weights, quantization takes a different approach: What if I could represent the numbers inside the model using fewer bits? That sounds like a small change. It turned out to make a surprisingly big difference. What Does “32 Bits → 8 Bits” Actually Mean? Neural networks commonly represent their weights and intermediate values using numerical formats such as 32-bit floating point , or FP32. So, conceptually, the model starts as: FP32 (32 bits per value) → INT8 (8 bits per value) INT8 quantization reducing an ECG TinyML neural network from FP32 to an 8-bit representation. In Beat2Bit, I converted the trained model to an INT8 representation , replacing the original 32-bit floating-point representation with 8-bit integers for the quantized model. The potential benefit is fairly intuitive. If each value can be represented using fewer bits, the model can require less storage. But there is an obvious problem. Less precision means less information. Converting FP32 to INT8 was the easy part. The real test was seeing whether the model would still behave the same way afterward. Making a model smaller is easy if you’re willing to sacrifice performance. The challenge is finding out how much you can remove before that trade-off becomes unacceptable. Why Can 8 Bits Be Enough? Think about storing a measurement. If I tell you that a room is: 23.472891°C I’m giving you a lot of numerical precision. Instead if I tell you: 23.5°C I’ve lost some precision. But if the only question is whether the room is comfortable, that extra precision might not matter. Quantization makes a similar trade. The goal isn’t necessarily to preserve every decimal place. It is to preserve the useful behaviour of the model . Neural networks can sometimes tolerate reduced numerical precision because not every tiny difference in a parameter necessarily changes the final prediction. But that’s only a hypothesis until you test the specific model. And that’s exactly what I wanted to find out with Beat2Bit. The Goal Wasn’t the Smallest Model This was an important distinction for the experiment. I wasn’t trying to win a competition for the smallest possible .tflite file. I wanted to find a useful balance between three things: Model size : How much storage does it need? Inference efficiency : How much computation does it require? Prediction quality: Does it still perform well enough for the task? A model that is tiny but performs poorly isn’t particularly useful. A highly accurate model that is too large for the intended hardware has a different problem. And a model that looks extremely fast on a benchmark isn’t enough if the benchmark doesn’t represent the actual deployment hardware. So I needed to keep all three in view. From 87.5 KB to 34.6 KB 📉 This was the first result that made me stop and look twice. Comparison of FP32 and INT8 neural network model size. The reported FP32 model was: 87.5 KB After INT8 quantization: 34.6 KB That’s a reduction of roughly 60% in model size . But the more interesting part wasn’t the size. It was what happened to the performance. ECG arrhythmia detection model performance before and after INT8 quantization. The reported accuracy stayed at 93.8% . Sensitivity stayed at 75.0% . Positive predictivity moved from 71.3% to 71.2% . So I had gone from: 87.5 KB → 34.6 KB without a meaningful change in those reported headline metrics. That was a much better result than I expected. But I didn’t want to stop at the headline numbers. Why 60% Smaller Doesn’t Mean 60% Less Intelligence There’s an important distinction here. Quantization doesn’t mean that I deleted 60% of the model’s learned knowledge. The 60% reduction refers to the reported model artifact size , going from 87.5 KB to 34.6 KB. The underlying idea is different: Instead of representing numerical values with the original FP32 representation, the quantized model uses a lower-precision INT8 representation. So: Smaller representation ≠ less learned information That’s why the performance results matter. If reducing numerical precision had caused a major degradation, the smaller model wouldn’t necessarily have been a useful trade. But in this experiment, the reported INT8 model retained the baseline’s accuracy and sensitivity , with only a very small change in positive predictivity. That made quantization look like a very promising first step. Did INT8 Quantization Make the Model Faster? Model size was only one part of the problem. The reported benchmark showed a substantial difference in inference time: FP32: 18.0 ms INT8: 0.073 ms That’s roughly 247× faster according to the project’s benchmark. That number definitely caught my attention. But there was an important detail behind it. The 0.073 ms measurement came from running the .tflite model on a desktop CPU , not on a physical microcontroller. So while the benchmark showed a big improvement, I still couldn’t tell how the model would perform on the hardware I ultimately wanted to target. That was something I would need to test for real. For now, the result was still useful. It showed that reducing the model’s numerical precision could have a much bigger effect than just cutting down its file size. And that made me wonder: What else could I remove without breaking the model? Neural Network Pruning: What Happened Next? This is where I moved from quantization to pruning . A neural network contains many weights, and not all of them contribute equally to the final prediction. Pruning takes advantage of that idea. Instead of asking: How can I represent all these weights more efficiently? it asks: Do I need all these weights in the first place? A neural network contains many weights, and not all of them contribute equally to the final prediction. Pruning takes advantage of that idea. The basic idea is to identify weights with relatively small magnitudes and set selected weights to zero Conceptually: Neural network pruning creating sparsity by setting low-magnitude weights to zero. where τ is a threshold. The result is a sparse network . For example: Before pruning: [0.82, -0.03, 0.71, 0.01, -0.44] After pruning: [0.82, 0.00, 0.71, 0.00, -0.44] Beat2Bit tested 50% and 60% pruning levels , followed by INT8 quantization. On paper, this sounded like the obvious next step. If INT8 had already made the model dramatically smaller, removing half the weights should make it smaller still. Right? Not exactly. Why Sparsity Isn’t the Same as Model Compression This was one of the most useful discoveries in the entire experiment. The 50% pruned + INT8 model was reported at: 34.6 KB The 60% pruned + INT8 model was also: 34.6 KB The same reported size as the INT8 model without pruning. That sounds strange at first. If half the weights are zero, shouldn’t the file be half the size? Not necessarily. There’s a difference between: A neural network containing many zero weights and A file format that actually stores those zero weights more efficiently. Consider: [0.82, 0.00, 0.71, 0.00, -0.44] If the representation still stores every position, including the zeros, then those zeros haven’t disappeared from the file. Pruning has created sparsity . It hasn’t necessarily created storage compression . And that’s what happened here. The serialized model remained 34.6 KB after both 50% and 60% pruning. So: 50% pruning ≠ 50% smaller model file and: 60% pruning ≠ 60% smaller model file That distinction completely changed how I thought about pruning. The Numbers Looked Good. Then I Looked Closer. Now the comparison became much more interesting: Comparison of INT8 quantization and pruning for TinyML ECG arrhythmia detection. And suddenly, the experiment wasn’t simply about compression anymore. It became a question about trade-offs . INT8 gave me a substantial reported reduction in model size while preserving the baseline’s reported accuracy and sensitivity. But pushing pruning further did something different. The reported model size didn’t decrease further. Meanwhile, positive predictivity dropped from 71.2% for INT8 to 61.2% at 50% pruning and 54.9% at 60% pruning . That changes the question completely. The goal shifted from compressing as much as possible to finding how much compression was actually useful. Why Smaller Isn’t Always Better for Edge AI This sounds obvious when you say it out loud. But it is surprisingly easy to forget when you’re optimizing a machine learning model. If you optimize only for model size, you might celebrate every reduction. If you optimize only for latency, you might celebrate every faster benchmark. If you optimize only for accuracy, you might ignore whether the model can actually run where you need it. Real deployment sits somewhere in the middle. Beat2Bit made that trade-off visible. INT8 quantization gave me the biggest win. The model became much smaller while its reported accuracy and sensitivity stayed the same. I then tried pruning , which removes weights the model seems to need less. But that came with a surprise: removing more weights didn’t make the model file any smaller, and its positive predictivity started to suffer. That taught me something important: An optimization is only useful if the thing you’re optimizing actually changes in the way you intended. Making a network sparse is one thing. Making the deployed artifact smaller is another. And improving a benchmark number is not automatically the same as improving a real deployment. So, What Actually Happened? Overview of INT8 quantization and neural network pruning for TinyML model compression The Real Question Wasn’t “How Small?” Beat2Bit started with the idea of making a model smaller. But the experiments showed me that smaller doesn’t automatically mean better . INT8 gave me a major reduction in model size while keeping the reported performance almost unchanged. Pruning went further, but the extra sparsity didn’t make the model file smaller and started to hurt positive predictivity. That changed how I think about optimization. The best model isn’t necessarily the smallest one but the one that makes the right trade-offs for where it needs to run. And that’s what makes edge AI interesting! 🔗 Want to explore the experiment yourself? Beat2Bit is open source. Explore the implementation on GitHub . What would you optimize first: size, speed, or performance? To answer that, I first needed a starting point.

The FP32 1D CNN had the following metrics on the reported MIT-BIH evaluation setup:

Reported FP32 baseline metrics on the MIT-BIH evaluation setup.

This was the model I was going to shrink.

The first compression experiment was INT8 quantization.

What if I could represent the numbers inside the model using fewer bits?

If each value can be represented using fewer bits, the model can require less storage.

But there is an obvious problem.

Less precision means less information.

Converting FP32 to INT8 was the easy part.

The real test was seeing whether the model would still behave the same way afterward.

Making a model smaller is easy if you’re willing to sacrifice performance.

The challenge is finding out how much you can remove before that trade-off becomes unacceptable.

Think about storing a measurement.

If I tell you that a room is: 23.472891°C

I’m giving you a lot of numerical precision.

Instead if I tell you: 23.5°C

The goal isn’t necessarily to preserve every decimal place.

It is to preserve the useful behaviour of the model.

Neural networks can sometimes tolerate reduced numerical precision because not every tiny difference in a parameter necessarily changes the final prediction.

But that’s only a hypothesis until you test the specific model.

And that’s exactly what I wanted to find out with Beat2Bit.

This was an important distinction for the experiment.

I wasn’t trying to win a competition for the smallest possible .tflite file.

The reported FP32 model was: 87.5 KB

After INT8 quantization: 34.6 KB

ECG arrhythmia detection model performance before and after INT8 quantization.

Sensitivity stayed at 75.0%.

Positive predictivity moved from 71.3% to 71.2%.

So I had gone from: 87.5 KB → 34.6 KB

That was a much better result than I expected.

But I didn’t want to stop at the headline numbers.

Instead of representing numerical values with the original FP32 representation, the quantized model uses a lower-precision INT8 representation.

So:

But in this experiment, the reported INT8 model retained the baseline’s accuracy and sensitivity, with only a very small change in positive predictivity.

That made quantization look like a very promising first step.

The reported benchmark showed a substantial difference in inference time:

FP32: 18.0 ms

INT8: 0.073 ms

That’s roughly 247× faster according to the project’s benchmark.

That number definitely caught my attention.

But there was an important detail behind it.

The 0.073 ms measurement came from running the .tflite model on a desktop CPU, not on a physical microcontroller.

So while the benchmark showed a big improvement, I still couldn’t tell how the model would perform on the hardware I ultimately wanted to target.

That was something I would need to test for real.

For now, the result was still useful. It showed that reducing the model’s numerical precision could have a much bigger effect than just cutting down its file size.

And that made me wonder:

What else could I remove without breaking the model?

Neural Network Pruning: What Happened Next?

This is where I moved from quantization to pruning.

A neural network contains many weights, and not all of them contribute equally to the final prediction.

Pruning takes advantage of that idea.

Instead of asking:

How can I represent all these weights more efficiently?

it asks:

Do I need all these weights in the first place?

A neural network contains many weights, and not all of them contribute equally to the final prediction.

Pruning takes advantage of that idea.

The basic idea is to identify weights with relatively small magnitudes and set selected weights to zero

Conceptually:

Neural network pruning creating sparsity by setting low-magnitude weights to zero.

where τ is a threshold.

The result is a sparse network.

For example:

Before pruning: [0.82, -0.03, 0.71, 0.01, -0.44]

After pruning: [0.82, 0.00, 0.71, 0.00, -0.44]

Beat2Bit tested 50% and 60% pruning levels, followed by INT8 quantization.

On paper, this sounded like the obvious next step.

If INT8 had already made the model dramatically smaller, removing half the weights should make it smaller still.

Right?

Not exactly.

Why Sparsity Isn’t the Same as Model Compression

This was one of the most useful discoveries in the entire experiment.

The 50% pruned + INT8 model was reported at: 34.6 KB

The 60% pruned + INT8 model was also: 34.6 KB

The same reported size as the INT8 model without pruning.

That sounds strange at first.

If half the weights are zero, shouldn’t the file be half the size?

Not necessarily.

There’s a difference between:

A neural network containing many zero weights

and

A file format that actually stores those zero weights more efficiently.

Consider:

[0.82, 0.00, 0.71, 0.00, -0.44]

If the representation still stores every position, including the zeros, then those zeros haven’t disappeared from the file.

Pruning has created sparsity.

It hasn’t necessarily created storage compression.

And that’s what happened here.

The serialized model remained 34.6 KB after both 50% and 60% pruning.

So:

50% pruning ≠ 50% smaller model file

and:

60% pruning ≠ 60% smaller model file

That distinction completely changed how I thought about pruning.

The Numbers Looked Good. Then I Looked Closer.

Now the comparison became much more interesting:

Comparison of INT8 quantization and pruning for TinyML ECG arrhythmia detection.

And suddenly, the experiment wasn’t simply about compression anymore.

It became a question about trade-offs.

INT8 gave me a substantial reported reduction in model size while preserving the baseline’s reported accuracy and sensitivity.

But pushing pruning further did something different.

The reported model size didn’t decrease further.

Meanwhile, positive predictivity dropped from 71.2% for INT8 to 61.2% at 50% pruning and 54.9% at 60% pruning.

That changes the question completely.

The goal shifted from compressing as much as possible to finding how much compression was actually useful.

Why Smaller Isn’t Always Better for Edge AI

This sounds obvious when you say it out loud.

But it is surprisingly easy to forget when you’re optimizing a machine learning model.

If you optimize only for model size, you might celebrate every reduction.

If you optimize only for latency, you might celebrate every faster benchmark.

If you optimize only for accuracy, you might ignore whether the model can actually run where you need it.

Real deployment sits somewhere in the middle.

Beat2Bit made that trade-off visible.

INT8 quantization gave me the biggest win. The model became much smaller while its reported accuracy and sensitivity stayed the same.

I then tried pruning, which removes weights the model seems to need less. But that came with a surprise: removing more weights didn’t make the model file any smaller, and its positive predictivity started to suffer.

That taught me something important:

An optimization is only useful if the thing you’re optimizing actually changes in the way you intended.

Making a network sparse is one thing.

Making the deployed artifact smaller is another.

And improving a benchmark number is not automatically the same as improving a real deployment.

So, What Actually Happened?Overview of INT8 quantization and neural network pruning for TinyML model compressionThe Real Question Wasn’t “How Small?”

Beat2Bit started with the idea of making a model smaller.

But the experiments showed me that smaller doesn’t automatically mean better.

INT8 gave me a major reduction in model size while keeping the reported performance almost unchanged.

Pruning went further, but the extra sparsity didn’t make the model file smaller and started to hurt positive predictivity.

That changed how I think about optimization.

The best model isn’t necessarily the smallest one but the one that makes the right trade-offs for where it needs to run.

And that’s what makes edge AI interesting!

🔗 Want to explore the experiment yourself? Beat2Bit is open source. Explore the implementation on GitHub.

What would you optimize first: size, speed, or performance?

How INT8 Quantization Made My Neural Network 60% Smaller: A TinyML Model Compression Experiment was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: 'It's going to hurt': How a surging student-loan payment is reshaping a family's future
items.summary: The Sprague family is determining the sacrifices they need to make to navigate higher student-loan payments. Alyssa Pointer for BI Jodi and Paul Sprague raised their daughters with a guiding principle: understand the value of a dollar. By elementary school, Evelyn and Olivia were learning about mortgages, car insurance, and basic accounting in the carpool lane. Early one June morning, before Evelyn, 17, and Olivia, 19, left for their summer jobs, Jodi sat them down with news that threw the Spragues' carefully managed budget into question. The student-loan payments the family had budgeted for since 2015 were surging from $404 to $1,014 monthly, starting in September. Jodi Sprague and her daughter, Olivia, are both facing looming student-debt burdens. Alyssa Pointer for BI She and Olivia began to cry. Olivia was about to start her sophomore year at Georgia Southern University, and while her parents helped her pay for housing, that likely wouldn't be possible in the upcoming semester. Her first thought when she learned of Jodi's payment increase: how would she afford her rent? The 150% increase comes from President Donald Trump's student-loan repayment overhaul , which took effect on July 1. It eliminated the Biden-era SAVE repayment plan , which gave Jodi and millions of other borrowers affordable monthly payments. The administration said its changes are intended to curb excessive borrowing, simplify a complex repayment system, and compel colleges to lower their tuition. Over the past year, more than a thousand borrowers have told Business Insider that they're taking on extra work, postponing retirement, and worrying they'll default because of higher monthly bills. This story is part of Business Insider's "Student Debt Spiral" series, which explores how rising student debt is changing the financial futures of millions. Do you have a story to share? Fill out this form , and we'll be in touch. Read more of our student-loan coverage here: 'A bunch of red tape': Student-loan borrowers can't get clear answers from the companies that manage their debt Student-loan borrowers are pushing off retirement , delaying children, and taking on 3 jobs to prep for repayment changes New student-loan repayment glitches are throwing borrowers' budgets into limbo The payment is in Jodi's name, but it will reshape decisions across the household. As Olivia prepares to borrow more for college and Evelyn weighs an expensive career path, Jodi and Paul have to decide how much more work, debt, and sacrifice the family can absorb. "When the kids were little, and there was a dollar in our checking account until payday, we made it," said Jodi, 54. Her student loans are no different. "It's going to hurt," she said, "but I'm going to pay them." Jodi's parents saw college as the key to wealth and pushed their daughters to attend. At 18, she borrowed a minimal amount to pursue a two-year degree at a small Bible college. Looking back, Jodi's shocked it was that easy to take on debt. After seven years as a stay-at-home mom left her depressed and unfulfilled, Jodi decided to go back to school. Teaching would offer the challenge she needed and the career she wanted. Paul, a city employee, worried about managing the cost of a degree while raising a family, but he had faith in Jodi. "She's always been very driven. Very smart." Jodi now has a $144,000 student-loan balance, from a history degree at Kennesaw State University and a master's in teaching from the University of West Georgia. Jodi said she is worried about making her student-loan payment before her next paycheck comes. Alyssa Pointer for BI "We took the maximum out," Jodi, now a middle school teacher, said. "We were able to survive because of the student-loan money." Survival has shaped the Spragues. Two years ago, a tree split open the roof of their home. For a whole school year, the family of four lived in a small rental with their dog Bailey, while their home underwent repairs. "It was absolutely devastating for our family to be literally displaced," Jodi said. "But again, we learned so much from it. We learned that we don't need that much." The first moment Evelyn and Olivia knew they weren't rich was when everyone at kindergarten had American Girl Dolls, but they didn't. They asked for Christmas presents in July to give their parents more time to save up; one year, Olivia got a bottle of Chick-fil-A Polynesian sauce while her friends were getting iPads and cash. When Evelyn's friends wanted to go out to dinner, she was often the one to say no — she had to wait for her next paycheck from Whataburger. In 2011, when the daughters were toddlers, Jodi accumulated credit card debt she couldn't repay, and the Spragues filed for bankruptcy . One day, she didn't know how she'd afford groceries — until an $80 refund check from a dentist appointment arrived in the mail. "I just broke down," Jodi said. "That's how tight it was." We've always had an open dialogue about money because my parents were the opposite. Evelyn and Olivia were too young to understand what bankruptcy meant. Jodi and Paul made it their mission to do what their parents hadn't. "We've always had an open dialogue about money because my parents were the opposite," Jodi said. "They didn't teach us anything. Everything was secret, secret." Jodi and Olivia show their matching tattoos (Evelyn is too young, but she has plans for ink the minute she turns 18). Alyssa Pointer for BI Olivia recalled an added pressure that came with those financial lessons. "I remember being in the car line in the morning, and my mom was like, 'You have to get good grades so you can go to school for free,'" Olivia said. "So it's always been in the back of my mind that school is really expensive." Ayelet Sheffey covers all things student debt, from the latest Education Department news to stories of borrowers navigating their loans. To stay up to date on her coverage, sign up to get email alerts for her new stories here . In high school, Olivia got an 89% on a biology test and cried so much that she had to go home; she worried the B+ would ruin her chances at a scholarship. In 7th grade, Evelyn started a spreadsheet mapping out potential college courses and their costs. "Unfortunately, it's probably put a lot of pressure on them," Paul said. "But that's what it is." Olivia received Georgia's HOPE scholarship, but it didn't cover her full tuition. So Jodi took out $19,000 in parent PLUS loans for Olivia's first year. Now, with the family's tighter budget, Olivia is taking out $6,000 this semester — the most she can borrow federally — to cover her rent and other expenses and prevent Jodi from borrowing further. "I can't really take the time to pick up another job because I'd be putting my schoolwork on the back burner," said Olivia, who's studying public relations. "So I'd rather just deal with it later, with my student loans." Evelyn is now applying to colleges, and while she dreams of playing in a band, she's pursuing forensic pathology instead. However, the cost of a medical degree has her second-guessing that route. Paul, 60, has looked into taking on a second job. He said retirement is "just not a reality right now." If it came down to it, he said he would look at using his life insurance to help his daughters pay off any debt they accumulate. The Spragues are coming together to navigate the student-loan increase, from cutting back on subscriptions to taking on more household chores. Alyssa Pointer for BI The family has also started making smaller sacrifices. They've cut back on their streaming subscriptions and canceled their September vacation to Florida. Paul is learning simple mechanical fixes for his car instead of taking it to the shop. Olivia decided not to rush a sorority because of the cost. Jodi has about three years of payments left toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness , which forgives student debt for government and nonprofit workers, like teachers, after 10 years of qualifying payments. She's concerned that the higher payments will push back that timeline if she falls behind. The stakes are also higher because the Education Department now requires PSLF payments on new income-driven repayment plans to be made exactly on the due date — there was previously a grace period — or they will not count toward PSLF progress. Other student-loan borrowers are facing similar pressures. More will start transitioning off the SAVE plan in the coming months and face higher payments. Some borrowers said they're concerned about defaulting and facing wage garnishment and the seizure of federal benefits, such as Social Security . Paul and Jodi said that while they believed setting Evelyn and Olivia up for college was in their best interests, they would still support them if they decided not to go. Jodi teaches her seventh-grade students that college isn't always worth the investment, and that they could be better off pursuing trade school. Paul learned that lesson decades ago. He paid his own way through a stint at community college before he met Jodi, but he quickly realized that his career mapping for city government didn't require a degree. So he dropped out — and avoided student debt of his own. "It was the greatest decision I ever made," Paul said. Read the original article on Business Insider

"I just broke down," Jodi said. "That's how tight it was."

We've always had an open dialogue about money because my parents were the opposite.

Evelyn and Olivia were too young to understand what bankruptcy meant. Jodi and Paul made it their mission to do what their parents hadn't.

"We've always had an open dialogue about money because my parents were the opposite," Jodi said. "They didn't teach us anything. Everything was secret, secret."

"It was the greatest decision I ever made," Paul said.

items.title: Glitch Tokens Compared to Fragile Tokens
items.summary: Contextual Copying Failures Beyond Isolated Token Probes Abstract Successful repetition of an isolated token does not establish that the token will be preserved in surrounding text. I study FragileTokens, vocabulary entries that pass an isolated copying probe but exhibit copying errors in context. Our protocol inserts fixed token IDs into shared banks of random common-word sequences, measures the probability of the expected token at its copy position, and examines selected decoding failures. Across eight open-weight models from the Qwen and OLMo families, a probability-based screen flags 0.4% to 10.9% of isolation-passing tokens in at least 10% of tested contexts. These values measure screening prevalence, not the prevalence of verified decoding errors. Per-token screening scores correlate at 0.82 to 0.95 between context halves, and stored examples demonstrate deletion, substitution, truncation, and translation, including errors made with concentrated output distributions. I also evaluate whether proximity to known or context-screened glitch tokens identifies this conditional population. The better of input- and output-embedding proximity achieves an AUROC of 0.744 to 0.881 on seven models, although static features improve on surface-feature baselines on only three. Selected candidates are preserved less often than stable controls in several instruction and simulated tool-use tasks. A separate natural-entity experiment finds no incremental predictive benefit beyond existing controls. The contribution is a controlled characterization of contextual susceptibility among tokens that pass an isolation probe, together with evidence about its reproducibility, geometric associations, and task-specific consequences. The results motivate contextual verification while leaving prospective discovery performance and prediction of individual triggering contexts unresolved. 1 Introduction A language model can reproduce a token when asked to copy that token alone and replace it when asked to copy a longer sequence containing the same token. This discrepancy matters whenever literal identity is part of an instruction: quoting a title, preserving an identifier, returning a list item, or placing a name in a tool query. A fluent response can satisfy the surrounding task while changing the item the task concerns. The OLMo-2‑7B token according provides a concrete example. It is token ID 4184, and decoding and re-encoding its string returns the same ID. Under an isolated repetition probe, the correct continuation has log-probability −0.001. In the sequence deliver rel behind according sent floor wrong, however, the model emits sent at the position assigned to according and then continues from that following word. The probability of this incorrect emission rounds to 1.000 and its entropy to 0.00 bits. Across 48 sampled contexts, the recorded continuations delete according in 44 and reproduce it with probability approximately 0.999 in the remaining four. The contrast concerns the same model, token ID, and copying instruction. Glitch-token research already studies failures to reproduce or manipulate particular vocabulary entries. It includes embedding-based detection, activation-based classification, prompt variation, and multi-task assessment (Land and Bartolo, 2024; Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026). The question addressed here is more specific: among tokens that pass a specified isolation probe, which remain susceptible when the same token is copied as part of surrounding text, and how consistently can we measure that susceptibility? I use FragileTokens for this conditional behavioral class. Membership depends on a model, a copying protocol, and a distribution of contexts. The term does not assert that vulnerability is independent of context, nor that every isolated-probe failure and contextual failure shares one mechanism. Our primary experiments use a probability screen to identify candidates for this class. I distinguish that screen from verified decoding errors throughout the paper. The study makes three contributions. First, it measures the passing isolated-token population using shared context banks and fixed token IDs, allowing comparison of token susceptibility across contexts, independent runs, and model configurations. Second, it tests whether geometric signals associated with established glitch tokens also distinguish candidates within this population, including comparisons with surface features and random reference sets. Lastly, it examines whether selected candidates are preserved in subsequent instructions and simulated tool interactions, while reporting an explicit negative result for natural entity-name prediction. The resulting claim empirically extends glitch-token assessment. I do not claim to introduce embedding-based glitch detection or to establish that prior research ignores all context. Instead, I show why an isolation result should be treated as one measurement condition rather than a general certificate of literal reliability. 2 Related Work and the Contribution Boundary Early observations documented unusual responses to particular tokens under varied prompts and connected some of those tokens to unusual embedding regions (Rumbelow and Watkins, 2023). Subsequent work developed systematic detectors and evaluation procedures. These studies provide both the methodological foundation and the relevant comparison for FragileTokens. Land and Bartolo’s (2024) Magikarp framework uses embedding-derived indicators to identify under-trained-token candidates and behavioral probes to verify them. Its analysis includes alternative prompts and examples involving copied code lists. Li et al. (2024) define glitch behavior broadly and evaluate repetition, spelling, and length; GlitchHunter uses an embedding graph and iterative clustering to locate problematic regions. Consequently, neither geometric candidate generation nor the use of surrounding prompt text is new to the present study. GlitchProber classifies tokens using attention and MLP features and studies mitigation by changing intermediate activations (Zhang et al., 2024). GlitchMiner uses entropy-guided discrete optimization with local embedding neighborhoods and verifies candidates under three repetition templates (Wu et al., 2026). Our experiments instead hold model weights fixed and evaluate contextual susceptibility after conditioning on success in an isolation probe. Low-entropy incorrect emissions are relevant to that evaluation, but their existence alone does not demonstrate that an entropy-guided detector will miss the corresponding token under every prompt. Tang et al. (2026) provide the closest behavioral comparison. GlitchQuiz evaluates eight tasks, including sentence and paragraph construction, repetition, and multi-turn recall. Their Figure 2 shows a token passing simple tests and failing another task, and Section 5.3 acknowledges possible failures beyond the full assessment. Our contribution is repeated measurement of a fixed copying operation over shared context banks within an isolation-passing population, followed by reproducibility and prediction analyses. An isolation pass in our experiment does not establish a pass on GlitchQuiz, and I also do not claim priority for task-dependent token failure. Table 1 summarizes the comparison. The present experiments directly compare available Magikarp labels for three model configurations. They do not constitute a head-to-head rerun of all five systems under a common contextual oracle; I make no comparative recall or efficiency claims for those systems. Table 1. Relationship to the closest detection and assessment methods. Descriptions concern the published procedures, not a claim that their authors regard context as irrelevant. Rarity is a further competing explanation. Yu et al. (2022) study how gradients affecting rare-token embeddings can contribute to representation degeneration. This motivates comparisons with rarity-related surface features, but it does not establish the training history or causal mechanism of the tokens studied here. Our token-ID feature is a vocabulary-order proxy, not a measurement of pretraining frequency. 3 Experimental Design 3.1 Models and sampling The main copying experiments cover eight open-weight models from two families: one OLMo-2 model and seven Qwen models spanning three generations. Table 2 gives the tested configurations. A separate representation analysis uses Pythia-1.4B and is reported as an auxiliary experiment in Section 7.2. Thus, claims from the eight-model copying study do not automatically extend to Pythia or other model families. For each model, we stratify the vocabulary sample by token-ID range. Sample sizes range from 4,200 to 8,400 IDs for the Qwen models. OLMo-2‑7B uses an initial sample of 2,098 IDs and a replication sample of 6,273. Each sampled token is inserted into every context in that run. The context banks contain random sequences of common words that individually pass the copying check; sequence lengths are 8, 16, 32, and 64, with a randomly chosen interior insertion slot. These are controlled common-word sequences, not samples of grammatical natural prose. Table 2. Configurations in the main copying study. Vocabulary values are embedding-row counts. “Tokens × contexts” describes the sampled copying matrix. Flash-Next and 235B use FP8 checkpoints. Appendix A includes full identifiers and framing details. The OLMo Team (2025) and Qwen Team (2025a, 2025b, 2026a, 2026b) describe the model families and releases. Differences among configurations include tokenizer, architecture, training, framing, and numerical precision. The model ladder is therefore a set of replications across configurations, not a controlled experiment on parameter count. 3.2 Copying protocol and token identity The copying prompt contains two demonstrations followed by a sequence containing the target token. The isolation probe uses the same template, with the target alone as the text. Appendix A provides the exact template. I assemble every test prompt from token IDs, so the target ID remains fixed even as its surroundings change. This choice is necessary to separate model behavior from re-tokenization. Adding a space to a decoded token string can change its segmentation before the model sees it. Direct ID insertion avoids that confound but also permits sequences that a tokenizer would not normally produce from an ordinary string. I therefore distinguish exact-ID copying from string preservation and restrict claims about normal text use accordingly. The canonical according example shows that the phenomenon is not confined to a noncanonical token string. Under teacher forcing, I supply the expected copied prefix before evaluating the next-token distribution at the target’s output position. Let q₀(t) be the model’s probability of target ID t under the isolation probe, and q(t,c) its probability at the corresponding position in context c. A low value measures poor support for the required token under a correct prefix. It does not by itself show what an unconstrained continuation will do after an earlier mistake. For the Qwen3.8 configurations, the copying instruction and demonstrations occupy the user turn of the model’s chat template, and Copy: open the assistant turn with thinking disabled. Other copying runs use a raw few-shot sequence. The framing is fixed within each model. This adjustment matters: under the raw cue, the Qwen3.8 models often start on a new line and change leading-space tokenization. Of 2,000 common-word checks, 3 copy under the raw framing, compared with 1,921 on 27B and 1,925 on Flash-Next under the chat framing. 3.3 Behavioral fragility and the probability screen Let ŷ(t,c) denote the greedy next token at the target’s copy position under the teacher-forced prefix. The empirical rate of target-position copying errors over a context bank C of size m is A behavioral FragileToken passes the specified isolated copying test and exhibits contextual errors. A quantitative class additionally requires a declared threshold on this error rate. Actual sequence-level copying failure is a separate outcome because it can involve errors before or after the target position. The aggregate experiments use a related probability screen. The primary isolation gate admits q₀(t) > 0.5, which guarantees that t is the unique greedy output in isolation. It is a sufficient condition for an isolated greedy pass, not an exhaustive characterization of such passes. A stricter gate, used in the OLMo sensitivity analysis, admits ln q₀(t) > −0.1, or q₀(t) > approximately 0.905. The contextual screen flags a cell if ln q(t,c) < −0.5, corresponding to q(t,c) < approximately 0.607. Its per-token susceptibility score is A screen-positive candidate passes the isolation gate and has S(t;C) ≥ 0.10. A stable control passes the gate and has S(t;C) = 0. Tokens with scores between these thresholds form an intermediate group. With 24 contexts, the candidate criterion requires at least 3 flagged cells; with 48 contexts, it requires at least 5. The probability screen and behavioral error rate must not be conflated. A token with probability 0.55, both alone and in context, passes the primary isolation gate and is flagged contextually, despite no probability decrease and a correct greedy output. Consequently, the reported screening prevalence is neither a direct estimate nor a guaranteed bound on the prevalence of behavioral FragileTokens. The stricter isolation gate removes this particular overlap, but contextual probability below 0.607 still does not establish a wrong argmax. I use decoded specimens to demonstrate actual errors and retain the aggregate probability results as screening measurements. 3.4 Reference classes and stored specimens OLMo-2‑7B has an independent reference set of 442 Magikarp-verified glitch tokens. None passes the primary isolation gate in these experiments, and their mean contextual screening score in the initial bank is 0.993. For models without this label set, reference construction combines poor isolation performance with a contextual screening score of at least 0.90. Appendix B reports the reference-set sizes used in the geometric analyses. This contextual check is necessary because poor isolation performance can reflect the prompt format rather than persistent copying difficulty. For inspected candidates and reference tokens, the specimen procedure retains three of the worst contextual cells and one control cell per token. Records include the context IDs, target slot, expected-token probability, top-five output IDs and probabilities, entropy, and a greedy continuation when generation is available. Provenance fields identify the model and checkpoint revision, precision, architecture metadata, and software versions. These records support case analysis; selecting the worst cells makes them unsuitable for estimating a representative distribution of confidence over all contextual errors. The descriptive failure categories are deletion, substitution, truncation, and translation, with script conversion recorded where appropriate. Deletion requires evidence that the model advances to the following text; an isolated top-token observation alone cannot establish how a full continuation proceeds. We use entropy below 2 bits as a concentration descriptor for a stored output distribution. It is not a calibrated measure of task correctness or of whether the model will verbally express uncertainty. 4 Contextual Susceptibility Among Isolation Passes 4.1 Screening prevalence Table 3 reports the primary-gate results. Candidate prevalence ranges from 15 of 4,047 gated tokens on Flash-Next (0.4%) to 684 of 6,277 on Qwen3‑235B (10.9%). The range is conditional on the sampled vocabulary, selected isolation gate, context distribution, and threshold. It is not a prevalence estimate for natural text occurrences or for all tokens that a model can greedily repeat in isolation. Table 3. Contextual screening under the primary isolation gate. Under the strict isolation gate, OLMo-2‑7B has 14 candidates among 873 tokens in the first bank (1.6%) and 29 among 1,888 in the replication bank (1.5%). These candidates have substantially higher isolation probability than the contextual threshold. They provide a sensitivity analysis against overlap of the two cutoffs, although verified argmax-error prevalence still requires direct measurement. Comparisons restricted to shared token IDs preserve some cross-configuration differences. Among 1,592 IDs passing both gates for Qwen3‑1.7B and Qwen3‑235B, the candidate rates are 2.0% and 6.2%. Among 1,569 shared passes for Qwen3‑32B and Qwen3‑235B, they are 0.8% and 4.3%. These comparisons reduce differences in sampled IDs but do not isolate the effects of scale from architecture, precision, or training. 4.2 Reproducibility and context effects Across the eight models, per-token scores correlate at 0.82 to 0.95 between context halves. A stronger replication on Qwen3‑32B doubles the token sample and draws a new context bank. Scores correlate at 0.984 over the 4,200 shared IDs, and 12 of the original 15 candidates meet the threshold again. Re-scoring stored Qwen3‑32B and Qwen2.5‑72B matrices on different hardware gives cell-level agreement of 0.999 and 0.996 and per-token score correlations of 0.9999 and 0.9996, respectively. The initial OLMo matrix assigns 95.2% of the reported variance to the token main effect, 0.1% to the context main effect, and 4.7% to the residual. Restricting to the strict-gate population changes these shares to 71.7%, approximately 0.0%, and 28.2%. The large reduction in the token share after gating is consequential: much of the variation over the full sample separates broadly problematic tokens from reliable ones. Substantial residual variation remains within the gated population. These observations support a reproducible token-level susceptibility under the sampled distribution. They do not establish that the triggering context is irrelevant. A small context main effect means that a particular carrier is not consistently difficult for every token; it can coexist with strong token-by-context variation. Consistent with this distinction, OLMo prediction of held-out cells reaches an AUROC of 0.94 using a token’s score in other contexts, compared with 0.56 using the carrier’s difficulty for other tokens. The tested token-context similarity features provide no additional predictive benefit. Context length also matters for some populations. On the strict-gate OLMo sample, the flagged-cell rates for lengths 8, 16, 32, and 64 are 0.005, 0.008, 0.008, and 0.008. Among Qwen2.5‑72B candidates, the corresponding comparison reported for the shortest and longest carriers is 33% versus 52%. The study therefore identifies a stable ranking of susceptibility more clearly than it identifies the conditions that produce any individual error. 4.3 Comparison with released Magikarp labels Table 4 compares the contextual candidate sets with available Magikarp records. None of the candidates in these three comparisons is a Magikarp-verified glitch token. Most are recorded as acceptable under that procedure; a small number are classified as undecodable and must not be counted as positively certified healthy tokens. The Qwen2.5‑7B comparison uses 294 candidates, whereas the screening summary in Table 3 reports 296; these analysis populations are reported separately. This shows that the contextual screen identifies behavior outside the available verified-glitch sets. It is not evidence that all contextual candidates are actual copying errors, nor that other detectors would fail to identify them under their own assessment tasks. A common-oracle comparison is required to quantify that broader claim. 4.4 Demonstrated errors and output concentration The motivating according case establishes an actual copy error despite near-certain success in isolation. Other stored cases show related behaviors across languages and model configurations. Table 5 gives representative observations. The screening score describes the token across its context bank; the final column describes a selected observed emission. These are different levels of evidence. Table 5. Selected contextual copying specimens. Probabilities are rounded as recorded. A score S summarizes threshold flags and is not necessarily the fraction of verified decoding errors. The table is illustrative and does not estimate failure-mode frequencies. Across the seven Qwen configurations, the fraction of selected stored failing specimens with entropy below 2 bits ranges from 14% to 74% (Appendix B). Some errors therefore occur under highly concentrated distributions, while others occur under diffuse distributions. These records support the existence of confident errors but do not support a universal claim that contextual errors are usually confident or never accompanied by uncertainty. 5 Embedding Associations and Prediction 5.1 Scores and prediction costs The geometric analysis asks whether the candidate population has a measurable relationship to a model’s glitch-reference set. Let e(t) be either an input-embedding row or an output-embedding row, and let N₅(t;G) contain the five reference tokens in G with the largest cosine similarity to t in that space. The proximity score is A second score projects the input embedding onto the direction from the vocabulary mean to the mean of the glitch-reference embeddings. The proximity score represents a local neighborhood; the projection represents one global direction. Neither score requires a model forward pass for a new token once the reference set and embeddings are available. Building a behaviorally screened reference set does require model evaluation, and its cost belongs in any end-to-end discovery comparison. The fitted prediction analysis compares four feature tiers. The surface baseline uses token ID, decoded character length, leading-space status, alphabetic status, and ASCII status. Static features comprise input and output row norms and centroid distances, nearest-neighbor similarities, a direct input-output self-score and competitor margin, and the glitch-direction projection. The static tier as evaluated does not include the five-neighbor glitch-proximity score. Dynamic features summarize the target-position representation over half of the contexts, including its dispersion, norm, and alignment with the target’s output row. Behavioral features use copying measurements from those contexts. The contextual and behavioral tiers predict the candidate label on the other half of the contexts. The reported fitted results use out-of-fold L2-regularized logistic regression and paired bootstrap comparisons with the surface baseline. Thus, the dynamic and behavioral tiers require forward passes and are not weight-only screens. Half-bank labels also produce different positive counts from the full-bank screening table. 5.2 Association with the glitch reference class Figure 1 and Appendix B report proximity separately for the input and output spaces. Selecting the better of the two spaces for each model gives an AUROC range of 0.744 to 0.881 across the seven configurations reported as having untied embeddings. This is a descriptive, model-wise selection of the better space, not the performance of one prespecified score applied uniformly to all models. We also retain the weaker values on Qwen3-1.7 B. Crosses show the token-ID score. The line at 0.5 marks chance ranking. The model-wise choice of the stronger space is descriptive. Table B1 reports sample counts and the remaining geometric scores. The informative space varies by model. On OLMo-2‑7B, input proximity gives 0.846 and output proximity 0.528. Qwen2.5‑72B shows the reverse pattern, with 0.685 and 0.798. A global direction is not always sufficient: its AUROC on Qwen2.5‑72B is 0.599. Conversely, Qwen3‑32B’s direction score, 0.898, exceeds either proximity score. The results support model-dependent geometric associations rather than a universal geometric form. Replacing the glitch-reference set with a random stable set of the same size gives mean AUROCs of 0.41 to 0.55 over ten draws. This comparison shows that arbitrary stable reference sets do not reproduce the reported ranking. It does not isolate glitch proximity from other competing explanations, including rarity, local embedding density, or how the reference set was selected. In particular, the token-ID baseline exceeds both proximity scores on Qwen2.5‑72B and Qwen3‑235B. The Qwen3‑1.7B results are insufficient to infer an effect of weight tying. Only one tied configuration is included, and the reported input- and output-proximity scores differ despite its tied-weight description. That discrepancy prevents a clean architectural interpretation of this row. 5.3 Projected distribution of contextual candidates Contextual candidates extend beyond the visible concentrations of the glitch-reference class. A geometric pre-screen is therefore plausible for prioritizing contextual testing, but the present results do not establish high-precision discovery at a fixed testing budget. AUROC measures ranking, not the precision of a selected shortlist. Demonstrating practical discovery would require a frozen score and reference set, disjoint candidates, a fixed verification budget, and comparisons with random, token-ID, and existing-detector selection under the same behavioral outcome. 6 Preservation in Generation and Tasks 6.1 Free generation and identity metrics Free-generation probes ask whether the model retains a supplied token while describing or responding to it. The OLMo experiment requests exact identification and an explanation, followed by the assistant prefix Let me think about this carefully. Other configurations use the token as the user turn under the model’s chat template. Outputs are generated for up to 256 tokens. These framing differences are part of the protocol and preclude treating the resulting counts as a controlled scale comparison. Two reproduction metrics are needed. The exact-ID metric asks whether the seed ID occurs anywhere in the generated IDs. The string metric asks whether the decoded seed string occurs anywhere in the output, allowing a different segmentation. Neither alone establishes correct identification or exact reproduction of an entire requested sequence. For Qwen2.5‑72B, for example, none of the 32 worst-isolation seeds reappear as their original IDs, while 12 reappear as strings. A seed such as _ghost can be written using multiple output tokens. Table C1 reports candidate-versus-control reproduction for the configurations with available generation. The candidate string-preservation rate is lower than the control rate in four of five comparisons and equal on Qwen3‑32B. Exact-ID rates are less consistent: Qwen2.5‑7B ties, and Qwen3‑32B reproduces 8 of 14 candidates versus 7 of 14 controls. A candidate can also be reproduced while being misidentified. These outcomes support task-dependent vulnerability rather than a universal inability to emit the candidate token. The 32 worst-isolation seeds used in separate generation probes are not interchangeable with context-screened glitch references. On Flash-Next, a teacher-forced check of these seeds assigns the expected token probability at least 0.5 in 71% of 768 cells, whereas the analogous rate on Qwen3‑235B is 0.1%. This disagreement is another reason to verify the behavior of a reference set in the relevant context. I did not run free generation, task probes, or specimen continuations on the two FP8 mixtures because the evaluation stack took about seven seconds per generated token, and I ran this with my own money; I would prefer not to go bankrupt. Their next-token observations must not be read as generated reasoning traces. We also did not run candidate-free generation on Qwen2.5‑72B. 6.2 Instructions requiring lexical preservation Five instruction templates require the model to preserve the target string: name a Python function, quote a document title, return a list item, correct spelling, and summarize while preserving proper nouns. Each class contributes ten selected tokens per model and five tasks, giving 50 episodes per class. Tokens are inserted by ID into the model’s chat template. Appendix C contains the full templates and per-task results. The primary metric asks whether the answer contains the given token string. It is deliberately narrower than complete task correctness. It does not verify whether generated code is valid, whether a function name is a legal Python identifier, or whether a summary is faithful in other respects. The spelling task also invites normalization, so its preservation rate must be interpreted in light of its wording. Table 7. Token-string preservation in simple instructions. The episode-bootstrap intervals exclude zero for OLMo-2‑7B, Qwen3.8‑27B, and both Qwen3‑32B modes, but not for Qwen2.5‑7B. Asked for the second item when the target is NSLocalizedString, it returns LocalizableString. Qwen3‑32B changes realtà to reality in the spelling task. These examples preserve much of the requested task form while altering the designated content. 6.3 Simulated tool interactions The tool experiment uses five assignments involving a target term: investigate a configuration key, prepare a background note, recommend whether to adopt a technology, explain a term, or check a release. Models can call search, open_page, and run_python for up to six rounds. Ten tokens per class again produce 50 episodes per configuration. The environment is constructed around the supplied token. A search containing its string returns relevant documentation, release notes, and an issue page. Other searches return no relevant hits and generic material. This design isolates whether the target reaches a tool call, but it does not estimate retrieval failure in a natural search engine. The selected token sets, repeated templates, and constructed environment limit generalization to autonomous systems operating on natural tasks. 6.4 A negative result on natural entity names A separate experiment evaluates 1,255 real code identifiers and proper nouns in a natural task. Adding the fragility of constituent tokens does not improve prediction of an incorrect entity name after controlling for entity rarity, constituent-token isolation scores, and the model probability of the complete entity. The reported change in AUROC is −0.001, with a 95% interval of [−0.008, +0.006]. This result limits the practical interpretation of the synthetic task findings. The current evidence does not establish that the contextual score explains natural entity-name errors beyond these existing predictors. It also does not show that rarity causes either outcome, or that every possible relationship between token fragility and hallucination has been excluded. The appropriate conclusion is that this experiment shows no incremental predictive power. 7 Auxiliary Analyses 7.1 Pair interactions and repetition A factorial copying experiment tests whether pairs of tokens produce damage beyond the contributions of their members. Carriers contain two slots at separations 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128, with two independent filler sequences at each separation. Each ordered pair is evaluated in four conditions: both targets, either target with a control, and two controls. The interaction contrast subtracts the two single-target scores from the joint score and adds the control score. The screen uses an additive fit within each carrier, standardized residuals, within-carrier permutations, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q = 0.05 (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995). Its declared count criterion compares the number of rejected pairs with the 95th percentile from twenty simulated additive-null datasets. No tested pool exceeds that criterion: the rejected-pair counts are 1 of 4,032 for each OLMo pool, 13 of 1,190 for Qwen3‑32B, and 1 of 2,256 for Qwen3‑235B (Appendix D). This finding is narrower than the absence of interaction. The maximum-statistic tests are significant for the OLMo pools and Qwen3‑32B, while Qwen3‑235B has p = 0.059. The two criteria assess different aspects of the interaction distribution and must both be retained. Mean repeated-token contrasts are positive in the reported tests, consistent with facilitation in these carriers. Neither result establishes universal additivity, the absence of rare harmful combinations, or a causal account based on induction. 7.2 Recoverability of token identity The Pythia-1.4B experiment places 36 verified glitch tokens and 1,088 controls at the ends of eight contexts. At each layer, the model matches a token’s contextual state to its state in another context within a pool of 1,124 candidates, after removing the component shared within each context. Biderman et al. (2023) describe Pythia. Identity-matching accuracy is 1.000 for glitch tokens from the embedding layer through layer 12 and 0.988 to 1.000 for controls. At the final layer it is 0.880 and 0.874, respectively. These results show that substantial token-identity information remains recoverable under the chosen comparison procedure. A logit-lens example also favors a continuation of a glitch token, idepress followed by ant, rather than reproduction of the input token itself. Decodability does not causally localize copying failure. The experiment does not show that the model uses the recoverable information in the copying computation, that identity is perfectly preserved, or that the output layer alone causes the error. It also concerns independently labeled glitch tokens on Pythia rather than the full candidate population in the eight-model study. Causal interventions would be needed to distinguish inadequate readout, context-dependent competition, and other explanations. 8 Discussion and Limitations The principal finding is a repeatable distinction between isolated copying success and contextual susceptibility. Shared context banks make it possible to estimate a per-token tendency without selecting an adversarial context for each token. Actual decoded examples establish that at least some of these discrepancies are literal copying errors, and the task experiments show that selected candidates can lose their identity beyond the copying template. Embedding associations connect this population to prior glitch-token research, while their variable incremental value prevents treating geometry as a complete explanation or a validated universal detector. Several limits determine the scope of that conclusion. First, the aggregate candidate class is defined by a probability threshold whose relationship to true decoding error is incomplete. Strict-gate results and inspected continuations strengthen the case for the phenomenon, but they do not replace a population-wide argmax-error analysis. A revised behavioral prevalence estimate must retain both the isolation outcome and contextual output identity for each cell. Second, the common-word carriers are artificial, and the model-dependent prompt framing affects what is measured. Direct ID insertion controls the experimental identity of the target but can create inputs unlike normal tokenizer output. String-preservation tasks partially address this concern, yet the study's strongest natural-entity test is negative after existing controls. There is no basis here to extrapolate candidate prevalence to everyday text or to treat a score as a context-independent property of a token. Third, eight copying configurations span only Qwen and OLMo, with differing precision and architecture. The auxiliary Pythia probe addresses another question. Generation coverage is incomplete, and some task classes contain only ten selected tokens. Episode-level bootstrap intervals do not fully account for dependence among five tasks using the same token. The reported intervals should therefore be read as descriptive evidence, with token-clustered or hierarchical uncertainty estimates needed for stronger population inference. Fourth, the geometric analyses evaluate associations with screen labels. Reference construction partly uses contextual behavior, and selection of the stronger embedding space is retrospective. Random stable references do not provide a rarity-matched or density-matched null. Static feature improvements occur on three models, while several token-ID baselines are already strong. The UMAP panels provide qualitative evidence about the plotted population; they do not measure original-space cluster coverage. No fixed-budget prospective discovery experiment or common-oracle comparison with the existing detectors is reported. Finally, the study does not identify which ordinary context will trigger a particular token’s error. Split-half prediction estimates average susceptibility under related context banks. Small context main effects do not eliminate token-context interactions, and the factorial experiment retains significant maximum-statistic results. Neither recoverable identity nor geometric proximity establishes a training mechanism. The evidence supports a measurement target and a set of associations; mechanistic explanation and context-specific prediction remain open. The most direct methodological extension is to freeze the isolation test, candidate score, reference construction, and context distribution before evaluation on disjoint data. Reporting target-position argmax error, full-sequence copying accuracy, and exact-string preservation alongside probability scores would connect screening sensitivity to observable failures. For discovery claims, precision and recall at a fixed verification budget would provide a more practical test than retrospective AUROC alone. 9 Reproducibility and Reporting Scope Reproduction requires the model and tokenizer revisions, sampled token IDs, complete context IDs and insertion slots, prompt framing, thresholds, precision, and scoring code. The procedure does not modify model weights. Appendix A provides public model identifiers and textual prompts; the run-specific matrices and environment metadata described in Section 3.4 are also necessary. Figure 2 additionally requires the plotted IDs and class masks, embedding preprocessing, UMAP parameters, and random seeds. Generation coverage is limited to the configurations explicitly listed in the corresponding tables. Analysis populations differ. Table 3 reports 296, 418, and 684 candidates for Qwen2.5‑7B, Qwen2.5‑72B, and Qwen3‑235B, while Table B1 reports 294, 417, and 682. Each analysis retains its associated counts. Half-bank prediction counts differ again because their labels use different contexts. Reconciling the remaining sample transitions exactly requires the underlying token manifests and exclusion masks. The recorded protocol includes amendments to the isolation gate, sample size, printable-seed filtering, and string-level reproduction scoring. Vocabulary sampling follows embedding-row counts, so padding reduces token-ID overlap between Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 samples. Matched-ID scaling within Qwen2.5 remains untested. These sampling and framing decisions form part of the experimental specification and constrain cross-model interpretation. 10 Conclusion FragileTokens studies contextual copying vulnerability among tokens that pass an isolation probe. Across eight configurations, screening scores are reproducible and decoded specimens confirm errors. Geometric proximity often ranks candidates above controls, with gains that vary across surface features. Selected candidates also show reduced lexical preservation in several tasks, while the natural-entity test finds no added predictive value. These findings support contextual verification and motivate direct evaluation of behavioral prevalence, prospective discovery, and individual triggering contexts.
