items.summary_html:
Contextual Copying Failures Beyond Isolated Token ProbesAbstract

Successful repetition of an isolated token does not establish that the token will be preserved in surrounding text. I study FragileTokens, vocabulary entries that pass an isolated copying probe but exhibit copying errors in context. Our protocol inserts fixed token IDs into shared banks of random common-word sequences, measures the probability of the expected token at its copy position, and examines selected decoding failures. Across eight open-weight models from the Qwen and OLMo families, a probability-based screen flags 0.4% to 10.9% of isolation-passing tokens in at least 10% of tested contexts. These values measure screening prevalence, not the prevalence of verified decoding errors. Per-token screening scores correlate at 0.82 to 0.95 between context halves, and stored examples demonstrate deletion, substitution, truncation, and translation, including errors made with concentrated output distributions. I also evaluate whether proximity to known or context-screened glitch tokens identifies this conditional population. The better of input- and output-embedding proximity achieves an AUROC of 0.744 to 0.881 on seven models, although static features improve on surface-feature baselines on only three. Selected candidates are preserved less often than stable controls in several instruction and simulated tool-use tasks. A separate natural-entity experiment finds no incremental predictive benefit beyond existing controls. The contribution is a controlled characterization of contextual susceptibility among tokens that pass an isolation probe, together with evidence about its reproducibility, geometric associations, and task-specific consequences. The results motivate contextual verification while leaving prospective discovery performance and prediction of individual triggering contexts unresolved.

1 Introduction

A language model can reproduce a token when asked to copy that token alone and replace it when asked to copy a longer sequence containing the same token. This discrepancy matters whenever literal identity is part of an instruction: quoting a title, preserving an identifier, returning a list item, or placing a name in a tool query. A fluent response can satisfy the surrounding task while changing the item the task concerns.

The OLMo-2‑7B token according provides a concrete example. It is token ID 4184, and decoding and re-encoding its string returns the same ID. Under an isolated repetition probe, the correct continuation has log-probability −0.001. In the sequence deliver rel behind according sent floor wrong, however, the model emits sent at the position assigned to according and then continues from that following word. The probability of this incorrect emission rounds to 1.000 and its entropy to 0.00 bits. Across 48 sampled contexts, the recorded continuations delete according in 44 and reproduce it with probability approximately 0.999 in the remaining four. The contrast concerns the same model, token ID, and copying instruction.

Glitch-token research already studies failures to reproduce or manipulate particular vocabulary entries. It includes embedding-based detection, activation-based classification, prompt variation, and multi-task assessment (Land and Bartolo, 2024; Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026). The question addressed here is more specific: among tokens that pass a specified isolation probe, which remain susceptible when the same token is copied as part of surrounding text, and how consistently can we measure that susceptibility?

I use FragileTokens for this conditional behavioral class. Membership depends on a model, a copying protocol, and a distribution of contexts. The term does not assert that vulnerability is independent of context, nor that every isolated-probe failure and contextual failure shares one mechanism. Our primary experiments use a probability screen to identify candidates for this class. I distinguish that screen from verified decoding errors throughout the paper.

The study makes three contributions. First, it measures the passing isolated-token population using shared context banks and fixed token IDs, allowing comparison of token susceptibility across contexts, independent runs, and model configurations. Second, it tests whether geometric signals associated with established glitch tokens also distinguish candidates within this population, including comparisons with surface features and random reference sets. Lastly, it examines whether selected candidates are preserved in subsequent instructions and simulated tool interactions, while reporting an explicit negative result for natural entity-name prediction.

The resulting claim empirically extends glitch-token assessment. I do not claim to introduce embedding-based glitch detection or to establish that prior research ignores all context. Instead, I show why an isolation result should be treated as one measurement condition rather than a general certificate of literal reliability.

2 Related Work and the Contribution Boundary

Early observations documented unusual responses to particular tokens under varied prompts and connected some of those tokens to unusual embedding regions (Rumbelow and Watkins, 2023). Subsequent work developed systematic detectors and evaluation procedures. These studies provide both the methodological foundation and the relevant comparison for FragileTokens.

Land and Bartolo’s (2024) Magikarp framework uses embedding-derived indicators to identify under-trained-token candidates and behavioral probes to verify them. Its analysis includes alternative prompts and examples involving copied code lists. Li et al. (2024) define glitch behavior broadly and evaluate repetition, spelling, and length; GlitchHunter uses an embedding graph and iterative clustering to locate problematic regions. Consequently, neither geometric candidate generation nor the use of surrounding prompt text is new to the present study.

GlitchProber classifies tokens using attention and MLP features and studies mitigation by changing intermediate activations (Zhang et al., 2024). GlitchMiner uses entropy-guided discrete optimization with local embedding neighborhoods and verifies candidates under three repetition templates (Wu et al., 2026). Our experiments instead hold model weights fixed and evaluate contextual susceptibility after conditioning on success in an isolation probe. Low-entropy incorrect emissions are relevant to that evaluation, but their existence alone does not demonstrate that an entropy-guided detector will miss the corresponding token under every prompt.

Tang et al. (2026) provide the closest behavioral comparison. GlitchQuiz evaluates eight tasks, including sentence and paragraph construction, repetition, and multi-turn recall. Their Figure 2 shows a token passing simple tests and failing another task, and Section 5.3 acknowledges possible failures beyond the full assessment. Our contribution is repeated measurement of a fixed copying operation over shared context banks within an isolation-passing population, followed by reproducibility and prediction analyses. An isolation pass in our experiment does not establish a pass on GlitchQuiz, and I also do not claim priority for task-dependent token failure.

Table 1 summarizes the comparison. The present experiments directly compare available Magikarp labels for three model configurations. They do not constitute a head-to-head rerun of all five systems under a common contextual oracle; I make no comparative recall or efficiency claims for those systems.

Table 1. Relationship to the closest detection and assessment methods. Descriptions concern the published procedures, not a claim that their authors regard context as irrelevant.

Rarity is a further competing explanation. Yu et al. (2022) study how gradients affecting rare-token embeddings can contribute to representation degeneration. This motivates comparisons with rarity-related surface features, but it does not establish the training history or causal mechanism of the tokens studied here. Our token-ID feature is a vocabulary-order proxy, not a measurement of pretraining frequency.

3 Experimental Design3.1 Models and sampling

The main copying experiments cover eight open-weight models from two families: one OLMo-2 model and seven Qwen models spanning three generations. Table 2 gives the tested configurations. A separate representation analysis uses Pythia-1.4B and is reported as an auxiliary experiment in Section 7.2. Thus, claims from the eight-model copying study do not automatically extend to Pythia or other model families.

For each model, we stratify the vocabulary sample by token-ID range. Sample sizes range from 4,200 to 8,400 IDs for the Qwen models. OLMo-2‑7B uses an initial sample of 2,098 IDs and a replication sample of 6,273. Each sampled token is inserted into every context in that run. The context banks contain random sequences of common words that individually pass the copying check; sequence lengths are 8, 16, 32, and 64, with a randomly chosen interior insertion slot. These are controlled common-word sequences, not samples of grammatical natural prose.

Table 2. Configurations in the main copying study. Vocabulary values are embedding-row counts. “Tokens × contexts” describes the sampled copying matrix. Flash-Next and 235B use FP8 checkpoints. Appendix A includes full identifiers and framing details.

The OLMo Team (2025) and Qwen Team (2025a, 2025b, 2026a, 2026b) describe the model families and releases. Differences among configurations include tokenizer, architecture, training, framing, and numerical precision. The model ladder is therefore a set of replications across configurations, not a controlled experiment on parameter count.

3.2 Copying protocol and token identity

The copying prompt contains two demonstrations followed by a sequence containing the target token. The isolation probe uses the same template, with the target alone as the text. Appendix A provides the exact template. I assemble every test prompt from token IDs, so the target ID remains fixed even as its surroundings change.

This choice is necessary to separate model behavior from re-tokenization. Adding a space to a decoded token string can change its segmentation before the model sees it. Direct ID insertion avoids that confound but also permits sequences that a tokenizer would not normally produce from an ordinary string. I therefore distinguish exact-ID copying from string preservation and restrict claims about normal text use accordingly. The canonical according example shows that the phenomenon is not confined to a noncanonical token string.

Under teacher forcing, I supply the expected copied prefix before evaluating the next-token distribution at the target’s output position. Let q₀(t) be the model’s probability of target ID t under the isolation probe, and q(t,c) its probability at the corresponding position in context c. A low value measures poor support for the required token under a correct prefix. It does not by itself show what an unconstrained continuation will do after an earlier mistake.

For the Qwen3.8 configurations, the copying instruction and demonstrations occupy the user turn of the model’s chat template, and Copy: open the assistant turn with thinking disabled. Other copying runs use a raw few-shot sequence. The framing is fixed within each model. This adjustment matters: under the raw cue, the Qwen3.8 models often start on a new line and change leading-space tokenization. Of 2,000 common-word checks, 3 copy under the raw framing, compared with 1,921 on 27B and 1,925 on Flash-Next under the chat framing.

3.3 Behavioral fragility and the probability screen

Let ŷ(t,c) denote the greedy next token at the target’s copy position under the teacher-forced prefix. The empirical rate of target-position copying errors over a context bank C of size m is

A behavioral FragileToken passes the specified isolated copying test and exhibits contextual errors. A quantitative class additionally requires a declared threshold on this error rate. Actual sequence-level copying failure is a separate outcome because it can involve errors before or after the target position.

The aggregate experiments use a related probability screen. The primary isolation gate admits q₀(t) > 0.5, which guarantees that t is the unique greedy output in isolation. It is a sufficient condition for an isolated greedy pass, not an exhaustive characterization of such passes. A stricter gate, used in the OLMo sensitivity analysis, admits ln q₀(t) > −0.1, or q₀(t) > approximately 0.905.

The contextual screen flags a cell if ln q(t,c) < −0.5, corresponding to q(t,c) < approximately 0.607. Its per-token susceptibility score is

A screen-positive candidate passes the isolation gate and has S(t;C) ≥ 0.10. A stable control passes the gate and has S(t;C) = 0. Tokens with scores between these thresholds form an intermediate group. With 24 contexts, the candidate criterion requires at least 3 flagged cells; with 48 contexts, it requires at least 5.

The probability screen and behavioral error rate must not be conflated. A token with probability 0.55, both alone and in context, passes the primary isolation gate and is flagged contextually, despite no probability decrease and a correct greedy output. Consequently, the reported screening prevalence is neither a direct estimate nor a guaranteed bound on the prevalence of behavioral FragileTokens. The stricter isolation gate removes this particular overlap, but contextual probability below 0.607 still does not establish a wrong argmax. I use decoded specimens to demonstrate actual errors and retain the aggregate probability results as screening measurements.

3.4 Reference classes and stored specimens

OLMo-2‑7B has an independent reference set of 442 Magikarp-verified glitch tokens. None passes the primary isolation gate in these experiments, and their mean contextual screening score in the initial bank is 0.993. For models without this label set, reference construction combines poor isolation performance with a contextual screening score of at least 0.90. Appendix B reports the reference-set sizes used in the geometric analyses. This contextual check is necessary because poor isolation performance can reflect the prompt format rather than persistent copying difficulty.

For inspected candidates and reference tokens, the specimen procedure retains three of the worst contextual cells and one control cell per token. Records include the context IDs, target slot, expected-token probability, top-five output IDs and probabilities, entropy, and a greedy continuation when generation is available. Provenance fields identify the model and checkpoint revision, precision, architecture metadata, and software versions. These records support case analysis; selecting the worst cells makes them unsuitable for estimating a representative distribution of confidence over all contextual errors.

The descriptive failure categories are deletion, substitution, truncation, and translation, with script conversion recorded where appropriate. Deletion requires evidence that the model advances to the following text; an isolated top-token observation alone cannot establish how a full continuation proceeds. We use entropy below 2 bits as a concentration descriptor for a stored output distribution. It is not a calibrated measure of task correctness or of whether the model will verbally express uncertainty.

4 Contextual Susceptibility Among Isolation Passes4.1 Screening prevalence

Table 3 reports the primary-gate results. Candidate prevalence ranges from 15 of 4,047 gated tokens on Flash-Next (0.4%) to 684 of 6,277 on Qwen3‑235B (10.9%). The range is conditional on the sampled vocabulary, selected isolation gate, context distribution, and threshold. It is not a prevalence estimate for natural text occurrences or for all tokens that a model can greedily repeat in isolation.

Table 3. Contextual screening under the primary isolation gate. Candidate counts use q₀ > 0.5 and S ≥ 0.10. “Zero score” is the percentage of gated tokens with S = 0. The correlation compares scores from even- and odd-indexed context halves. The final column is the context main-effect share of the reported variance decomposition.

Under the strict isolation gate, OLMo-2‑7B has 14 candidates among 873 tokens in the first bank (1.6%) and 29 among 1,888 in the replication bank (1.5%). These candidates have substantially higher isolation probability than the contextual threshold. They provide a sensitivity analysis against overlap of the two cutoffs, although verified argmax-error prevalence still requires direct measurement.

Comparisons restricted to shared token IDs preserve some cross-configuration differences. Among 1,592 IDs passing both gates for Qwen3‑1.7B and Qwen3‑235B, the candidate rates are 2.0% and 6.2%. Among 1,569 shared passes for Qwen3‑32B and Qwen3‑235B, they are 0.8% and 4.3%. These comparisons reduce differences in sampled IDs but do not isolate the effects of scale from architecture, precision, or training.

4.2 Reproducibility and context effects

Across the eight models, per-token scores correlate at 0.82 to 0.95 between context halves. A stronger replication on Qwen3‑32B doubles the token sample and draws a new context bank. Scores correlate at 0.984 over the 4,200 shared IDs, and 12 of the original 15 candidates meet the threshold again. Re-scoring stored Qwen3‑32B and Qwen2.5‑72B matrices on different hardware gives cell-level agreement of 0.999 and 0.996 and per-token score correlations of 0.9999 and 0.9996, respectively.

The initial OLMo matrix assigns 95.2% of the reported variance to the token main effect, 0.1% to the context main effect, and 4.7% to the residual. Restricting to the strict-gate population changes these shares to 71.7%, approximately 0.0%, and 28.2%. The large reduction in the token share after gating is consequential: much of the variation over the full sample separates broadly problematic tokens from reliable ones. Substantial residual variation remains within the gated population.

These observations support a reproducible token-level susceptibility under the sampled distribution. They do not establish that the triggering context is irrelevant. A small context main effect means that a particular carrier is not consistently difficult for every token; it can coexist with strong token-by-context variation. Consistent with this distinction, OLMo prediction of held-out cells reaches an AUROC of 0.94 using a token’s score in other contexts, compared with 0.56 using the carrier’s difficulty for other tokens. The tested token-context similarity features provide no additional predictive benefit.

Context length also matters for some populations. On the strict-gate OLMo sample, the flagged-cell rates for lengths 8, 16, 32, and 64 are 0.005, 0.008, 0.008, and 0.008. Among Qwen2.5‑72B candidates, the corresponding comparison reported for the shortest and longest carriers is 33% versus 52%. The study therefore identifies a stable ranking of susceptibility more clearly than it identifies the conditions that produce any individual error.

4.3 Comparison with released Magikarp labels

Table 4 compares the contextual candidate sets with available Magikarp records. None of the candidates in these three comparisons is a Magikarp-verified glitch token. Most are recorded as acceptable under that procedure; a small number are classified as undecodable and must not be counted as positively certified healthy tokens. Some candidates had entered Magikarp’s geometric candidate set but were rejected by its behavioral verification.

Table 4. Contextual candidates and Magikarp records. Counts describe the samples used in this comparison. “Rejected” refers to rejection of glitch status by the prior verification step. The Qwen2.5‑7B comparison uses 294 candidates, whereas the screening summary in Table 3 reports 296; these analysis populations are reported separately.

This shows that the contextual screen identifies behavior outside the available verified-glitch sets. It is not evidence that all contextual candidates are actual copying errors, nor that other detectors would fail to identify them under their own assessment tasks. A common-oracle comparison is required to quantify that broader claim.

4.4 Demonstrated errors and output concentration

The motivating according case establishes an actual copy error despite near-certain success in isolation. Other stored cases show related behaviors across languages and model configurations. Table 5 gives representative observations. The screening score describes the token across its context bank; the final column describes a selected observed emission. These are different levels of evidence.

Table 5. Selected contextual copying specimens. Probabilities are rounded as recorded. A score S summarizes threshold flags and is not necessarily the fraction of verified decoding errors. The table is illustrative and does not estimate failure-mode frequencies.

Across the seven Qwen configurations, the fraction of selected stored failing specimens with entropy below 2 bits ranges from 14% to 74% (Appendix B). Some errors therefore occur under highly concentrated distributions, while others occur under diffuse distributions. These records support the existence of confident errors but do not support a universal claim that contextual errors are usually confident or never accompanied by uncertainty.

5 Embedding Associations and Prediction5.1 Scores and prediction costs

The geometric analysis asks whether the candidate population has a measurable relationship to a model’s glitch-reference set. Let e(t) be either an input-embedding row or an output-embedding row, and let N₅(t;G) contain the five reference tokens in G with the largest cosine similarity to t in that space. The proximity score is

A second score projects the input embedding onto the direction from the vocabulary mean to the mean of the glitch-reference embeddings. The proximity score represents a local neighborhood; the projection represents one global direction. Neither score requires a model forward pass for a new token once the reference set and embeddings are available. Building a behaviorally screened reference set does require model evaluation, and its cost belongs in any end-to-end discovery comparison.

The fitted prediction analysis compares four feature tiers. The surface baseline uses token ID, decoded character length, leading-space status, alphabetic status, and ASCII status. Static features comprise input and output row norms and centroid distances, nearest-neighbor similarities, a direct input-output self-score and competitor margin, and the glitch-direction projection. The static tier as evaluated does not include the five-neighbor glitch-proximity score. Dynamic features summarize the target-position representation over half of the contexts, including its dispersion, norm, and alignment with the target’s output row. Behavioral features use copying measurements from those contexts.

The contextual and behavioral tiers predict the candidate label on the other half of the contexts. The reported fitted results use out-of-fold L2-regularized logistic regression and paired bootstrap comparisons with the surface baseline. Thus, the dynamic and behavioral tiers require forward passes and are not weight-only screens. Half-bank labels also produce different positive counts from the full-bank screening table.

5.2 Association with the glitch reference class

Figure 1 and Appendix B report proximity separately for the input and output spaces. Selecting the better of the two spaces for each model gives an AUROC range of 0.744 to 0.881 across the seven configurations reported as having untied embeddings. This is a descriptive, model-wise selection of the better space, not the performance of one prespecified score applied uniformly to all models. We also retain the weaker values on Qwen3-1.7 B.

Figure 1. Geometric association with the contextual candidate label. Points and horizontal bars show the reported proximity AUROC and 95% bootstrap interval in each embedding space. Crosses show the token-ID score. The line at 0.5 marks chance ranking. The model-wise choice of the stronger space is descriptive. Table B1 reports sample counts and the remaining geometric scores.

The informative space varies by model. On OLMo-2‑7B, input proximity gives 0.846 and output proximity 0.528. Qwen2.5‑72B shows the reverse pattern, with 0.685 and 0.798. A global direction is not always sufficient: its AUROC on Qwen2.5‑72B is 0.599. Conversely, Qwen3‑32B’s direction score, 0.898, exceeds either proximity score. The results support model-dependent geometric associations rather than a universal geometric form.

Replacing the glitch-reference set with a random stable set of the same size gives mean AUROCs of 0.41 to 0.55 over ten draws. This comparison shows that arbitrary stable reference sets do not reproduce the reported ranking. It does not isolate glitch proximity from other competing explanations, including rarity, local embedding density, or how the reference set was selected. In particular, the token-ID baseline exceeds both proximity scores on Qwen2.5‑72B and Qwen3‑235B.

The Qwen3‑1.7B results are insufficient to infer an effect of weight tying. Only one tied configuration is included, and the reported input- and output-proximity scores differ despite its tied-weight description. That discrepancy prevents a clean architectural interpretation of this row.

5.3 Projected distribution of contextual candidates

Contextual candidates extend beyond the visible concentrations of the glitch-reference class. Figure 2 shows UMAP projections of the output-embedding rows using cosine distance (McInnes et al., 2018). In Qwen3‑1.7B, Qwen3.8‑27B, and Qwen3‑235B, red candidate points appear throughout substantial portions of the gray population while black reference points remain comparatively concentrated. Qwen2.5‑7B and OLMo-2‑7B show both candidates near reference concentrations and candidates among the gray points. These patterns describe the plotted candidate population under the probability screen in Section 3.3.

Figure 2. Contextual candidates in projected output-embedding space. Gray shows the screened background; red denotes candidates passing the isolation gate with S ≥ 0.10; black denotes the model-specific glitch-reference class (Section 3.4). Panels retain the original projection coordinates and are arranged in model order. Orientations and scales vary by panel. Colors encode screening and reference labels, not independent verification of every plotted candidate.

Li et al. (2024, Figure 4 and Section 5) report that glitch tokens tend to cluster in embedding space and use this observation to motivate GlitchHunter’s iterative graph clustering. Our projections raise a question about the scope of that characterization: does the geometry of a glitch-reference class also describe contextual candidates that pass an isolation probe? The dispersed red points suggest that the visible reference concentrations incompletely describe this conditional population.

Tang et al. (2026, Section 6.1) also report clustering, supported by Euclidean-distance and entropy comparisons on Llama2‑7B-chat and Mistral2‑7B-it, and associate it with insufficient embedding differentiation. Their account concerns the input embedding layer described in Section 2.1. Our cosine-based output-embedding projections therefore do not directly test that explanation. For untied models, evaluate the input and output matrices separately; a dispersed output projection alone cannot establish that input embeddings lack the reported crowding.

This observation is compatible with the proximity associations in Section 5.2. A population can occupy several regions while retaining useful local similarity to reference tokens. An informative ranking score therefore does not require a visibly separate candidate cluster. UMAP also changes density and can introduce apparent separations (UMAP developers, n.d.), so the panels do not rule out clustering in the original space.

These projections motivate comparing geometric characterization across detection protocols. Our reference sets follow Section 3.4 and are not outputs of GlitchHunter or GlitchQuiz. A direct test would compare original-space neighborhoods and contextual-failure coverage on the same checkpoints, with matched embedding spaces and metrics, independently verified errors, and labels from each assessment.

5.4 Incremental value beyond surface features

Table 6 compares the fitted tiers on held-out context-half labels. Static features have a positive improvement interval over surface features on Qwen2.5‑7B, OLMo-2‑7B, and Flash-Next. They do not improve on the other five models, and the interval is negative on Qwen2.5‑72B. Table B2 reports the corresponding intervals.

Table 6. Out-of-fold AUROC for predicting the held-out context-half candidate label. The positive count is defined on the held-out half. Static, dynamic, and behavioral columns denote the reported feature tiers relative to the surface baseline. These targets are probability-screen labels, not independently verified argmax-error labels.

Dynamic features improve on surface features with intervals excluding zero on five models: OLMo-2‑7B, Qwen3.8‑27B, Qwen2.5‑72B, Flash-Next, and Qwen3‑235B. This supports a relationship between contextual representations and susceptibility beyond the particular surface baseline. It does not imply that a representation-based procedure is cheaper than directly measuring copying under the same contexts.

The behavioral tier reaches AUROC 0.945 to 1.000. These results agree with the split-half correlations: observing a token in some contexts effectively predicts its screening label in other contexts from the same construction process. They provide evidence for repeatability, but the labels and features share a copying task and context distribution. Performance under new natural-text distributions remains unmeasured.

A geometric pre-screen is therefore plausible for prioritizing contextual testing, but the present results do not establish high-precision discovery at a fixed testing budget. AUROC measures ranking, not the precision of a selected shortlist. Demonstrating practical discovery would require a frozen score and reference set, disjoint candidates, a fixed verification budget, and comparisons with random, token-ID, and existing-detector selection under the same behavioral outcome.

6 Preservation in Generation and Tasks6.1 Free generation and identity metrics

Free-generation probes ask whether the model retains a supplied token while describing or responding to it. The OLMo experiment requests exact identification and an explanation, followed by the assistant prefix Let me think about this carefully. Other configurations use the token as the user turn under the model’s chat template. Outputs are generated for up to 256 tokens. These framing differences are part of the protocol and preclude treating the resulting counts as a controlled scale comparison.

Two reproduction metrics are needed. The exact-ID metric asks whether the seed ID occurs anywhere in the generated IDs. The string metric asks whether the decoded seed string occurs anywhere in the output, allowing a different segmentation. Neither alone establishes correct identification or exact reproduction of an entire requested sequence. For Qwen2.5‑72B, for example, none of the 32 worst-isolation seeds reappear as their original IDs, while 12 reappear as strings. A seed such as _ghost can be written using multiple output tokens.

Table C1 reports candidate-versus-control reproduction for the configurations with available generation. The candidate string-preservation rate is lower than the control rate in four of five comparisons and equal on Qwen3‑32B. Exact-ID rates are less consistent: Qwen2.5‑7B ties, and Qwen3‑32B reproduces 8 of 14 candidates versus 7 of 14 controls. A candidate can also be reproduced while being misidentified. These outcomes support task-dependent vulnerability rather than a universal inability to emit the candidate token.

The 32 worst-isolation seeds used in separate generation probes are not interchangeable with context-screened glitch references. On Flash-Next, a teacher-forced check of these seeds assigns the expected token probability at least 0.5 in 71% of 768 cells, whereas the analogous rate on Qwen3‑235B is 0.1%. This disagreement is another reason to verify the behavior of a reference set in the relevant context.

I did not run free generation, task probes, or specimen continuations on the two FP8 mixtures because the evaluation stack took about seven seconds per generated token, and I ran this with my own money; I would prefer not to go bankrupt. Their next-token observations must not be read as generated reasoning traces. We also did not run candidate-free generation on Qwen2.5‑72B.

6.2 Instructions requiring lexical preservation

Five instruction templates require the model to preserve the target string: name a Python function, quote a document title, return a list item, correct spelling, and summarize while preserving proper nouns. Each class contributes ten selected tokens per model and five tasks, giving 50 episodes per class. Tokens are inserted by ID into the model’s chat template. Appendix C contains the full templates and per-task results.

The primary metric asks whether the answer contains the given token string. It is deliberately narrower than complete task correctness. It does not verify whether generated code is valid, whether a function name is a legal Python identifier, or whether a summary is faithful in other respects. The spelling task also invites normalization, so its preservation rate must be interpreted in light of its wording.

Table 7. Token-string preservation in simple instructions. Each row contains 50 episodes per class. C denotes selected contextual candidates, S stable controls, and G the model’s glitch-reference class. The reported interval for C − S is a bootstrap interval over episodes; repeated use of each token across tasks limits independence.

Candidates are preserved less frequently than controls in all five configurations. The episode-bootstrap intervals exclude zero for OLMo-2‑7B, Qwen3.8‑27B, and both Qwen3‑32B modes, but not for Qwen2.5‑7B. Coarse task completion is reported at 0.96 to 1.00 while lexical preservation varies, illustrating why successful-looking task structure is insufficient for this measurement.

The transcripts make the discrepancy concrete. Asked for a function named according, OLMo-2‑7B writes sum_list. In the spelling template, it changes according to correct. Asked for the second item when the target is NSLocalizedString, it returns LocalizableString. Qwen3‑32B changes realtà to reality in the spelling task. These examples preserve much of the requested task form while altering the designated content.

6.3 Simulated tool interactions

The tool experiment uses five assignments involving a target term: investigate a configuration key, prepare a background note, recommend whether to adopt a technology, explain a term, or check a release. Models can call search, open_page, and run_python for up to six rounds. Ten tokens per class again produce 50 episodes per configuration.

The environment is constructed around the supplied token. A search containing its string returns relevant documentation, release notes, and an issue page. Other searches return no relevant hits and generic material. This design isolates whether the target reaches a tool call, but it does not estimate retrieval failure in a natural search engine. Qwen models use their native tool templates; OLMo follows a textual protocol, which further limits cross-model comparisons.

Table 8. Preservation during simulated tool use. Values are the fractions of 50 episodes in which the target string appears. Intervals are the reported episode-bootstrap intervals for C − S. Plain and thinking configurations are shown separately.

Qwen3‑32B in plain mode preserves stable targets in 96% of first queries and final answers. Candidates appear in 74% of first queries and 68% of final answers. The glitch-reference targets appear in neither measure in any of the 50 episodes. Some responses proceed from generic retrieved material after the term disappears or changes in the first query.

Qwen3.8‑27B has a similar first-query contrast but a different completion pattern. In plain mode, glitch episodes finish within the round limit in 14% of cases, versus 66% for stable controls and 58% for candidates. Identical tool calls recur in 28%, 10%, and 14% of cases, respectively. Thinking mode changes these completion rates and also changes the stable baseline. These results show that losing a target can lead to either a completed generic answer or repeated tool use, depending on the configuration.

The experiment does not establish widespread fabrication of specific retrieved facts. The recorded version-number fabrication rates are only 0.00 to 0.02 per class and configuration, with isolated nonzero cells in both glitch and control-related groups (Table C4). The clearer measured effect is loss of the literal target in a query or answer. The selected token sets, repeated templates, and constructed environment limit generalization to autonomous systems operating on natural tasks.

6.4 A negative result on natural entity names

A separate experiment evaluates 1,255 real code identifiers and proper nouns in a natural task. Adding the fragility of constituent tokens does not improve prediction of an incorrect entity name after controlling for entity rarity, constituent-token isolation scores, and the model probability of the complete entity. The reported change in AUROC is −0.001, with a 95% interval of [−0.008, +0.006].

This result limits the practical interpretation of the synthetic task findings. The current evidence does not establish that the contextual score explains natural entity-name errors beyond these existing predictors. It also does not show that rarity causes either outcome, or that every possible relationship between token fragility and hallucination has been excluded. The appropriate conclusion is that this experiment shows no incremental predictive power.

7 Auxiliary Analyses7.1 Pair interactions and repetition

A factorial copying experiment tests whether pairs of tokens produce damage beyond the contributions of their members. Carriers contain two slots at separations 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128, with two independent filler sequences at each separation. Each ordered pair is evaluated in four conditions: both targets, either target with a control, and two controls. The interaction contrast subtracts the two single-target scores from the joint score and adds the control score.

The screen uses an additive fit within each carrier, standardized residuals, within-carrier permutations, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q = 0.05 (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995). Its declared count criterion compares the number of rejected pairs with the 95th percentile from twenty simulated additive-null datasets. No tested pool exceeds that criterion: the rejected-pair counts are 1 of 4,032 for each OLMo pool, 13 of 1,190 for Qwen3‑32B, and 1 of 2,256 for Qwen3‑235B (Appendix D).

This finding is narrower than the absence of interaction. The maximum-statistic tests are significant for the OLMo pools and Qwen3‑32B, while Qwen3‑235B has p = 0.059. The two criteria assess different aspects of the interaction distribution and must both be retained. Mean repeated-token contrasts are positive in the reported tests, consistent with facilitation in these carriers. Neither result establishes universal additivity, the absence of rare harmful combinations, or a causal account based on induction.

7.2 Recoverability of token identity

The Pythia-1.4B experiment places 36 verified glitch tokens and 1,088 controls at the ends of eight contexts. At each layer, the model matches a token’s contextual state to its state in another context within a pool of 1,124 candidates, after removing the component shared within each context. Biderman et al. (2023) describe Pythia.

Identity-matching accuracy is 1.000 for glitch tokens from the embedding layer through layer 12 and 0.988 to 1.000 for controls. At the final layer it is 0.880 and 0.874, respectively. These results show that substantial token-identity information remains recoverable under the chosen comparison procedure. A logit-lens example also favors a continuation of a glitch token, idepress followed by ant, rather than reproduction of the input token itself.

Decodability does not causally localize copying failure. The experiment does not show that the model uses the recoverable information in the copying computation, that identity is perfectly preserved, or that the output layer alone causes the error. It also concerns independently labeled glitch tokens on Pythia rather than the full candidate population in the eight-model study. Causal interventions would be needed to distinguish inadequate readout, context-dependent competition, and other explanations.

8 Discussion and Limitations

The principal finding is a repeatable distinction between isolated copying success and contextual susceptibility. Shared context banks make it possible to estimate a per-token tendency without selecting an adversarial context for each token. Actual decoded examples establish that at least some of these discrepancies are literal copying errors, and the task experiments show that selected candidates can lose their identity beyond the copying template. Embedding associations connect this population to prior glitch-token research, while their variable incremental value prevents treating geometry as a complete explanation or a validated universal detector.

Several limits determine the scope of that conclusion. First, the aggregate candidate class is defined by a probability threshold whose relationship to true decoding error is incomplete. Strict-gate results and inspected continuations strengthen the case for the phenomenon, but they do not replace a population-wide argmax-error analysis. A revised behavioral prevalence estimate must retain both the isolation outcome and contextual output identity for each cell.

Second, the common-word carriers are artificial, and the model-dependent prompt framing affects what is measured. Direct ID insertion controls the experimental identity of the target but can create inputs unlike normal tokenizer output. String-preservation tasks partially address this concern, yet the study's strongest natural-entity test is negative after existing controls. There is no basis here to extrapolate candidate prevalence to everyday text or to treat a score as a context-independent property of a token.

Third, eight copying configurations span only Qwen and OLMo, with differing precision and architecture. The auxiliary Pythia probe addresses another question. Generation coverage is incomplete, and some task classes contain only ten selected tokens. Episode-level bootstrap intervals do not fully account for dependence among five tasks using the same token. The reported intervals should therefore be read as descriptive evidence, with token-clustered or hierarchical uncertainty estimates needed for stronger population inference.

Fourth, the geometric analyses evaluate associations with screen labels. Reference construction partly uses contextual behavior, and selection of the stronger embedding space is retrospective. Random stable references do not provide a rarity-matched or density-matched null. Static feature improvements occur on three models, while several token-ID baselines are already strong. The UMAP panels provide qualitative evidence about the plotted population; they do not measure original-space cluster coverage. No fixed-budget prospective discovery experiment or common-oracle comparison with the existing detectors is reported.

Finally, the study does not identify which ordinary context will trigger a particular token’s error. Split-half prediction estimates average susceptibility under related context banks. Small context main effects do not eliminate token-context interactions, and the factorial experiment retains significant maximum-statistic results. Neither recoverable identity nor geometric proximity establishes a training mechanism. The evidence supports a measurement target and a set of associations; mechanistic explanation and context-specific prediction remain open.

The most direct methodological extension is to freeze the isolation test, candidate score, reference construction, and context distribution before evaluation on disjoint data. Reporting target-position argmax error, full-sequence copying accuracy, and exact-string preservation alongside probability scores would connect screening sensitivity to observable failures. For discovery claims, precision and recall at a fixed verification budget would provide a more practical test than retrospective AUROC alone.

9 Reproducibility and Reporting Scope

Reproduction requires the model and tokenizer revisions, sampled token IDs, complete context IDs and insertion slots, prompt framing, thresholds, precision, and scoring code. The procedure does not modify model weights. Appendix A provides public model identifiers and textual prompts; the run-specific matrices and environment metadata described in Section 3.4 are also necessary. Figure 2 additionally requires the plotted IDs and class masks, embedding preprocessing, UMAP parameters, and random seeds. Generation coverage is limited to the configurations explicitly listed in the corresponding tables.

Analysis populations differ. Table 3 reports 296, 418, and 684 candidates for Qwen2.5‑7B, Qwen2.5‑72B, and Qwen3‑235B, while Table B1 reports 294, 417, and 682. Each analysis retains its associated counts. Half-bank prediction counts differ again because their labels use different contexts. Reconciling the remaining sample transitions exactly requires the underlying token manifests and exclusion masks.

The recorded protocol includes amendments to the isolation gate, sample size, printable-seed filtering, and string-level reproduction scoring. Vocabulary sampling follows embedding-row counts, so padding reduces token-ID overlap between Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 samples. Matched-ID scaling within Qwen2.5 remains untested. These sampling and framing decisions form part of the experimental specification and constrain cross-model interpretation.

10 Conclusion

FragileTokens studies contextual copying vulnerability among tokens that pass an isolation probe. Across eight configurations, screening scores are reproducible and decoded specimens confirm errors. Geometric proximity often ranks candidates above controls, with gains that vary across surface features. Selected candidates also show reduced lexical preservation in several tasks, while the natural-entity test finds no added predictive value. These findings support contextual verification and motivate direct evaluation of behavioral prevalence, prospective discovery, and individual triggering contexts.

Values originally reported as 0.000 are displayed as <0.001 to avoid implying an exact zero probability; the underlying permutation resolution is required for more precise reporting.

Table D2. Mean joint copy score and interaction by ordered pair type. R denotes reliable and I intermittent. These means summarize the mixed pools; positive mean interactions do not rule out negative individual interactions.

The repeated-token OLMo contrast is reported as +0.005 at separation 2 and +0.018 at separation 128. In the mixed-pool carrier failures, five OLMo tokens account for 47% of failing carriers and five Qwen3‑32B tokens for 57%. This concentration motivates token-level susceptibility as a useful summary, while failures that do not recur across filler sequences also demonstrate the limits of interpreting that summary as context independence.

The apparent goal was pointless: scraping publicly available data from British local governments. OpenAI reportedly never told those affected. items.title: Support for Unions Is Spiking as AI Threatens Jobs
items.summary: As the triple-threat of AI-fueled unemployment, rampant inflation, and further erosion of workers’ rights take their toll, US workers are throwing their support behind a long-neglected institution: labor unions. According to a new survey by polling firm Gallup, a full 47 percent of Americans now say they want unions to have more influence than they do today. That’s up from 43 percent in 2023 and a dismal 25 percent in 2009 — setting, per Gallup, a new record for the 21st century. At the same time, the percentage of Americans harboring anti-labor sentiment — those who want unions to have even “less influence” than they do today — have also set a record for the new millennium, reaching just 23 percent. Even that share is shrinking, though: i t’s down from 26 percent in 2023, and is nearly half the record 21st century highs of 42 percent, set in 2009. What’s more, overall “approval” of labor unions has reached a whopping 71 percent, on par with Gallup’s polling from May of 1965, a period marked by an unrecognizably strong fervor for labor protections — but also the beginning of the long decline of organized labor in the US. Yet despite similar pro-labor attitudes, the differences between 1965 and 2026 could not be more pronounced. At that point some 60 years ago, nearly one in three Americans belonged to a union, compared to just one in ten in 2025. According to data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the volume of work stoppages grew steadily throughout the 1960s, with the average duration of all worker-led shutdowns peaking at a whopping 25 days in 1965. But union militancy didn’t become what it was through popular sentiment alone. It took decades of organizing and hard-won concessions in the face of rising industrialization, a cause for which many everyday workers selflessly dedicated their lives with no guarantee of success. Sure enough, the decades following the 1960s were characterized by a major drop-off in union power, as both union activity and popular support began to wane. Now, years of de-industrialization — economic policy now culminating in the rising threat of AI automation — have forced workers onto their heels , as once-ardent labor groups capitulate to pro-business forces . But it doesn’t have to remain this way. If the broad collective of US workers can tap into the long-forgotten legacy of the 20th century labor movement, it could mean the revival of union militancy, and for some, possibly one last chance to carve out protections against an automated future through workplace organizing. items.title: Mercury Is Shrinking Way Faster Than We Thought, Scientists Discover
items.summary: Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that got dumped, went high, shrank in size, and got the blues. First, you’ve heard of getting a feather in your cap, but what about a feather in some crap? That’s the upshot of a new study about rare bird remains found in dino doodoo. Then: a walk on titanosaur eggshells, the contractions of Mercury, and a luxe fishpond painting. As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens , or subscribe to my personal newsletter the BeX Files . Birds of a feather are pooped out together O'Connor, Jingmai et al. “Bird feathers from a Late Cretaceous coprolite.” Current Biology. Some 66 million years ago, a bird ate a fish, and then a dinosaur—perhaps a T. rex —ate that bird. Subsequent to these events, the dinosaur took a dump. Time passed. The poop fossilized. A space rock hit Earth and wiped out most life. Fast forward to 2016, when the dino dookie was unearthed at the Hell Creek Formation in Montana, complete with exquisitely-preserved feathers from the bird, and fish scales from its last meal. This incredible story is reported by scientists who have spent years studying the fossilized feces, known as a coprolite, with advanced imaging techniques. By sheer luck, this fossil contains extremely rare feathers from the Late Cretaceous, including “arguably the best-preserved feather ever recovered from Mesozoic lithic deposits,” according to the study. A feather found in poop. Image: Credit: O’Connor et al “Here we report on an exceptionally preserved three-dimensional pennaceous feather preserved in a medium-sized theropod dinosaur coprolite,” said researchers led by Jingmai O’Connor of the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago. The specimen “begins to fill in a critical gap in our understanding of feather morphology in the Late Cretaceous.” The fossil record contains some feathers from extinct birds, pterosaurs, and dinosaurs, which can be found etched into stone or encased in amber. But hardly any feathers from the final days of the age of dinosaurs, the Late Cretaceous, have survived. This gap in the record has stymied efforts to explain why only one family of birds, the Neornithes, survived the Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) extinction event to become the ancestors of all modern birds. Concept art of a theropod eating a bird eating a fish. Turtles look on. Image: Andrey Atuchin Sometimes the answer to profound existential questions is hidden in unexpected places, like a very old piece of poop. O’Connor and her colleagues determined that the coprolite contains the first known feathers from a family of aquatic birds known as hesperornithiformes, which did not survive the asteroid impact. The team speculate that the birds’ plumage might have been less efficient at insulating the birds compared to Neornithean feathers, dooming the former lineage to death. “These primitive plumaceous morphotypes may have been less effective for trapping air, resulting in extinction during the asteroid-induced impact winter largely responsible for the K-Pg mass extinction,” the researchers said. The whole sequence of events reminds me of an infamous scene in Jurassic World in which a woman is captured by a pterosaur that is then swallowed by a giant mosasaur. I shudder to imagine what that coprolite would look like. In other news… If you want to make a titanosaur omelette… Tanaka, Kohei et al. “Titanosaur eggshells from the latest Cretaceous of Patagonia, Argentina: implications for nesting at high latitude.” Royal Society Open Science. What a treat—there is even more breaking news from the Late Cretaceous! Paleontologists have discovered a clutch of fossilized titanosaur eggs at the Chorrillo Formation of Patagonia, shedding new light on the breeding behaviors of the largest animals ever to walk on land. The biggest titanosaurs tipped the scales at 70 metric tonnes—as heavy as the Space Shuttle, or ten African elephants in a trenchcoat—and they exceeded 120 feet in length. (If you ever visit the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, I recommend checking out the scale model of a titanosaur to behold the sheer spectacle of these extinct behemoths.) Closeup of surface of eggshell from Fusioolithus oosp. from the Chorrillo Formation, southernmost Patagonia. Image: Tanaka, Kohei et al. But even heavyweights start small; titanosaur hatchlings weighed in at six to eight pounds, on par with human newborns. Most of their eggshells have been discovered at low latitudes, suggesting that the animals preferred to lay their young in warm regions with maximum sunlight to aid incubation. But the new specimens were laid in a cool climate at unprecedented latitudes, around 55 to 60°S, and were likely buried under vegetation and warmed by microbial activity above them. “These eggshells provide, to our knowledge, the first indication that titanosaurs nested at relatively high latitudes,” said researchers led by Kohei Tanaka of the University of Tsukuba “The eggs…would have been incubated in nests buried by nesting materials and would have used the heat generated by decaying vegetation” in order to nest in habitats “where sufficient heat from solar radiation was probably unavailable.” Poopy feathers from the North and the eggshells of giants from the South?What a bounty of global offerings from the orifices of long-lost dinosaurs. A shrinking planetary violet Nishiyama, Gaku et al. “Underestimation of Planetary Contraction due to 2 Obscuration by Surface Roughness: The Case of 3 Mercury.” Geophysical Research Letters. Mercury is the solar system’s smallest planet, with a surface area roughly comparable to the size of the Indian Ocean. But scientists have discovered that the planet was much bigger at its birth, with a radius that may have been anywhere from four to six miles longer than it is today. While it has long been known that Mercury has shrunk as it cooled over time, the extent of this “planetary contraction” may have been “underestimated by 10–30 percent,” according to a new study. By examining updated maps of the planet’s surface, scientists noticed that the rocky wrinkles left by its contraction, known as “shortening structures,” are not evenly distributed across its terrain, as predicted by models. The team realized that the messy fallout left over from impacts on the planet, known as “ejecta,” is obscuring a lot of these shortening structures, leading to previous underestimates of its shrinkage. Mercury’s pockmarked surface. Image: NASA “Our correction for Mercury’s radial contraction provides new insights into the planet’s thermal evolution” and “has a wide range of implications for the interior structure of the planet,” said researchers led by Gaku Nishiyama of the German Aerospace Center. Fortunately, the mercurial nature of this world will be explored in more detail by BepiColombo, a European-Japanese space mission that is currently on track to scooch into orbit around the planet this November. Though this is the only planet in the solar system to be outranked by mere moons—Jupiter’s Ganymede and Saturn’s Titan are both bigger than Mercury—it still has plenty of big secrets left to spill. Out of the Egyptian blue Dilaria, Simone et al. “An Uncommon Instance of Egyptian Blue in the “Pigmented Intonachino” of the Fishpond Wall Painting From the Roman Villa of Torre di Pordenone (Northeast Italy).” Archaeometry. To close, let’s step back in time 2,000 years to visit a luxury villa decorated with ostentatious displays of wealth, including a captivating painting of a fishpond. This colorful artwork once adorned the wall of the “Torre di Pordenone,” a resplendent home near Friuli-Venezia-Giulia in northeast Italy, and which now survives only as puzzle-piece remnants. Scientists have now discovered that the painting included the famous pigment “Egyptian blue,” which is considered the world’s oldest synthetic hue, dating back at least 5,000 years. The pigment was deliberately mixed with lime "to obtain homogeneous, pale blue tones for the marine background” offering “a rare example of Roman ‘blue lime-painted mortar,’ according to a new study. The process of making the marine painted wall. Image: Dilaria, Simone et al. Apart from one other similar painting found at Tivoli, “the case of the Roman villa of Torre di Pordenone seems to represent a singular instance within the Roman wall painting production,” said researchers led by Simone Dilaria of the University of Padua, who added the pigment was “utilized with a notable degree of abundance, an ‘excess’ that permitted its direct incorporation into the mortar matrix itself.” “Beyond merely reflecting the immense wealth of the villa's owner, this scale of consumption of Egyptian blue at Torre prompts a reconsideration of the pigment's value, availability, and modes of use in antiquity,” the team said. “Ultimately, this evidence suggests that while Egyptian blue remained a valuable commodity, its supply in ancient markets was significantly more consistent and well established than traditionally assumed, with quantities sufficient to support large-scale, high-quality decorative programs.” While the full painting itself no longer survives, its fragments open a fascinating window into the luxury commodities of the era—and the timeless compulsion for the ultra-wealthy to splurge on flashy status symbols. Thanks for reading! See you next week.

Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that got dumped, went high, shrank in size, and got the blues.

First, you’ve heard of getting a feather in your cap, but what about a feather in some crap? That’s the upshot of a new study about rare bird remains found in dino doodoo. Then: a walk on titanosaur eggshells, the contractions of Mercury, and a luxe fishpond painting.

As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter the BeX Files. 

Birds of a feather are pooped out together

O'Connor, Jingmai et al. “Bird feathers from a Late Cretaceous coprolite.” Current Biology.

Some 66 million years ago, a bird ate a fish, and then a dinosaur—perhaps a T. rex—ate that bird. Subsequent to these events, the dinosaur took a dump. 

Time passed. The poop fossilized. A space rock hit Earth and wiped out most life. Fast forward to 2016, when the dino dookie was unearthed at the Hell Creek Formation in Montana, complete with exquisitely-preserved feathers from the bird, and fish scales from its last meal.

This incredible story is reported by scientists who have spent years studying the fossilized feces, known as a coprolite, with advanced imaging techniques. By sheer luck, this fossil contains extremely rare feathers from the Late Cretaceous, including “arguably the best-preserved feather ever recovered from Mesozoic lithic deposits,” according to the study.

A feather found in poop. Image: Credit: O’Connor et al

“Here we report on an exceptionally preserved three-dimensional pennaceous feather preserved in a medium-sized theropod dinosaur coprolite,” said researchers led by Jingmai O’Connor of the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago. The specimen “begins to fill in a critical gap in our understanding of feather morphology in the Late Cretaceous.” 

The fossil record contains some feathers from extinct birds, pterosaurs, and dinosaurs, which can be found etched into stone or encased in amber. But hardly any feathers from the final days of the age of dinosaurs, the Late Cretaceous, have survived. This gap in the record has stymied efforts to explain why only one family of birds, the Neornithes, survived the Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) extinction event to become the ancestors of all modern birds.

Concept art of a theropod eating a bird eating a fish. Turtles look on. Image: Andrey Atuchin

Sometimes the answer to profound existential questions is hidden in unexpected places, like a very old piece of poop. O’Connor and her colleagues determined that the coprolite contains the first known feathers from a family of aquatic birds known as hesperornithiformes, which did not survive the asteroid impact. The team speculate that the birds’ plumage might have been less efficient at insulating the birds compared to Neornithean feathers, dooming the former lineage to death.

“These primitive plumaceous morphotypes may have been less effective for trapping air, resulting in extinction during the asteroid-induced impact winter largely responsible for the K-Pg mass extinction,” the researchers said.

The whole sequence of events reminds me of an infamous scene in Jurassic World in which a woman is captured by a pterosaur that is then swallowed by a giant mosasaur. I shudder to imagine what that coprolite would look like.

In other news…

If you want to make a titanosaur omelette…

Tanaka, Kohei et al. “Titanosaur eggshells from the latest Cretaceous of Patagonia, Argentina: implications for nesting at high latitude.” Royal Society Open Science.

What a treat—there is even more breaking news from the Late Cretaceous! Paleontologists have discovered a clutch of fossilized titanosaur eggs at the Chorrillo Formation of Patagonia, shedding new light on the breeding behaviors of the largest animals ever to walk on land.

The biggest titanosaurs tipped the scales at 70 metric tonnes—as heavy as the Space Shuttle, or ten African elephants in a trenchcoat—and they exceeded 120 feet in length. (If you ever visit the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, I recommend checking out the scale model of a titanosaur to behold the sheer spectacle of these extinct behemoths.) 

Closeup of surface of eggshell from Fusioolithus oosp. from the Chorrillo Formation, southernmost Patagonia. Image: Tanaka, Kohei et al.

But even heavyweights start small; titanosaur hatchlings weighed in at six to eight pounds, on par with human newborns. Most of their eggshells have been discovered at low latitudes, suggesting that the animals preferred to lay their young in warm regions with maximum sunlight to aid incubation. But the new specimens were laid in a cool climate at unprecedented latitudes, around 55 to 60°S, and were likely buried under vegetation and warmed by microbial activity above them. 

“These eggshells provide, to our knowledge, the first indication that titanosaurs nested at relatively high latitudes,” said researchers led by Kohei Tanaka of the University of Tsukuba

“The eggs…would have been incubated in nests buried by nesting materials and would have used the heat generated by decaying vegetation” in order to nest in habitats “where sufficient heat from solar radiation was probably unavailable.”

Poopy feathers from the North and the eggshells of giants from the South?What a bounty of global offerings from the orifices of long-lost dinosaurs. 

A shrinking planetary violet

Nishiyama, Gaku et al. “Underestimation of Planetary Contraction due to 2 Obscuration by Surface Roughness: The Case of 3 Mercury.” Geophysical Research Letters.

Mercury is the solar system’s smallest planet, with a surface area roughly comparable to the size of the Indian Ocean. But scientists have discovered that the planet was much bigger at its birth, with a radius that may have been anywhere from four to six miles longer than it is today.

While it has long been known that Mercury has shrunk as it cooled over time, the extent of this “planetary contraction” may have been “underestimated by 10–30 percent,” according to a new study. By examining updated maps of the planet’s surface, scientists noticed that the rocky wrinkles left by its contraction, known as “shortening structures,” are not evenly distributed across its terrain, as predicted by models. 

The team realized that the messy fallout left over from impacts on the planet, known as “ejecta,” is obscuring a lot of these shortening structures, leading to previous underestimates of its shrinkage.  

Mercury’s pockmarked surface. Image: NASA

“Our correction for Mercury’s radial contraction provides new insights into the planet’s thermal evolution” and “has a wide range of implications for the interior structure of the planet,” said researchers led by Gaku Nishiyama of the German Aerospace Center.

Fortunately, the mercurial nature of this world will be explored in more detail by BepiColombo, a European-Japanese space mission that is currently on track to scooch into orbit around the planet this November. Though this is the only planet in the solar system to be outranked by mere moons—Jupiter’s Ganymede and Saturn’s Titan are both bigger than Mercury—it still has plenty of big secrets left to spill.

Out of the Egyptian blue

Dilaria, Simone et al. “An Uncommon Instance of Egyptian Blue in the “Pigmented Intonachino” of the Fishpond Wall Painting From the Roman Villa of Torre di Pordenone (Northeast Italy).” Archaeometry.

To close, let’s step back in time 2,000 years to visit a luxury villa decorated with ostentatious displays of wealth, including a captivating painting of a fishpond. This colorful artwork once adorned the wall of the “Torre di Pordenone,” a resplendent home near Friuli-Venezia-Giulia in northeast Italy, and which now survives only as puzzle-piece remnants. 

Scientists have now discovered that the painting included the famous pigment “Egyptian blue,” which is considered the world’s oldest synthetic hue, dating back at least 5,000 years. The pigment was deliberately mixed with lime "to obtain homogeneous, pale blue tones for the marine background” offering “a rare example of Roman ‘blue lime-painted mortar,’ according to a new study.

The process of making the marine painted wall. Image: Dilaria, Simone et al.

Apart from one other similar painting found at Tivoli, “the case of the Roman villa of Torre di Pordenone seems to represent a singular instance within the Roman wall painting production,” said researchers led by Simone Dilaria of the University of Padua, who added the pigment was “utilized with a notable degree of abundance, an ‘excess’ that permitted its direct incorporation into the mortar matrix itself.”

“Beyond merely reflecting the immense wealth of the villa's owner, this scale of consumption of Egyptian blue at Torre prompts a reconsideration of the pigment's value, availability, and modes of use in antiquity,” the team said. “Ultimately, this evidence suggests that while Egyptian blue remained a valuable commodity, its supply in ancient markets was significantly more consistent and well established than traditionally assumed, with quantities sufficient to support large-scale, high-quality decorative programs.”

While the full painting itself no longer survives, its fragments open a fascinating window into the luxury commodities of the era—and the timeless compulsion for the ultra-wealthy to splurge on flashy status symbols.

Thanks for reading! See you next week.

items.title: A developer emailed Claude Code's creator about AI slop. Boris Cherny wrote back.
items.summary: Boris Cherny shared his response to a developer worried about AI slop. Bloomberg/Getty Images A developer emailed Claude Code creator Boris Cherny that AI coding had created "friction." Cherny posted his full response to the engineer. The developer's job is to "hold the bar on code quality," Cherny wrote. Developers are worried about AI. The creator of Claude Code has a response. On Thursday, Anthropic's Boris Cherny posted an email a developer wrote to him on X. The email was titled: "What to do about slop?" Cherny wrote that he receives emails like this every day and that he tries to respond to as many as possible. It's no surprise that developers are reaching out to Cherny with their worries. AI has radically changed coding , shifting job descriptions and turning engineers into reviewers. Some engineers love the ease; others call it lonely and tedious . In the email, the unnamed developer wrote that the shift to AI coding was causing "friction." He broke it down into two views and asked Cherny to broker the dispute. The first view was a more restrained use of AI tools: We create code similar to before, accelerated by AI. We may not review all of it, but it should be reviewable. The person submitting the code should be able to explain it. It should be built in such a way to make it as easy to maintain — or easier — than before, by human agents. The second view was more permissive. This was the vibe coding position: We treat the code as a black box. We don't worry about it. We just check the output. The developer wrote that many people were incapable of doing option 1 — the more restrained approach — but worried about getting laid off . "A lot of people are just forcing it," they wrote. Cherny posted his response in full. As for the two options the developer provided, Cherny said there was room for both. On the "don't worry" approach: Prototypes and other throw-away code can be treated as totally black box. If you're going to throw it away anyway, and if the blast radius of it breaking is low, it doesn't need to be perfect. And, on cautious reviewing: Production code written by Claude should have a higher bar than if it was written by a human. At Anthropic, we have many guardrails in place to make sure this is happening: lots of lint rules, lots of tests, Claude-driven end to end tests, Claude-powered fuzzers running daily, automated code reviews and security reviews, automated code refactoring, and so on. Without these, you can end up with a mess that is hard to maintain down the line. Luckily, the model makes it increasingly easy to do these well — run a few daily routines, use Claude Code Review, etc. The developer's job is to "hold the bar on code quality," Cherny wrote. AI leaders use different terms for this role, such as " mini CEO ." It's the developer's job to act like a manager, stopping bad code in its tracks. If all else fails, Cherny said the developer could be more hands-on with Claude or ask it to rewrite the codebase. "Or, wait for the next model," he wrote.
