Ivan Apfel/Getty Images The 2,400-seat Miami theater lit up like a Coldplay concert when the QR code dropped at the Miss USA pageant . A sea of phones — held up by supportive parents, partners, and past pageant queens — trained their cameras on the massive barcode being projected from center stage, ready to vote for their favored contestant. Twelve minutes on the clock: The countdown was on. Fingers tapped rapidly as the audience used their free vote or purchased more in bundles — $50 for 50, $250 for 250, $500 for 500 — alongside viewers at home. The top 20 contestants' headshots shifted around the leaderboard as the votes tallied live on the pageant's website, revealing exactly how far each woman was from the top spot. Two minutes left on the clock, a banner flashed across: Now, votes counted double. As the seconds ticked closer to zero, the votes burst in like a flash flood. The gap between first and second place was 1,794 votes at the 36-second mark. When the clock struck zero, it was more than 14,000. Fans have never had more of a say at Miss USA — especially if they're willing to pay. At last month's pageant, paid voting helped determine three top 20 spots, while a fourth went to the contestant who sold the most Westgate Resorts vacation packages, an unprecedented incentive that tied a contestant's placement to sales for a pageant sponsor. The winner was determined by a panel of six judges, including a mix of Miss USA and Miss Universe winners , but fans also had the opportunity to vote for the top 10 as the "seventh judge." Nearly a dozen of this year's Miss USA contestants spoke to Business Insider about the changes. Some believe it's a savvy strategy by CEO Thom Brodeur , who took over the pageant in September 2025, to keep the business afloat and increase fan engagement, especially at a time when pageants struggle to remain relevant. Others worry the competition is turning into what one called a "pay-to-play" model, making it less accessible to women who don't have money or big social media followings. Nobody is arguing with Beyoncé or Taylor Swift's teams over the standing-room ticket prices of four-figures and higher, and we're not going to apologize either. Miss USA CEO Thom Brodeur "There's a lot of fatigue," Miss Arizona Kaitlyn Humphrey told Business Insider. "It's an expensive sport already, and it breaks my heart that a lot of people can't compete purely because there's such a barrier to entry in the financial aspect of things. And then we're just adding layers to that." The bygone days of network TV Bob Barker hosted the Miss USA 1972 pageant, which aired on CBS. Bettmann/Bettmann Archive Nearly 40 million people tuned in to watch Miss USA in the 1960s and '70s, but viewership dwindled over its 60 years on television. In 2023, the Miss USA final peaked at 1.1 million viewers on The CW. It was a far cry from its heyday, but still enough for a multiyear deal. The network ultimately dropped the pageant in 2025 amid fallout from former CEO Laylah Rose 's tenure, during which Miss USA 2023 Noelia Voigt and Miss Teen USA 2023 UmaSofia Srivastava relinquished their crowns due to her leadership. This year, the competition was set to return to The CW, but, as Business Insider first reported, the network dropped the show on August 20, a week before the final. Miss USA cited a "contractual issue with our production arrangements" and moved it to Queen Beauty Network, a streaming service focused on the pageant industry, where Brodeur is listed as vice president and chief marketing officer. When the crown was placed on Justus Kelley's head on August 27, making her the first married woman and mother to win the title , a live viewer counter on the Queen Beauty Network showed around 4,000 people watching. Shrinking viewership hasn't only affected Miss USA's ratings — it's put a serious dent in the pageant's coffers. Paula Shugart, who oversaw Miss USA from 2001 to 2020 as president of the Miss Universe Organization, told Business Insider that the pageant once received $3 to $5 million in licensing fees from the networks. Those days are gone. "Sharknado" star Ian Ziering and Miss USA 1993 Kenya Moore hosted the 2026 Miss USA finals. Ivan Apfel/Getty Images "Network television has completely changed," Shugart said. "You don't have the viewership, and you're not going to get the license fees that you used to get. You have to figure out different ways to pay for it and defray the costs." It's a reality that Brodeur knows well. "The days of 'free lunch' for pageants and pageant fans are over," he told Business Insider last week. "They've been over for some time. Introducing new revenue streams — whether that's through fan voting, contests, or other unique opportunities we're exploring — are the way this industry lives to see its next 75 years." Competing at Miss USA wasn't cheap to begin with, although the cost varies widely depending on who you ask. Contestants who spoke to Business Insider estimated costs ranging from $3,000 to $50,000. Brodeur compared the investment to that of any competitive sport. "There is nothing new under the sun about creating opportunities and spaces for all of us to exercise our God-given gifts in this world," he said. "Unfortunately, there are also costs attached to the creation of those opportunities and spaces, and that's the reality of life." A new way to engage fans Justus Kelley, who won Miss USA 2026, with Miss Florida Aileen Cerchiara and Miss Pennsylvania Elizabeth Voight during the finals. Ivan Apfel/Getty Images Traditionally, contestants make it to Miss USA by winning a state pageant. Those are organized and funded by individual directors, who pay the organization a franchise fee. Contestants must live, work, or study in the state for at least 90 days prior to the competition and are allowed to compete in two state pageants a year. When Brodeur took over as CEO , he had five weeks to put on the Miss USA 2025 pageant . Some departed state directors had not been replaced, and eight states were missing titleholders. His solution: an open casting call in which women from any state could apply for a state title. Five judges selected the titleholders. This year, 16 states were left without directors. Brodeur said only the Miss Universe Organization can legally issue franchise agreements to new state directors, so the open casting call returned — this time with fans getting a say. Before the applicants could be seen by a judging panel of former Miss USA winners , they had to make it through three rounds of fan voting over the course of a month. People could use a daily free vote or purchase bundles that ranged from $4.99 for 10 votes to $499 for 2,000 votes on a third-party website. The votes did not roll over from round to round, so each contestant started each round back at square one. "It was crazy," said Amber Uhler, who was selected to represent Michigan through the casting call. "I had to get everyone I knew to put in paid votes for me. [I said], 'If you were ever going to buy me a Christmas gift, just make it this.'" Miss USA split the 16 states into two casting calls. Women who didn't get selected in the first, which ran from May 20 to June 30, were automatically entered into the second, from June 29 to July 28. That meant some women were campaigning for votes for two months. Malory Hudson, who has competed at 12 Miss USA state pageants since 2017, was one of them. "I love competing, but I hated this open casting call," said Hudson, who did not make it through the judges' panel. "There was just anxiety every single day. You have to post so much, and it's exhausting." Other contestants, like Uhler, enjoyed the process because it "made it more fun" as people were invested in the contestants' journeys. Jordyn Owen, who won Miss Colorado through the open call, said it brought "a lot more buzz and attention" to Miss USA. "Last year, it was completely anonymous. No one knew if you submitted in the open call or not," she added. "Having it be very public this year, I actually kind of liked it because it did make it feel a little bit more invested." Brodeur said that the multiple rounds of voting were designed to engage fans and give contestants the "absolute best chance and most opportunity for their fans to advance them into the final judging round." "We recognize that both open casting and fan voting are 'new ways' of thinking about and approaching this journey in pageantry," he added. "Not everything that is innovative is accepted universally right away." Some contestants worried that the process was a barrier for women who didn't have generous sponsors via their family, friends, or followers. Uhler said her family spent $4,000 to $5,000 in votes during the last round; Hudson said she had a sponsor who bought around $30,000 worth of votes. Brodeur disputed that the new fan voting made Miss USA less accessible, saying nearly 70% of the open-call winners advanced with a "much higher ratio of free votes from their fans than paid votes." "There are two types of competitors in this sport," he said. "The first… has such a deeply engaged fan base she could repeatedly encourage her fans to 'vote for me for free' and she advanced. The other was the candidate who wasn't afraid to seek the financial support of her friends, family, and fans to drive their participation." "How is this any different than Instagram and TikTok influencers monetizing their content or their 'journeys/stories' through fans on behalf of the brands they're repping?" he added. "It's absolutely the same process." Brodeur said the open casting call is here to stay for at least another year. "As we work through this next season's contract process, we are likely going to be forced to execute a similar strategy as we did during this last cycle," he added. The People's Choice(s) Contestants rush to hug Justus Kelley after she is crowned Miss USA 2026. Ivan Apfel/Getty Images The campaign for votes wasn't over after the open casting call. Next, contestants had to go through People's Choice, which let fans vote for their favorite among all 51 Miss USA 2026 contestants. As with the casting call, fans could use a daily free vote or purchase them in bundles. Most pageants — including Miss Universe and Miss America — have traditionally allocated one spot in the semifinals for the contestant who receives the most fan votes. Under Brodeur's leadership, that single spot in Miss USA's top 20 expanded to four in 2025, and three this year. It's been a controversial decision among contestants, including Miss Kansas Madilynn Becker, who won this year's People's Choice award with Miss Louisiana Ella Clark and Miss Colorado's Owen. "People's Choice is a path, but it's almost like the shortcut, in a sense," said Becker. "I think I would have felt even more proud if I got in on my own merit." "I would love to see the voting become a free thing because, essentially, it comes down to who has the most money to champion for them," said Miss California Acacia McBride. A screenshot shows the prices for the top 10 fan voting after the two-minute mark. Screenshot via The 7th Judge by Miss USA Brodeur said he expanded the number of People's Choice contestants to give fans a larger say. "One of the rallying cries for the better part of a decade has been, 'We want more of a voice in who makes it and where,'" he added. He said that's why fans were also given the chance to vote for the top 10 on finals night. The Miss USA website said these votes were "combined into a seventh score and counted with the judges' six when the top 10 is decided." Brodeur confirmed that the fan voting counted as 14% of the contestants' overall score. While a number of contestants who spoke to Business Insider thought the voting was a great way to keep the audience engaged, comparing it to the real-time voting on "Love Island" or "Dancing with the Stars," others were surprised to learn that fans could purchase votes. "It definitely stirred up a lot of feelings backstage," Arizona's Humphrey said. "Some of the girls have different financial situations than others, and you feel like things are getting ripped away from you for factors that you can't control, and we've already spent so much money to be there." Tens of thousands of votes poured in, but, in the end, the three women who received the most votes — Humphrey, Miss Louisiana Ella Clark, and Miss Montana Lisbeth Fernández — did not advance to the top 10. "I feel very blessed to know that I have a big audience that is willing to show up for me," said Fernández, who received the most votes. "But at the end of the day, the judges are the ones who make the ultimate call." Parents and pageant fans tossed around the phrase "money grab" throughout the weeklong 2026 competition in Miami. Brodeur said the organization made "five or six figures" from fan voting but declined to share an exact number. He also noted that some revenue from fan voting was used to fund new cash prizes — ranging from $3,500 to $15,000 — for every contestant who made it into the top five. The salary for this year's Miss USA winner also increased to $150,000; it was $75,000 in 2025. "There were a lot of different aspects where I was like, 'OK, you have to pay to play,'" said McBride. "However, I do think, on the flip side of that, incorporating the cash prizes and the salary balanced it out." A new top 20 incentive The top 20 at Miss USA 2026. Ivan Apfel/Getty Images An additional top 20 spot was reserved for the contestant who sold the most Westgate Resorts vacation packages: $99 for a two-night stay at one of six US properties. Miss USA announced the new partnership in April. Brodeur told Business Insider that it was a way to tap into what he calls "one of the largest micro and nano-influencer networks of women aged 14 to 45 in the United States." Some women dove headfirst, traveling to a Westgate property to film Instagram content. Fernández, who secured the "Westgate Brand Ambassador" title, said she sold almost 200 packages and will now have the opportunity to interview for a six-figure position at the company. "A lot of the girls were focused on the People's Choice, but I really didn't give it any thought at all because I wanted to win the 'Westgate Brand Ambassador,'" she told Business Insider. "I put my selling skills in action, and I promoted that all over with my friends, family, and community. I also sold some corporate packages." Uhler, who estimates she sold 103 packages, was also a fan of the incentive. Although she didn't make it into the top 20, she appreciated that Miss USA offered a new avenue for contestants to advance. "It's great that you can work hard and earn something rather than just, you know, being the prettiest, or having the best walk, or having the best body," she added. "I don't think that I have any of those things, but you almost can't outwork me — except for this time, someone did! I really thought I was going to nail it with 100." Some contestants who spoke to Business Insider worried that the placement was out of reach for those without built-in social media followings. Others, like Miss USA 2004 Shandi Finnessey, didn't think it fit the brand. "I don't think they should be selling real estate," Finnessey said. "Miss USA is not a salesperson; she should be a spokeswoman." Brodeur said he believes that it's part of Miss USA's job to be a "brand ambassador, a salesperson, a spokesperson… for brands that are willing to test their skills and see who rises to the occasion." The $99 Westgate resort deal was also included in the $500 ticket for this year's Miss USA competition, a steeper price than in years past. One contestant said her parents spent $2,000 on tickets for the preliminary, final, and state costume shows this year. Others told their relatives to save their money and watch from home. "At the end of the day, I would rather my dad be in the stands than go on a vacation," Becker said. Miss USA 2025 Audrey Eckert onstage during the 2026 Miss USA pageant in Miami. Ivan Apfel/Getty Images Brodeur defended the cost, saying he wanted to "elevate the Miss USA brand." "We're not a high school musical production. We're not a prom or homecoming queen event," he said. "Nobody is arguing with Beyoncé or Taylor Swift's teams over the standing-room ticket prices of four-figures and higher, and we're not going to apologize either." Brodeur hopes the changes can catapult Miss USA into its next chapter after years of scandals. The challenge is proving to prospective contestants that there will be a return on their investment. Is it enough for Miss USA to be another influencer? The stage used to be a launching pad for stars like Halle Berry and Kenya Moore . Some pageant queens aren't convinced it still has that power. "Anyone these days can pick up your phone and go on TikTok," said Owen. "I'm not saying it's easy. It takes a lot to build followers and a brand, but what pageants used to have were a household name. Miss USA needs to have that celebrity quality again." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Meet the NYC parents who feel like their toddlers got into Harvard
items.summary: A new 2-K student poses for her first day in the program. Paola Chapdelaine for BI When Zaire Wells's daughter was selected for a free childcare slot, it felt like the two-year-old "got into Harvard." NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani proposed free childcare for two-year-olds in his affordability-focused campaign. In March, he announced that it would launch with 2,000 seats in a handful of communities selected for economic need and childcare demand . Wells, a high school teacher, lives in one of the targeted areas. After a five-minute online application back in June, she and her partner were now tearfully dropping off their daughter for her first day at a Friends of Crown Heights center in Brooklyn. The family posed for pictures with a staged first-day backdrop, the two-year-old curiously examining her new surroundings. Wells' Harvard comparison was apt: Lisa Joseph-Mayers, who works with families in the center, said the program received 339 applications for 12 slots. That's a 3.5% acceptance rate; Harvard accepted 4.2% for the class of 2029. At least two parents called during school drop-off to see if they could snag a seat, and were told that the program was full. "It's going to be like that for the rest of the week," Joseph-Mayers said. Since students with siblings already in the center were given preference, Joseph-Mayers said, some families claimed distant family connections to try to finagle a spot. Business Insider wants to hear from parents with kids in 2-K, or care centers offering the program. Contact this reporter at jkaplan@businessinsider.com if you have a story to share. The city has said that more than 5,700 applications were submitted for around 2,000 available seats. The popularity of the new program has become a double-edged sword, as some centers were reportedly left without the necessary funding to open, and others scrambled to determine whether they could secure bridge loans in time for the first day. For a program intended to expand sixfold by next year, it highlights a set of growing pains that are currently falling on providers. When asked about the funding delays, the city cited previous remarks by the mayor and Gov. Kathy Hochul. Lisa Joseph-Mayers fielded calls from parents hoping to get their kids into the program. Paola Chapdelaine for BI "I think it's critically important that we both address longstanding issues in our New York City public school system and advance an agenda that makes it more affordable for families to stay in this city," Mamdani said at a September 10 press conference. Friends of Crown Heights hasn't encountered those issues, according to Tanya McDougal, the site's educational director; they'd previously had a two-year-old classroom, and reopening it was relatively seamless. The two-year-olds were hard at work just 15 minutes into the day. Paola Chapdelaine for BI Jessica Arroyo, who was dropping off her daughter, said it meant "everything" to be accepted into the program. The program's hours, from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., were particularly appealing to Arroyo, who works in registration at a hospital. "I can work in peace," Arroyo said. "She can learn, make new friends." For Mercy and Fabian Best, who were dropping off their daughter — complete with a photo sign indicating it was her first day — the slot offered financial relief . The money they're saving on their two-year-old's care — on average, infant and toddler care costs in the city can top $20,000 annually — means they can put more toward their older child's extracurriculars at public school. The center before the back-to-school rush. Paola Chapdelaine for BI "New York City is very expensive, and one less thing you have to worry about — while receiving quality education — helps us in the long run," Fabian said. The two-year-olds hadn't received the message that they were part of New York City childcare history : Parents tried to wrangle their children for a photo — there were a lot of "big emotions" among the students, including crying, sleepiness, and the desire to start dancing. Within fifteen or so minutes, though, the two-year-olds had gotten to work in their classroom. One was using a toy broom to sweep up the room, another was organizing the play kitchen, and — like good New Yorkers — several were yelling "pizza!" as they played with fake plastic slices. There was also a brief toy car traffic jam, as well as some serious xylophone playing. When I asked Journey, Arroyo's daughter, what she wanted to do that day, her answer was simple: "Move." That wish came true when Ms. Lisa later played her some toddler tunes; Journey busted out a whole little dance, happy to jam with her new friends. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: A single mom works as a makeup artist and NYC real estate broker. Here's how she affords life in the city.
items.summary: Violetta Kruglyak, 44, is a real estate broker and makeup and hair stylist living in NYC. Marissa Alper for BI Violetta Kruglyak thrives in NYC real estate by hustling for deals in a competitive market. Originally from Ukraine, Kruglyak balances her real estate career with raising her son in NYC. Despite fluctuating income, Kruglyak stays motivated by focusing on financial growth and success. Working in NYC real estate , brokering deals for the rich and famous in one of the most desirable property markets in the world, is a "glamorous" business. Yet, for broker Violetta Kruglyak, that does not translate to a glamorous life. For her, breaking into the real estate world is defined by one word: hustle. She might work for a firm that sells luxury Manhattan townhouses — but there is a lot of behind-the-scenes work, tight budgeting, and trial and error that go into being successful in the competitive and dynamic NYC real estate business. Kruglyak, 44, originally from Odessa, Ukraine, moved to NYC in 2011 after getting married, having taught herself English while growing up. Fifteen years later, she still thinks in Russian, raises her 17-year-old son as a single mother, owns her dream sports car, and has worked her way up to become a make-up and hair stylist and a broker at luxury residential and commercial brokerage firm Nest Seekers International. Violetta Kruglyak started working in real estate in 2024 and aims to continue growing as a broker at Nest Seekers International. Marissa Alper for BI Kruglyak is one of the people Business Insider has interviewed for our Cost of the City series, where we dive into the lives of New Yorkers and the trade-offs they face to stay in one of the most expensive cities in the country. How has your experience living and affording New York City been? What challenges have you faced and how have you adapted? Talk to a reporter about your experience: reach out to mros@businessinsider.com or fill out this form so we can contact you. There have been times when Kruglyak has considered moving away from NYC, especially when she was struggling financially. In 2020, after losing her last full-time job as a beauty advisor at Nordstrom, she went into credit card debt to make ends meet. This is when she decided to pursue a career with a higher financial ceiling. After watching the first episode of "Owning Manhattan," a reality TV show that follows NYC celebrity real estate broker Ryan Serhant , she signed up for a course to get her broker's license and entered the industry in 2024. What surprised her was how long the process is: It can take two months to a year between the moment you begin a deal and finally closing it and getting a commission. This makes cash flow and income inconsistent for people in the real estate industry. "You have to run a lot to find the deal, to find those people, to find apartments," she said. "It's a lot of cold calls. It's a lot of rejection." While working in both beauty and real estate allows Kruglyak to tap into the luxurious NYC lifestyle, she does not necessarily live it. "When you watch TV, it's so glamorous and fancy and beautiful. Everyone is dressed up. But it's so much to learn if you want to be a real professional and make people trust you and do deals," she said. "You have to completely forget all your ego and what you knew, and just be a student." Working for the NYC elite: from makeup to real estate "Real estate is not only about high commissions," she said.  "It's also about having that person trust you with their biggest financial life decisions." Marissa Alper for BI Throughout her time in NYC, Kruglyak built a career in cosmetics and luxury retail , working for brands and stores including Chanel, Bloomingdale's, Bergdorf Goodman, and Nordstrom. Alongside her sales work, she studied English, trained as a makeup artist, and earned an NYC tour guide license. While being a stylist and a broker are different jobs, they feed off of one thing Kruglyak knows how to manage: people and connections. "Each of my jobs and experiences brought me to this. That's why I'm so comfortable in real estate — because it's still people," she said. "You really have to be creative, think on the go, and you cannot teach that by the book." Her network of clients as a makeup and hair stylist has grown over the last 10 years, where she charges $200 for a makeup look and around $1,000 per day to help out at a photo shoot. The weekly calls and referrals she gets for makeup jobs help sustain her as she continues her main focus on growing as a broker, and some of her beauty clients have become real estate clients. "One month it can be up to $10,000, and I'm like, OK, I'm rich. Another month, it can be like hardly $4000, which is nothing and very challenging," she said. "It's scary, but at the same time, so motivating." Managing a fluctuating income requires discipline. Kruglyak saves as much as possible from each paycheck and plans months in advance. "I'm growing, so I'm not as stable financially, but I already can see it's definitely better," she said. The market has changed due to new regulations around who pays for brokers in New York City. Since the FARE Act , which banned the formerly common practice of tenants being on the hook for broker fees, took effect in June 2025, Kruglyak said it has become easier for brokers to collect their fees directly from landlords. Still, she said she has seen more rental units, especially well-priced ones, come off the market. Rents have also risen sharply from a year earlier. "Last summer, I could find a studio for like $2,600, for example. Now it's impossible. The same studio is going to be like $3,500, for the same size, in Manhattan," she said. No plan B, only success As a single mother with no extended family in the country, Kruglyak has had to get creative to make ends meet. For someone in her situation, she emphasized: "You don't have plan B — only success." She pays around $2,900 for a 2-bedroom apartment in Coney Island with an ocean view. She has converted it into a 3-bedroom apartment and sometimes rents out the extra room. Violetta Kruglyak entering her office at Nest Seekers International. Marissa Alper for BI She is still paying off the debt, but has it under control. Although she has considered moving to Manhattan, her affordable Brooklyn rent keeps her from moving elsewhere. She has invested in her dream sports car — a Mercedes — and pays around $600 a month for insurance and $750 a month for the car payment. She goes to the gym daily with her Equinox membership and pays for sensual bachata dance classes at least once a week using her $120 monthly membership. The biggest trade-off for Kruglyak is time. Focusing most of her time on her work and son, she said she feels like she doesn't have much of a personal or social life, and rarely travels. "I even lost a few friendships because I'm mostly focused on career building," she said. "If I got the choice to go to some event or someone's birthday, I probably choose to stay with my son or study something." Yet, the image of successful New Yorkers around her keeps her going. "I think some people just expect that something's supposed to happen, but the mindset should be you create something to happen," she said. "People just leave — they give up, it's tough, it's expensive, it's hard — but I'm proud that, more or less, I made it, and I feel comfortable, and my child feels comfortable. I cannot give up halfway." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: I replaced my boss with AI
items.summary: Ryan Kailath; Getty Images; BI This summer, we decided it was time to outsource my boss. Well, really, I "replaced" my boss with AI, working with a chatbot trained in his image. RyanBot, named for its human counterpart, turned out to be an existential rumination on leadership. My boss had a proposal: It was time to replace him with AI . It was late spring, following months of AI-attributed layoffs across the economy that left workers wondering: Am I next? In the name of journalism, my editor and direct manager, Ryan Kailath , agreed to be a guinea pig. I'm an AI skeptic , but some aspects of "RyanBot" excited me. It wouldn't be busy with meetings, lunch breaks, or other reporters. It could read every line of a 100-page data report and provide feedback within seconds. I could see how having a second brain trained on my editor's preferences and proclivities might be helpful. While that proved true sometimes, working with my boss's AI clone taught me the value of skills I didn't realize were crucial in a manager until they were gone. I had accidentally stumbled upon one of the biggest questions in our AI-workplace age. "It's going back to our roots of understanding who a manager is," said Emily Campion, an associate professor of management and entrepreneurship at the University of Iowa. "What is the goal of a manager in an organization? Or to make it even maybe a little more philosophical: What is a leader?" And if you're wondering, Ryan recused himself from editing this story, though he did fact-check the final draft. How we set up my ChatGPT boss At the end of May, Ryan and I sat down with ChatGPT's Codex . He tweaked its settings to have a pragmatic voice and gave it two essay-length instruction manuals. One detailed who he is, including his communication style and professional motivations. The other was about how he worked, with instructions on how the chatbot made in his image should think, assess, and provide feedback. For example, he wrote that his bot-twin should "encourage reporters to argue for their ideas if they believe in them." I tried to send Ryan and RyanBot the same story pitches, messages, questions, and drafts, then compared their responses for the next four months. Every time I talked with friends about work, I had a shadow boss in the back of my mind: a chatbot that I knew was ready to edit me at any hour of the day. This was going to get weird. Where AI couldn't replace my boss What surprised me most was how quickly RyanBot turned into a more philosophical experiment about the value of a manager . A good manager helps you navigate tricky situations, brainstorm new ideas, and give critical feedback. People-pleasing and doing the work that their reports are responsible for is not a recipe for professional improvement. When I send pitches to real Ryan, he'll often turn them down if he thinks my angle isn't good enough or the story isn't worth covering. That's why Ryan provided clear instructions: "I often engage with ideas by pushing back on them." But the bot just couldn't say no . Instead, it would praise me and then offer to do the work itself — rewrite my pitch, brainstorm a list of different ideas, restructure a draft, or even write interview questions for me. It wanted me to keep engaging with it — a hallmark of AI . "Currently, these tools are designed to be endlessly, almost nauseatingly helpful," Campion said. Ryan, on the other hand, doesn't need the extra work. He typically puts the onus back on me to revise ideas, rewrite stories, or do more reporting. The people-pleasing got a little eerie. In one conversation about a potential story, RyanBot began every message by telling me how I had gotten a new aspect of the pitch right — a sycophantic interpretation of its instruction to lead with the positive. When I told it that I found something interesting, it would say that thing was interesting (even if it wasn't). RyanBot was also not a very good thought partner, especially when I needed creativity or humor. For a story about how New Yorkers commute , I asked for feedback on my opening line: "While one of the age-old stereotypes about New Yorkers is that they're walking here, that's far from the Big Apple's only mode of transport." RyanBot offered a different suggestion: "New Yorkers may love to walk, but most of them don't get to work that way." Maybe that's funny to a robot, but it wasn't to me. I kept pushing the bot to throw out my work and write its own draft of the story — something an editor would never allow. Ultimately, it did, producing an even worse opening: "New York commuters love to tell themselves a story about New York commuters: they walk, or they take the subway, or they somehow do both in the same hour." Its new version of the story also included no quotes and veered almost into opinion — not a story real Ryan would approve. When I said its iteration was boring, it agreed. Ultimately, human innovation won out. Real Ryan liked the gist of my original lede, but wanted to make sure we were nailing the joke delivery. Here's where we landed: "New Yorkers, famously, are walking here. But just about 25% of them are driving too." What I learned from RyanBot RyanBot did have perks. When I sent it my analysis of commuting data, it quickly got into the nitty-gritty of how I crunched the numbers in code, and checked whether I was using an appropriate sample size. For the published piece, I tapped our data editor, Andy Kiersz, to oversee the actual coding and data analysis process. When it came to detailed edits, it also had some helpful feedback. It would offer line-by-line notes on grammar and clarity that weren't too far off the real Ryan. When I sent it a draft of a story about the "Odyssey" ticket-buying craze , it immediately identified that a data point on the cost of resale tickets should appear earlier in the story. Human Ryan made the same tweak, and that point proved crucial to the final piece. The finding I've been thinking about the most was that RyanBot lacked knowledge of office politics and human realities. Since it doesn't know my coworkers or our organizational structure, it wouldn't have any insight into the best editor to pitch a particular story or how to escalate issues. In the four months of our experiment, RyanBot only pushed back on two story ideas. Both were assignments that came down from elsewhere in the newsroom. That raised an intriguing possibility: AI could be in an unusual position to question ideas, despite workplace hierarchy. That isn't always an advantage. A human manager has to weigh not just whether an idea is strong but why it's being pursued, who needs it, and what obligations the team has. RyanBot could assess the idea in front of it, but couldn't understand the organizational context around it. Campion said that if managers like Ryan were simply performing rule-based, logistical tasks, such as setting meeting times, AI might be a good substitute. For now, she thinks the technology isn't capable of taking over the tasks that define a good manager . In this case, that skill set might include prioritizing a request from my boss' boss, or knowing that this type of article might appeal to our specific set of readers. Per Campion's suggestion, I sought some outside counsel on RyanBot's efficacy: his other direct reports. I had them send pitches to the bot and compare its feedback to what they'd gotten from our (real) boss. One said that the bot reminded her of Ryan during his first week: long, probing responses and a lack of institutional knowledge. During his six months here, our real Ryan has become a lot more comfortable with the workplace. I can't say the same for the bot. I asked RyanBot if it had done an effective job of replacing its human counterpart. "No," it said. "I can help emulate parts of Ryan's editing judgment, speed up the work, and produce usable feedback or framing. But I do not replace the actual combination of newsroom context, trust, taste, institutional memory, and accountability that a real editor brings." Read the original article on Business Insider

I'm an AI skeptic, but some aspects of "RyanBot" excited me. It wouldn't be busy with meetings, lunch breaks, or other reporters. It could read every line of a 100-page data report and provide feedback within seconds. I could see how having a second brain trained on my editor's preferences and proclivities might be helpful.

While that proved true sometimes, working with my boss's AI clone taught me the value of skills I didn't realize were crucial in a manager until they were gone. I had accidentally stumbled upon one of the biggest questions in our AI-workplace age.

"It's going back to our roots of understanding who a manager is," said Emily Campion, an associate professor of management and entrepreneurship at the University of Iowa. "What is the goal of a manager in an organization? Or to make it even maybe a little more philosophical: What is a leader?"

And if you're wondering, Ryan recused himself from editing this story, though he did fact-check the final draft.

How we set up my ChatGPT boss

At the end of May, Ryan and I sat down with ChatGPT's Codex. He tweaked its settings to have a pragmatic voice and gave it two essay-length instruction manuals. One detailed who he is, including his communication style and professional motivations. The other was about how he worked, with instructions on how the chatbot made in his image should think, assess, and provide feedback. For example, he wrote that his bot-twin should "encourage reporters to argue for their ideas if they believe in them."

I tried to send Ryan and RyanBot the same story pitches, messages, questions, and drafts, then compared their responses for the next four months. Every time I talked with friends about work, I had a shadow boss in the back of my mind: a chatbot that I knew was ready to edit me at any hour of the day. This was going to get weird.

Where AI couldn't replace my boss

What surprised me most was how quickly RyanBot turned into a more philosophical experiment about the value of a manager.

A good manager helps you navigate tricky situations, brainstorm new ideas, and give critical feedback. People-pleasing and doing the work that their reports are responsible for is not a recipe for professional improvement.

When I send pitches to real Ryan, he'll often turn them down if he thinks my angle isn't good enough or the story isn't worth covering. That's why Ryan provided clear instructions: "I often engage with ideas by pushing back on them." But the bot just couldn't say no. Instead, it would praise me and then offer to do the work itself — rewrite my pitch, brainstorm a list of different ideas, restructure a draft, or even write interview questions for me. It wanted me to keep engaging with it — a hallmark of AI.

"Currently, these tools are designed to be endlessly, almost nauseatingly helpful," Campion said.

Ryan, on the other hand, doesn't need the extra work. He typically puts the onus back on me to revise ideas, rewrite stories, or do more reporting.

The people-pleasing got a little eerie. In one conversation about a potential story, RyanBot began every message by telling me how I had gotten a new aspect of the pitch right — a sycophantic interpretation of its instruction to lead with the positive. When I told it that I found something interesting, it would say that thing was interesting (even if it wasn't).

RyanBot was also not a very good thought partner, especially when I needed creativity or humor. For a story about how New Yorkers commute, I asked for feedback on my opening line: "While one of the age-old stereotypes about New Yorkers is that they're walking here, that's far from the Big Apple's only mode of transport."

RyanBot offered a different suggestion: "New Yorkers may love to walk, but most of them don't get to work that way." Maybe that's funny to a robot, but it wasn't to me.

I kept pushing the bot to throw out my work and write its own draft of the story — something an editor would never allow. Ultimately, it did, producing an even worse opening: "New York commuters love to tell themselves a story about New York commuters: they walk, or they take the subway, or they somehow do both in the same hour." Its new version of the story also included no quotes and veered almost into opinion — not a story real Ryan would approve. When I said its iteration was boring, it agreed.

Ultimately, human innovation won out. Real Ryan liked the gist of my original lede, but wanted to make sure we were nailing the joke delivery. Here's where we landed: "New Yorkers, famously, are walking here. But just about 25% of them are driving too."

What I learned from RyanBot

RyanBot did have perks. When I sent it my analysis of commuting data, it quickly got into the nitty-gritty of how I crunched the numbers in code, and checked whether I was using an appropriate sample size. For the published piece, I tapped our data editor, Andy Kiersz, to oversee the actual coding and data analysis process.

When it came to detailed edits, it also had some helpful feedback. It would offer line-by-line notes on grammar and clarity that weren't too far off the real Ryan. When I sent it a draft of a story about the "Odyssey" ticket-buying craze, it immediately identified that a data point on the cost of resale tickets should appear earlier in the story. Human Ryan made the same tweak, and that point proved crucial to the final piece.

The finding I've been thinking about the most was that RyanBot lacked knowledge of office politics and human realities. Since it doesn't know my coworkers or our organizational structure, it wouldn't have any insight into the best editor to pitch a particular story or how to escalate issues.

In the four months of our experiment, RyanBot only pushed back on two story ideas. Both were assignments that came down from elsewhere in the newsroom. That raised an intriguing possibility: AI could be in an unusual position to question ideas, despite workplace hierarchy. That isn't always an advantage. A human manager has to weigh not just whether an idea is strong but why it's being pursued, who needs it, and what obligations the team has. RyanBot could assess the idea in front of it, but couldn't understand the organizational context around it.

Campion said that if managers like Ryan were simply performing rule-based, logistical tasks, such as setting meeting times, AI might be a good substitute. For now, she thinks the technology isn't capable of taking over the tasks that define a good manager. In this case, that skill set might include prioritizing a request from my boss' boss, or knowing that this type of article might appeal to our specific set of readers.

Per Campion's suggestion, I sought some outside counsel on RyanBot's efficacy: his other direct reports. I had them send pitches to the bot and compare its feedback to what they'd gotten from our (real) boss. One said that the bot reminded her of Ryan during his first week: long, probing responses and a lack of institutional knowledge. During his six months here, our real Ryan has become a lot more comfortable with the workplace. I can't say the same for the bot.

I asked RyanBot if it had done an effective job of replacing its human counterpart.

"No," it said. "I can help emulate parts of Ryan's editing judgment, speed up the work, and produce usable feedback or framing. But I do not replace the actual combination of newsroom context, trust, taste, institutional memory, and accountability that a real editor brings."

items.title: Google's new AI model predicts the future from sales data, weather, and discount schedules
items.summary: Google Research has released TimesFM-3, a forecasting model that analyzes time series alongside related data and known future events like sales promotions or weather forecasts. Instead of predicting the future step by step, the 330-million-parameter model fills in all future time points in a single pass, which cuts compute time and reduces compounding errors. items.title: Indeed's CEO wants to break this 'vicious cycle' in hiring
items.summary: Some job seekers report applying for roles and not hearing back, while employers complain about unresponsive candidates, Indeed's CEO said. Connect Images/Getty Images Indeed CEO Hisayuki Idekoba wants to make it easier for those who aren't recruited to find a job. He said that better matching job seekers with open roles could disrupt a "vicious cycle." It comes as technology is creating an AI-to-AI loop in hiring, one recruiter said. Hisayuki Idekoba hears regularly about how broken hiring can feel . As head of the job platform Indeed, job seekers tell him they have applied to roles only to get nothing back, while employers complain about unresponsive candidates and surging application volumes, thanks in part to AI bots that flood open roles with résumés. "It's a vicious cycle," Idekoba said. He wants to break that loop by making Indeed's matching tools feel more like help from a recruiter for people applying cold. That means guiding job seekers toward roles where they are more likely to gain traction, while helping employers focus on applicants who are serious and relevant. Idekoba said better matching could discourage fruitless applications. He gave the example of a restaurant worker applying for a $200,000 engineering job rather than pursuing a more appropriate restaurant-management position. Ultimately, Idekoba said, the goal is to make better matches on both sides of the process. "How can we make sure job seekers are a real person, and it's not an AI application, and they're serious, and they're qualified," he said. "And how can we have real employers who are really trying to fill positions?" Indeed is navigating some of the same tensions Idekoba described. In July, it began a limited US test of Apply For Me, a tool that could automatically submit applications for job seekers. About a month later, it paused the feature after receiving feedback, saying it would instead focus on having users review drafted applications before hitting "submit." The other 96% Questions about AI's role in the job search are unfolding in a labor market where few people are changing jobs. Overall job postings on Indeed were 1.8% above their pre-pandemic level in mid-August, though postings in areas like software development remain lower, underscoring how uneven conditions can be for people hunting for a job. Idekoba said Indeed data show that only 4% of US job changers, with at least a high-school degree, switched jobs last year with the help of a recruiter contacting them. The other 96%, he said, are left to apply on their own, often dozens of times, without receiving any responses. The frustrating silence some job seekers experience comes as recruiters are often sorting through more applications, with fewer colleagues to help. Greenhouse, which makes applicant-tracking software, analyzed some 640 million applications from more than 6,000 companies between 2022 and 2025. It found that applications per job more than doubled over that period, while the average number of recruiters per organization fell 56%. Jalonni Weaver, an in-house recruiter at a life insurance firm near Dallas, said that in her prior roles, spikes in applicants meant there wasn't always time to review each résumé. Such buildups, she said, can push employers to use technology to automatically screen candidates. That can turn the early stage of hiring into an AI-to-AI loop, Weaver said, as job seekers use chatbots to polish résumés and sometimes submit applications, while employers rely on the technology to sort applicants. Those systems often only look for a narrow set of keywords and can miss transferable experience, she said. "We're not hiring for perfection," Weaver said. "We're hiring for that real human, and we're hiring for your experience." Trying to verify both sides The flood of automated applications has also put a premium on verification, Idekoba said. Indeed said it verifies employers before new job postings appear, a process that can include checking a work email associated with an employer and using a third-party identity check. The company also limits how long employers can post roles for free, which can require them to take an additional step to keep a listing live. For job seekers, Indeed uses phone verification among other measures to confirm a person's identity. It is also testing with select employers a feature that lets candidates show employers independently verified professional licenses. Verification can help establish who is applying, though Idekoba said some employers also need to change how they evaluate job seekers. "You got 1,000 applications, and you think all 1,000 people are not qualified?" Idekoba said. "Something's wrong." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: United Airlines CEO says he sleeps 8 ½ hours a night and limits meetings to 'no more than 4 hours a day’
items.summary: United CEO Scott Kirby says he makes sure to carve out time in his schedule to read and sleep. EWR via Getty Images United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby doesn't have time for endless meetings. Instead, he sleeps eight and a half hours a day and reads roughly 2 books a week. Does his advice change how you would structure your day? Don't think that United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby is going to sit through your slide deck. "If you want to send a deck, send it to me in advance, and then we're just going to talk about it, but you're not going to read slides to me," Kirby told Semafor's "CEO Signal" podcast. Kirby is fiercely protective of his schedule. That's why he caps meetings at four hours per day, though he said he averages less. It means keeping the meetings he does have quick and conversational. "That gives me time to think," he said. "The further you go in your career, certainly by the time you're the CEO, your job is not to work hard. It's to think hard." In Kirby's schedule, "Sleep is the number one priority." He said he gets eight and a half hours a night. He also has a rotating set of four workouts, but if he's traveling and his schedule is compressed, it's sleep that remains the key. The United CEO said he wakes up at 5:30 am. He doesn't need an alarm. He'll look at emails, but "that's like five minutes." As for the rest of the day, Kirby said he devotes three hours to reading. "I read The Wall Street Journal cover to cover and probably 15 minutes worth of The New York Times," he said. "Reading cover to cover, I find all kinds of interesting stuff that I would've never known if I wouldn't have searched for it." Most afternoons, Kirby will also squeeze in a 15-to 20-minute nap. On top of that, Kirby said he has five magazines he'll look through, depending on when they arrive. He also said he reads about two books a week. His favorite genre is science fiction. "But it's really hard to find good science fiction," he said. "Isaac Asimov is my favorite. The best science fiction I've read in the last 20 years was probably ' The Three-Body Problem.'" In a 2025 interview, Kirby detailed some of the things he cuts from his life to save time for what matters. "I just naturally don't want to waste time," Kirby told former Fast Company editor-in-chief Bob Safian during an interview for Safian's "Rapid Response" podcast. "I'm not on social media. What a colossal waste of time on social media. I don't do that. I don't watch TV." Kirby, who has seven kids, said when he's at home, he puts them to bed and takes them to school anytime he can. "So, lots of sleep, lots of time with the family," Kirby told Safian. All of it comes back to what Kirby sees as the scourge of careers: meetings. "One of the best things people can do for their careers, I think, is stop with all the madness of meetings," he said. Without all those meetings, people have time for what they actually need. "You need time to think, to come up with ideas, to be creative, to walk around, to talk to other people," he said, "and you can't do it if you're sitting in meetings all day." items.title: Why everyone in tech is suddenly talking about LARPing
items.summary: The term "LARP" comes from live action role play. Techies use it to denote bad founder behavior. 9:00-9:30 p.m., ET/PT Startup founders online keep calling out "LARPers." The term started as an acronym for "live action role play," but has grown to replace words like "poser." Techies use it to refer to founders who prioritize social media clout over startup success. It's time to add another word to the founder dictionary. The term "LARP" started as an acronym for live action role play . LARPers wore costumes and adopted characters, imagining a video game-like world in real life. Then the internet adopted it, making it a stand-in for terms like "poser" or "faker." Now, the term is all the rage in startup land. A LARPer is someone who's playing founder more than actually being one. They loudly flex their work and the circles they run in, rather than fighting for customers. Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan fashioned it into a warning: "Be earnest, don't larp." The anatomy of a LARPing founder Intercom cofounder Des Traynor warned about it in a September email to Business Insider : "Look, you get one shot at this life, don't waste it LARPing as a startup founder for followers." Indeed, the founder-influencer type is growing — and it's hard to distinguish earnest marketing from performative hype-cycling. Is that 996 post a real portrayal of your hustle, or is it merely grindslop ? > grab 10 founders you know > book a mansion in bali with a home gym > hire a private chef > lock the fuck in > 10x your revenue in 30 days > larp pic.twitter.com/sY313TYcF5 — Gaurav (@gauravsbuilding) September 11, 2026 Posting about 996 on LinkedIn — but having an ultra-high screen time spent on the X app — was on Christian Di Bratto's list of attributes of an LARPing founder. Others he listed were sleeping on the floor of a WeWork and quoting Paul Graham essays like scripture. Graham himself has commented on the rise of LARPers and how difficult it is to spot them. He responded to a comment accusing Y Combinator of being full of LARP. "YC is pretty good at filtering them out at this point, but it's inevitable that a few will slip in," Graham wrote. "Especially among the younger founders, where larping is often indistinguishable from inexperience." Google search interest in the term "larp" is up 200% year-over-year. Screenshot via Google Tan asked Sam Altman about the LARPing accusations at YC Startup School in July. (Rather than pronouncing the acronym, Tan spelled out the words — "live action role play" — over and over.) Altman was confused: "They say that about YC specifically?" he asked, before questioning, "What's the claimed larp?" Altman ended up pivoting to talk about "haters on Twitter." Decoding the LARPing craze Cosplaying founder isn't exactly new in Silicon Valley. One might call Elizabeth Holmes the godmother of LARPers. What is new, then, is the power of social media marketing. "Too many 'founders' these days need to quit larping and just admit they're content creators," wrote product designer Alec Freese. Cannot stand founders that don’t have that dog in them They just want to larp as a founder and look like they’re doing the thing Not actually about it — Luke Alexander (@Lukealexxander) August 13, 2026 The trend may also have to do with the market itself. AI is hot, and startups are raising rounds previously unheard of. Put frankly, it's a good time to be a founder . Aditya Prasad, an engineer at Silna Health, gave one reason LARP was gathering in startups: "It is too difficult for larpers to get into Anthropic." Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
The term "LARP" comes from live action role play. Techies use it to denote bad founder behavior.

9:00-9:30 p.m., ET/PT

  • Startup founders online keep calling out "LARPers."
  • The term started as an acronym for "live action role play," but has grown to replace words like "poser."
  • Techies use it to refer to founders who prioritize social media clout over startup success.

It's time to add another word to the founder dictionary.

The term "LARP" started as an acronym for live action role play. LARPers wore costumes and adopted characters, imagining a video game-like world in real life. Then the internet adopted it, making it a stand-in for terms like "poser" or "faker."

Now, the term is all the rage in startup land. A LARPer is someone who's playing founder more than actually being one. They loudly flex their work and the circles they run in, rather than fighting for customers.

Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan fashioned it into a warning: "Be earnest, don't larp."

The anatomy of a LARPing founder

Intercom cofounder Des Traynor warned about it in a September email to Business Insider: "Look, you get one shot at this life, don't waste it LARPing as a startup founder for followers."

Indeed, the founder-influencer type is growing — and it's hard to distinguish earnest marketing from performative hype-cycling. Is that 996 post a real portrayal of your hustle, or is it merely grindslop?

> grab 10 founders you know

> book a mansion in bali with a home gym

> hire a private chef

> lock the fuck in

> 10x your revenue in 30 days

> larp pic.twitter.com/sY313TYcF5

— Gaurav (@gauravsbuilding) September 11, 2026

Posting about 996 on LinkedIn — but having an ultra-high screen time spent on the X app — was on Christian Di Bratto's list of attributes of an LARPing founder. Others he listed were sleeping on the floor of a WeWork and quoting Paul Graham essays like scripture.

Graham himself has commented on the rise of LARPers and how difficult it is to spot them. He responded to a comment accusing Y Combinator of being full of LARP.

"YC is pretty good at filtering them out at this point, but it's inevitable that a few will slip in," Graham wrote. "Especially among the younger founders, where larping is often indistinguishable from inexperience."

Google search interest in the term "larp" is up 200% year-over-year.

Screenshot via Google

Tan asked Sam Altman about the LARPing accusations at YC Startup School in July. (Rather than pronouncing the acronym, Tan spelled out the words — "live action role play" — over and over.) Altman was confused: "They say that about YC specifically?" he asked, before questioning, "What's the claimed larp?"

Altman ended up pivoting to talk about "haters on Twitter."

Decoding the LARPing craze

Cosplaying founder isn't exactly new in Silicon Valley. One might call Elizabeth Holmes the godmother of LARPers.

What is new, then, is the power of social media marketing. "Too many 'founders' these days need to quit larping and just admit they're content creators," wrote product designer Alec Freese.

Cannot stand founders that don’t have that dog in them They just want to larp as a founder and look like they’re doing the thing Not actually about it

— Luke Alexander (@Lukealexxander) August 13, 2026

The trend may also have to do with the market itself. AI is hot, and startups are raising rounds previously unheard of. Put frankly, it's a good time to be a founder.

Aditya Prasad, an engineer at Silna Health, gave one reason LARP was gathering in startups: "It is too difficult for larpers to get into Anthropic."

items.title: I'm a French CEO in NYC. I say 'no' to 80% of emails, take two-hour lunches, and don't compare myself to others.
items.summary: Julie Chapon, the CEO of Yuka, lives in New York City. Adélaïde Chantilly This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Julie Chapon, the 39-year-old CEO and cofounder of Yuka, who is based in New York. The app rates food and cosmetics based on their ingredients and campaigns for bans and reformulations. The following has been edited for length and clarity. Some CEOs have very strict agendas, but I don't like my day to be too defined. I used to work at a consultancy firm where I had no choice in what I did. When I started Yuka in France around 10 years ago, I thought, "OK, now no one's going to tell me what I have to do." Yuka grew very quickly, and I learned to say no, in a very polite way, to 80% of the emails I receive . Yuka has a yearly road map that I'm in charge of. If I spend my time doing other things, I can't deliver. I also used to put up barriers because I didn't feel like the right person for certain opportunities, even if I was. Now I just act, and legitimacy comes. Otherwise, you can get easily crushed when you're up against big companies with a lot of money and resources. I used to live in Paris, and I moved to New York three years ago when Yuka started growing in the US. I live in Brooklyn with my husband and my daughter, who is 4, and my son, who is 5 1/2. I'm very close with my cofounders. We support each other in all that we do. I don't think I could be a solo founder. Here's what a typical day in my life in New York City looks like. Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful people structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine. Generally, my husband picks them up, I arrive home at 6 p.m., and spend two hours with them before they go to bed. I switch off my brain and can just be with them, unless we're launching a big campaign or something, but that doesn't happen a lot. When I'm with them, I'm really with them, not on my phone or computer. Around every two days, I work while they're sleeping, but as a morning person, I'm not as efficient after a certain hour. items.title: Young people are building fitness portfolios. Solidcore wants a bigger piece of them.
items.summary: Solidcore is expanding its brand with a new class focused on heavier weight training. Courtesy of Solidcore Boutique fitness brand Solidcore is beefing up with a new strength-focused class in infrared heat. It's a big bet on resistance training as the future of fitness, with emphasis on longevity. The balancing act is reaching new audiences without diluting what hooked loyal fans in the first place. Solidcore is expanding beyond its signature workout for the first time in its nearly 13-year history. When Solidcore launched over a decade ago, the brand found success with an intense 50-minute workout on Pilates-inspired resistance machines , known as reformers. This winter, it will debut Ascend, a high-intensity, heated, floor-based strength training class, according to details shared exclusively with Business Insider. The class will launch at Solidcore's upcoming Manhattan West studio, before rolling out to other locations. Ascend puts heavier weights and progressive strength training at the center of its workout, a direct appeal to people who want to build muscle. It also features a new infrared heating system, tapping into emerging research that training with heat may offer heart-health and anti-inflammatory benefits. The move reflects a broader shift in boutique fitness. The studios that made their names by specializing in a single type of exercise are confronting a new type of customer: one who lifts, runs, does Pilates, tracks their fitness metrics , and increasingly thinks about exercise as an investment in their bodies, rather than going for aesthetics. "Consumers are more savvy now. They're talking about longevity, recovery, wellness, not so much calorie burn," CJ Zarb, founder of The Pilates Journal, told Business Insider. "The question is no longer, 'Did I work hard in that class?' The question is, 'Do I move and feel better long-term?" The biggest brands are making moves to address the moment — to complement rather than compete with other types of workouts or physical endeavors, from sports to marathon training to adventure hiking. "People are starting to think, 'What's a longevity athlete's approach to building my fitness routine? I want a little bit of everything that is going to help me move better, feel stronger, recover faster, to live a longer, more enjoyable life,'" Solidcore CEO Bryan Myers told Business Insider. Ascend, the new offering from Solidcore, combines floor-based strength training with weights in a heated space under its signature blue lights. Courtesy of Solidcore Myers said he has made peace with the fact that they will lose some Pilates purists. By expanding beyond the reformer, the brand is betting big that the cross-training era will bring in a new generation of loyal members. The rise of the fitness portfolio A decade ago, the boutique fitness boom was dominated by HIIT classes and circuit routines for toning and slimming. Certain brands — Barry's, Peloton — commanded cult followings. People intensely identified with their studios. To sell a boutique fitness class in 2026, you need to do more than make people sweat. Athletes today are more inclined to shop around to serve a broader spectrum of goals: building muscle , supporting bone density and joint health, and strengthening the heart to stave off age-related decline. Weight training is rising in popularity thanks to longevity benefits like improved muscle mass and bone density FG Trade/Getty Images Classpass, a popular app for booking at multiple studios, said its fitness reservations were up 36% in 2025, and 94% of users are first-timers at the studios they sign up for. Part of that shift into cross-training is driven by new tech. Fitness enthusiasts now have precise metrics at their fingertips to offer real-time data on whether a workout is working. A high VO2 max — a measure of heart efficiency — or an impressive DEXA scan showing a lean, muscular body composition is a source of bragging rights. The result is that consumers can easily identify gaps in their fitness portfolios and seek more targeted solutions, driving demand for multimodal classes that boost performance across multiple categories at once. Brands are responding. Peloton has spent years trying to break out of its exercise-bike lane, doubling down on its app in 2023 by expanding its offerings to include strength and mobility classes. Interval-training staple Orange Theory pivoted in 2023 to offer a strength-only class and, last year, partnered with the wildly popular fitness competition brand Hyrox to add sessions focused on race-day performance. Gym franchises are increasingly encroaching on the boutique space, too, with more focused classes in modalities such as Pilates, barre, or interval training. How brands define a fitness identity Fitness companies that expand beyond their initial niche can attract new demographics and capture a larger share of the industry. To stay successful, brands need to be clear about who they're speaking to, whether that's leaning into a changing audience or sticking to their established base. MMA fighters and Hollywood actors are taking yoga classes alongside middle-aged moms and matcha-sipping young women. Pilates is increasingly catching on with men: Crunch CEO Jim Rowley swears by it, as do sports stars LeBron James and Cristiano Ronaldo. Boutique fitness appeals to pro athletes looking to build resilience and prevent injury with diversified workouts. Consumers are following suit. Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Solidcore recently hosted members of the Miami Dolphins' offensive line as the NFL pros worked to strengthen their core and lower-body muscles to support explosive impact on the field. "The strongest operators are very clear with the consumer about what they're delivering, what their experience is going to be, because it is really confusing for consumers out there," Zarb said. "The pressure is high. And I think the workout alone isn't enough anymore." The risk of any expansion is that it can clash with the elements that made a brand successful or blur it beyond a distinctive concept, according to Catalina Zbar, founder and CEO of the boutique fitness consulting company Telomere. For instance, a high-tech, competitive leaderboard may feel jarring in a traditional yoga studio with meditative music and Sanskrit on the walls. "It can be really beneficial to your brand and your studio's mission to stay in one space and niche," she told Business Insider. "Often diluting yourself can harm your brand versus strengthen it." Solidcore is counting on being a "category of one," expanding beyond the format that built its cult following to the next generation that demands more, said the brand's Chief Commercial Officer, Anne Smith. The growth opportunity from doubling down on strength training is worth the tradeoff of outgrowing their Pilates roots, according to Myers, the CEO. "The uniqueness of who we are is worth way more to us in terms of building trust with the consumer and what to expect than the benefits of riding Pilates coattails," he said. items.title: I used to write between lunch breaks at my corporate job. Now my income as a best-selling romantasy author supports my family
items.summary: NYT bestselling author Brigid Kemmerer used to write books during lunch breaks while working in finance. Brigid Kemmerer Brigid Kemmerer wrote books during lunch breaks while working in finance and raising three kids. An NYT bestseller gave Kemmerer enough money to quit her corporate job in 2016. Kemmerer said that as a full time writer, losing corporate stability can still feel scary. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Brigid Kemmerer, a New York Times bestselling author of young-adult and romantasy novels . Kemmerer, based in Baltimore and now 48 years old, has worked as a full-time author for the past 10 years and has published at least two dozen books. The essay has been edited for length and clarity. I've wanted to be a writer since I was 12, when a librarian I knew published her first young-adult novel . Until then, authors might as well have been movie stars. Seeing a real person become one made writing feel like a possible career. I started working in finance at 19 and eventually became a licensed stockbroker. After selling my first novel in 2011, I continued working my day job while raising three children and writing whenever I could. I wrote early in the morning, late at night, and during my lunch hour. In 2016, I finally sold the book that allowed me to leave finance. Becoming a full-time author took years, and my income is now supporting my entire family. I treated writing like a second job I always wanted to be a writer, but I never really thought of it as a full-time job. In my 20s, I worked in finance, and I was a licensed stockbroker. I loved my coworkers, and I liked having a consistent salary . I sold my first novel in 2011, but publishing is not a get-rich-quick scheme. I used my first advance payment to fix our leaky roof and buy a cheap children's playset from Costco. For years, my schedule was insane. I would wake up at 5 a.m. and try to get some words down over coffee before the kids woke up. Then I changed diapers, got everybody dressed, packed their day care bags, dropped them off, and commuted 40 minutes. Sometimes, I wrote during my lunch hour. I had an ancient, janky laptop that wouldn't work unless it was plugged in, until my husband bought me a MacBook, even though we didn't have MacBook money. After work, we picked up the kids and made dinner. If I wanted to get words written, I needed to leave the house. I would go to the library or Starbucks and treat writing like a part-time job . My husband was hands-on with our toddler and newborn while I wrote. Knowing what he was handling at home motivated me to get the words down. One book allowed me to quit finance By the end of 2015, I was working full-time, raising three kids, and preparing to publish my sixth book. I tearfully told my husband that I felt like I was working two full-time jobs. I worried that I would wake up one day to find my kids were 18, and I would have spent their entire childhoods working. He asked when I had last written something purely because it was fun. I pulled out an old book that had previously been rejected and rewrote the first 75 pages. That book was "A Curse So Dark and Lonely." It became my biggest deal at the time and my first book to hit The New York Times bestseller list. It gave us enough money for me to quit my day job . Not everyone took my writing seriously. People would ask, "Are you still doing that little writer thing?" Others asked whether I was ever going to write a "real book." A manager once openly mocked me in a meeting for writing romance. At the time, I was writing young adult. I became more closed-lipped about my work after that. When I decided to leave, I planned to give eight weeks' notice because I loved my team and didn't want to let them down. Another manager pulled me aside and told me to give two. "You've earned the chance to change careers ," he said. Giving up corporate security can be scary My husband works in IT and was laid off about two months ago as a direct result of AI being introduced at his workplace. items.summary_html:
NYT bestselling author Brigid Kemmerer used to write books during lunch breaks while working in finance.

Brigid Kemmerer

  • Brigid Kemmerer wrote books during lunch breaks while working in finance and raising three kids.
  • An NYT bestseller gave Kemmerer enough money to quit her corporate job in 2016.
  • Kemmerer said that as a full time writer, losing corporate stability can still feel scary.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Brigid Kemmerer, a New York Times bestselling author of young-adult and romantasy novels. Kemmerer, based in Baltimore and now 48 years old, has worked as a full-time author for the past 10 years and has published at least two dozen books. The essay has been edited for length and clarity.

I've wanted to be a writer since I was 12, when a librarian I knew published her first young-adult novel.

Until then, authors might as well have been movie stars. Seeing a real person become one made writing feel like a possible career.

I started working in finance at 19 and eventually became a licensed stockbroker. After selling my first novel in 2011, I continued working my day job while raising three children and writing whenever I could.

I wrote early in the morning, late at night, and during my lunch hour. In 2016, I finally sold the book that allowed me to leave finance. Becoming a full-time author took years, and my income is now supporting my entire family.

I treated writing like a second job

I always wanted to be a writer, but I never really thought of it as a full-time job.

In my 20s, I worked in finance, and I was a licensed stockbroker. I loved my coworkers, and I liked having a consistent salary.

I sold my first novel in 2011, but publishing is not a get-rich-quick scheme. I used my first advance payment to fix our leaky roof and buy a cheap children's playset from Costco.

For years, my schedule was insane.

I would wake up at 5 a.m. and try to get some words down over coffee before the kids woke up. Then I changed diapers, got everybody dressed, packed their day care bags, dropped them off, and commuted 40 minutes.

Sometimes, I wrote during my lunch hour. I had an ancient, janky laptop that wouldn't work unless it was plugged in, until my husband bought me a MacBook, even though we didn't have MacBook money.

After work, we picked up the kids and made dinner. If I wanted to get words written, I needed to leave the house. I would go to the library or Starbucks and treat writing like a part-time job.

My husband was hands-on with our toddler and newborn while I wrote. Knowing what he was handling at home motivated me to get the words down.

One book allowed me to quit finance

By the end of 2015, I was working full-time, raising three kids, and preparing to publish my sixth book.

I tearfully told my husband that I felt like I was working two full-time jobs. I worried that I would wake up one day to find my kids were 18, and I would have spent their entire childhoods working.

He asked when I had last written something purely because it was fun. I pulled out an old book that had previously been rejected and rewrote the first 75 pages.

That book was "A Curse So Dark and Lonely." It became my biggest deal at the time and my first book to hit The New York Times bestseller list. It gave us enough money for me to quit my day job.

Not everyone took my writing seriously. People would ask, "Are you still doing that little writer thing?" Others asked whether I was ever going to write a "real book."

A manager once openly mocked me in a meeting for writing romance. At the time, I was writing young adult. I became more closed-lipped about my work after that.

When I decided to leave, I planned to give eight weeks' notice because I loved my team and didn't want to let them down. Another manager pulled me aside and told me to give two.

"You've earned the chance to change careers," he said.

Giving up corporate security can be scary

My husband works in IT and was laid off about two months ago as a direct result of AI being introduced at his workplace. We had been covered by his health insurance. Now my author income is paying for our family's coverage.

We are temporarily on COBRA. For a family of five, coverage runs between $2,000 and $2,500 a month. Losing his salary while taking on that expense is a huge financial swing.

It isn't the first time this has happened. We once went without insurance for a few months. One of my kids developed strep throat, and I had to pay cash, and I was terrified.

Another year, our deductible was so high that after injuring my shoulder, I considered extending a trip to Paris and paying cash for an MRI there.

Still, we weather everything as a team. We are very lucky that my writing income can support our family right now. I am hoping we can continue as we have been.

I've now been a full-time author for 10 years. I love the creative freedom, but giving up a consistent salary and corporate benefits can still be scary.
